claims.statement: Nukekubi names a rokurokubi whose head detaches completely.
claims.statement_id: Nukekubi adalah rokurokubi yang kepalanya dapat terlepas.
claims.quote: her head can go flying off, either at the end of a greatly extended snakelike neck or completely detached from her body (in which case she may be called a nukekubi

claims.statement: Its separated head can fly away from the body.
claims.statement_id: Kepala itu dapat terbang meninggalkan tubuhnya.
claims.quote: her head can go flying off, either at the end of a greatly extended snakelike neck or completely detached from her body

claims.statement: Stories and pictures of rokurokubi became popular in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Kisah dan gambar rokurokubi populer pada zaman Edo.
claims.quote: Tales about rokurokubi and depictions in art first became especially popular in the Edo period (1603–1868)

claims.statement: Lafcadio Hearn included a related story in Kwaidan.
claims.statement_id: Lafcadio Hearn memuat kisah serupa dalam Kwaidan.
claims.quote: In Kwaidan , the classic collection of weird tales by Lafcadio Hearn , there is a story called “Rokuro-kubi” in which a priest stays with a family of what turn out to be these creatures.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, nukekubi are a variant type of rokurokubi, similar in most respects except that the head detaches completely from the body instead of the neck elongating.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nukekubi adalah jenis varian rokurokubi yang serupa dalam banyak hal, kecuali bahwa kepalanya terlepas sepenuhnya dari tubuh, bukan lehernya yang memanjang.
claims.quote: Nukekubi are a variant type of rokurokubi. They are similar in most respects, except that a nukekubi's head detaches itself completely from its body rather than elongating like a rokurokubi's neck.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, nukekubi thirst for blood and are more violent than rokurokubi; their flying head sucks the blood of victims like a vampire.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nukekubi haus darah dan lebih ganas daripada rokurokubi; kepalanya yang terbang mengisap darah korban seperti vampir.
claims.quote: Nukekubi possess a thirst for blood, and are more violent than rokurokubi. Their flying head sucks the blood of victims like a vampire.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Edo-period scientists believed nukekubi suffered from an affliction similar to sleepwalking, except that the patient's entire soul and head leave the body.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, para ilmuwan zaman Edo mengira nukekubi menderita penyakit mirip berjalan dalam tidur, hanya saja seluruh jiwa dan kepala penderita meninggalkan tubuh.
claims.quote: Edo period scientists believed that nukekubi suffered from an infliction similar to somnambulism; only instead of walking about at night the patient's entire soul and head depart from the body.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, in lore from Hitachi a man married to a nukekubi heard from a peddler that the liver of a white-haired dog could remove the curse.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, dalam cerita dari Hitachi, seorang lelaki yang beristri nukekubi mendengar dari pedagang keliling bahwa hati anjing berbulu putih dapat menghilangkan kutukan itu.
claims.quote: According to lore from Hitachi, a man married to a nukekubi heard from a peddler that the liver of a white-haired dog could remove the curse.

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, nukekubi are rokurokubi whose heads come off and float about.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, nukekubi adalah rokurokubi yang kepalanya lepas dan melayang-layang.
claims.quote: The nukekubi are rokurokubi whose heads come off and float about.

claims.statement: It is theorized that the nukekubi has a weakness while sleeping with its head floating: if the body is moved, the head cannot reunite with it.
claims.statement_id: Diteorikan bahwa nukekubi punya kelemahan saat tidur dan kepalanya melayang: jika tubuhnya dipindahkan, kepala tidak dapat menyatu kembali dengan tubuh.
claims.quote: It is theorized that the nukekubi has a weakness when it is sleeping and the head is floating around: if the body moves, then the head cannot be re-united to the body.

claims.statement: Sometimes the head separating from the body is seen as the soul wandering away from the body, i.e. somnambulism.
claims.statement_id: Terkadang lepasnya kepala dari tubuh dipandang sebagai jiwa yang mengembara keluar dari tubuh, yaitu berjalan dalam tidur.
claims.quote: Sometimes, the action of the head separating from the body is seen as the soul wandering away from the body, i.e. somnambulism.

claims.statement: Although rokurokubi and nukekubi are usually female, the Edo-period tale Shōsai Hikki has a male nukekubi.
claims.statement_id: Meskipun rokurokubi dan nukekubi biasanya perempuan, dalam kisah zaman Edo Shōsai Hikki ada nukekubi lelaki.
claims.quote: Although rokurokubi and nukekubi are usually female, in Shousai Hikki (蕉斎筆記), an Edo period tale, there is a nukekubi that is male.

claims.statement: In the Sorori Monogatari (1663), in the chapter on a woman's wild thoughts wandering, the head separating from the body is interpreted as the woman's soul wandering while asleep.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Sorori Monogatari (1663), bab tentang pikiran liar seorang perempuan yang mengembara, kepala yang terpisah dari tubuh ditafsirkan sebagai jiwa perempuan itu yang mengembara saat tidur.
claims.quote: in the Sorori Monogatari (曾呂利物語, 1663 CE), in the chapter A Woman's Wild Thoughts Wandering Around (女の妄念迷ひ歩く事, Onna no Mōnen Mayoiaruku Koto) the head separating from the body interpreted to be the woman's soul wandering while asleep.

claims.statement: The dictionary describes the rokurokubi as a Japanese yōkai phenomenon of a human neck stretching or the head separating from the body, recorded in many Edo-period works such as Sorori Monogatari and Kasshi Yawa; the type whose head separates is also called nukekubi.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menyebut rokurokubi sebagai yōkai Jepang berupa leher manusia yang memanjang atau kepala yang terpisah dari tubuh, dicatat dalam banyak pustaka zaman Edo seperti Sorori Monogatari dan Kasshi Yawa; yang kepalanya terpisah disebut juga nukekubi.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。人の首が長く伸びる、身体から首が分離するなどの怪異。江戸時代の「曾呂利物語」、「甲子夜話」など多くの文献に記述がある。首が身体と分離するものは「抜け首」ともいう。

claims.statement: According to Edo-period essays, all the people of a land called Hitōban are rokurokubi with a red mark on the neck; at night they fly off using their ears as wings to eat insects, and return at dawn.
claims.statement_id: Menurut esai-esai zaman Edo, semua orang di negeri bernama Hitōban adalah rokurokubi dengan bekas merah di leher; pada malam hari mereka terbang dengan telinga sebagai sayap untuk memakan serangga lalu kembali saat fajar.
claims.quote: 近世の随筆類によると、飛頭蛮(ひとうばん)という国の人はみなろくろ首で、首に赤い痕(あと)があり、夜は両耳を翼として飛んで行って虫を食い、明け方には帰ってきてもとのようになるという。

claims.statement: The encyclopedia author notes that the Chinese Soushenji (Liu Chao era tales) contains a story of the head of a general Wu's maidservant flying out every night, so tales of flying heads were probably imported from China.
claims.statement_id: Penulis ensiklopedia menyatakan bahwa Sōshinki, kumpulan kisah dari zaman Enam Dinasti Tiongkok, memuat cerita kepala pelayan perempuan seorang jenderal Wu yang terbang keluar setiap malam, sehingga kisah kepala terbang kemungkinan berasal dari Tiongkok.
claims.quote: 中国の六朝(りくちょう)時代の説話などを集めた『捜神記(そうじんき)』には、呉(ご)将軍の召使いだった下女の首が、夜ごとに飛び出した話があるから、首が飛行する話は中国伝来のものであろう。

claims.statement: Ōkubi is a giant-headed yōkai in Japanese tales.
claims.statement_id: Ōkubi adalah yōkai berkepala besar dalam cerita Jepang.
claims.quote: Ōkubi (大首) (おおくび) (the giant head) is a Japanese yōkai.

claims.statement: It is commonly pictured as a large female head with blackened teeth.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya sering berupa kepala perempuan besar bergigi hitam.
claims.quote: Its image is mostly a huge female head and has the characteristics of a married woman's teeth painted black.

claims.statement: Some accounts interpret it as a vengeful human spirit.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian kisah mengaitkannya dengan arwah manusia pendendam.
claims.quote: Their true identities are said to be human vengeful spirits and obsessions turned into yōkai.

claims.statement: A tale about the figure appears in an Edo-period collection of monster stories.
claims.statement_id: Sosok ini muncul dalam kumpulan cerita makhluk dari zaman Edo.
claims.quote: There is such a story in Tōtei Bukkairoku, a collection of monster stories in the mid-Edo period.

claims.statement: Some say Ōkubi is not a monster from Japanese folklore but was created to satirize monks who broke their precepts.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian orang berpendapat Ōkubi bukan monster dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, melainkan diciptakan untuk menyindir biksu yang melanggar sila.
claims.quote: Some say that Ōkubi is not a Japanese monster in folklore but was created to satirize monks who broke their precepts.

claims.statement: In the tale the protagonist opened his storage room one day and saw a huge old woman's face.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu, sang tokoh utama membuka ruang penyimpanannya suatu hari dan melihat wajah perempuan tua yang sangat besar.
claims.quote: When the protagonist opened his storage room one day, he saw a huge old woman's face.

claims.statement: The protagonist poked the giant face with tongs but Ōkubi did not respond, and when he touched it by hand it felt sticky.
claims.statement_id: Tokoh utama menusuk wajah raksasa itu dengan capit, tetapi Ōkubi tidak bereaksi; ketika disentuh dengan tangan, terasa lengket.
claims.quote: The protagonist poked the giant face with tongs, but Okubi didn't respond, and when he touched it with his hands, it felt sticky.

claims.statement: Ōkubi is said to be able to make people sick; the mid-Edo haiku poet Hori Bakusui wrote about Ōkubi in his works.
claims.statement_id: Ōkubi disebut dapat membuat orang sakit; penyair haiku zaman Edo pertengahan, Hori Bakusui, menulis tentang Ōkubi dalam karyanya.
claims.quote: Ōkubi has the ability to make people sick. The mid-Edo period haiku poet Hori Bakusui wrote about Ōkubi in his works.

claims.statement: In that account an Ōkubi blew on someone, and the part touched by its breath at once turned yellow and swollen; later a doctor prescribed a medicated bath to cure it.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu, Ōkubi menghembus seseorang sehingga bagian yang terkena napasnya langsung menguning dan bengkak; kemudian dokter meresepkan mandi obat untuk menyembuhkannya.
claims.quote: This Ōkubi blew on someone, and the part touched by the breath immediately turned yellow and swollen. Later, the doctor prescribed a medicated bath to cure it.

claims.statement: There is a story titled Ōkubi in the short story collection Hyakkiyakou-yō (百鬼夜行―陽) by Natsuhiko Kyogoku.
claims.statement_id: Ada cerita berjudul Ōkubi dalam kumpulan cerpen Hyakkiyakou-yō (百鬼夜行―陽) karya Natsuhiko Kyogoku.
claims.quote: There is a story titled Ōkubi in the short story collection Hyakkiyakou-yō (百鬼夜行―陽) by Natsuhiko Kyogoku.

claims.statement: The image of Ōkubi has also appeared in Japanese manga and anime, including as a villain monster in Shigeru Mizuki's GeGeGe no Kitaro.
claims.statement_id: Citra Ōkubi juga muncul dalam manga dan anime Jepang, termasuk sebagai monster penjahat dalam karya Shigeru Mizuki, GeGeGe no Kitaro.
claims.quote: The image of Okubi also appeared in Japanese manga and anime, and appeared as a villain monster in Shigeru Mizuki's work GeGeGe no Kitaro.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: the Edo-period Toriyama Sekien included a yōkai picture of this name in Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki; its caption has a giant severed female head with blackened teeth appearing in the rainy night sky, but this is pointed out as not a traditional yōkai and rather a creation satirizing precept-breaking monks of the time.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Toriyama Sekien dari zaman Edo memuat gambar yōkai bernama ini dalam Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki; keterangannya menyebut kepala perempuan raksasa bergigi hitam muncul di langit malam berhujan, tetapi hal ini dinilai bukan yōkai dari tradisi, melainkan ciptaan yang menyindir biksu pelanggar sila pada masa itu.
claims.quote: 江戸時代の鳥山石燕の妖怪画集『今昔画図続百鬼』にこの名の妖怪画があり、解説文によれば、お歯黒をつけた巨大な女の生首が雨の夜空に現れるものとされるが、これは伝承上にある妖怪ではなく、実際には当時の破戒僧を風刺した創作と指摘されている。

claims.statement: Old Edo-period kaidan and essays contain many cases of a giant female severed head appearing; almost all are female, typically with blackened teeth (ohaguro) as a mark of a married woman.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah ganjil dan esai kuno zaman Edo terdapat banyak contoh kepala perempuan raksasa yang muncul; hampir semuanya perempuan, dengan ciri gigi dihitamkan (ohaguro) sebagai tanda perempuan menikah.
claims.quote: 江戸時代の怪談や随筆などの古書には、巨大な女の生首が現れたという事例が多数あり、ほとんどは女性で、既婚女性の証としてお歯黒を付けていることが特徴である。

claims.statement: Their true identity is said to be a human vengeful spirit or obsession turned into a yōkai, or else a fox or tanuki in disguise.
claims.statement_id: Wujud aslinya disebut sebagai arwah pendendam atau kegigihan manusia yang menjelma menjadi yōkai, atau rubah dan tanuki yang menyamar.
claims.quote: それらの正体は、人間の怨霊や執念が妖怪と化したもの、あるいはキツネやタヌキが化けたものといわれている。

claims.statement: The Iwakuni (Yamaguchi) kaidan collection Ganson Kaidanroku, in an entry titled "Koshiro no bakemono no koto", says a woman met a female severed head one jō (about 3 meters) in size on a mountain called Oshiroyama, which smiled at her.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kumpulan kisah ganjil Iwakuni, Prefektur Yamaguchi, Ganson Kaidanroku, di bawah judul "Koshiro no bakemono no koto" seorang perempuan bertemu kepala perempuan setinggi satu jō (sekitar 3 meter) di gunung Oshiroyama yang tersenyum kepadanya.
claims.quote: 山口県岩国の怪談集『岩邑怪談録』には「古城の化物の事」と題し、ある女が御城山という山で一丈（約3メートル）の女の生首に遭い、にこにこと笑いかけられたとある。

claims.statement: It is recorded that already in the Heian period, before the Edo period, a giant female-head yōkai called 面女 (tsura-onna) appeared.
claims.statement_id: Disebutkan bahwa sejak zaman Heian, sebelum zaman Edo, telah muncul yōkai kepala perempuan raksasa bernama 面女 (tsura-onna).
claims.quote: 江戸時代よりさかのぼって平安時代にも、「面女（つらおんな）」と呼ばれる巨大な女の首の妖怪が出現したとある。

claims.statement: In the Bunka-era reading book Kinsei Kaidan Shimoyo no Hoshi, said to be the prototype of Yotsuya Kaidan, the vengeful spirit of a woman who took her life after being entrapped appears as a giant ōkubi in Kamakura.
claims.statement_id: Dalam buku bacaan zaman Bunka Kinsei Kaidan Shimoyo no Hoshi, yang disebut bentuk awal Yotsuya Kaidan, arwah pendendam perempuan yang mengakhiri hidup karena dijebak digambarkan muncul sebagai ōkubi raksasa di Kamakura.
claims.quote: 『四谷怪談』の祖形といわれる文化時代の読本『近世怪談霜夜星』では、策略に陥れられて命を絶った女性の怨霊が、鎌倉の地で巨大な大首となって現れた姿が描かれている。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Ōkubi appear as enormous severed heads that fly through the sky; in most accounts they look female, and quite commonly have blackened teeth.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Ōkubi tampak sebagai kepala terpenggal yang sangat besar dan terbang di langit; dalam kebanyakan kisah berwujud perempuan, dan cukup sering bergigi hitam.
claims.quote: Ōkubi appear as enormous, severed heads, which fly through the sky. In most accounts they are female in appearance. Quite commonly they have blackened teeth.

claims.statement: Their most common activity is to fly about harassing people: grinning at them, blowing away their umbrellas, or otherwise scaring them.
claims.statement_id: Kegiatan paling umum mereka adalah terbang mengganggu orang: menyeringai, meniup pergi payung, atau menakut-nakuti dengan cara lain.
claims.quote: Their most common activity is to fly about harassing people: grinning at them, blowing away their umbrellas, or otherwise scaring them.

claims.statement: On a night after rain, when the moon came out and thunder sounded, an Ōkubi about 2 meters high appeared on top of the wall.
claims.statement_id: Pada malam setelah hujan, saat bulan muncul dan terdengar guntur, seekor Ōkubi setinggi sekitar 2 meter muncul di atas tembok.
claims.quote: It was a night after the rain, when the moon came out, and with the sound of thunder, a Ōkubi about 2 meters high appeared on the top of the wall.

claims.statement: Like Ōkubi, Japanese folklore has some other yōkai whose heads are prominent features; the article points to Rokurokubi and Wanyūdō.
claims.statement_id: Seperti Ōkubi, cerita rakyat Jepang juga memiliki beberapa yōkai yang kepalanya menjadi ciri utama; artikel merujuk ke Rokurokubi dan Wanyūdō.
claims.quote: Like Ōkubi, Japanese folklore also has some yōkai whose heads are prominent features. See also Rokurokubi and Wanyūdō

claims.statement: Sabnock is one of the demons in demonology.
claims.statement_id: Sabnock adalah salah satu iblis dalam demonologi.
claims.quote: サブナック（Sabnac、Sabnachまたは、Sabnack）は悪魔学における悪魔の一人。

claims.statement: The Goetia calls him its forty-third spirit and a marquis.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menyebutnya roh ke-43 dan seorang markis.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の50の軍団を率いる序列43番の偉大にして強大なる侯爵。

claims.statement: He appears as a lion-headed soldier on a pale horse.
claims.statement_id: Ia tampil sebagai prajurit berkepala singa di atas kuda pucat.
claims.quote: Sabnock is depicted as a soldier with armor and weapons, the head of a lion, and riding a pale horse.

claims.statement: The text credits him with building towers, castles and cities.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu menyebut ia dapat membangun menara, kastel, dan kota.
claims.quote: He builds high towers, castles and cities, furnishing them with weapons, ammunition, etc., gives good familiars

claims.statement: In the Goetia text the forty-third spirit is called Sabnock or Savnok, a mighty marquis who appears as an armed soldier with a lion's head riding a pale-coloured horse.
claims.statement_id: Dalam teks Goetia, roh ke-43 disebut Sabnock atau Savnok, seorang markis yang perkasa, tampil sebagai prajurit bersenjata berkepala singa yang menunggang kuda berwarna pucat.
claims.quote: The Forty-third Spirit, as King Solomon commanded them into the Vessel of Brass, is called Sabnock, or Savnok. He is a Marquis, Mighty, Great and Strong, appearing in the Form of an Armed Soldier with a Lion's Head, riding on a pale-coloured horse.

claims.statement: His office is to build high towers, castles and cities and furnish them with armour; he can also afflict people for many days with wounds and sores that are rotten and full of worms.
claims.statement_id: Tugasnya membangun menara, kastel, dan kota yang tinggi serta melengkapinya dengan persenjataan; ia juga dapat menyiksa manusia selama berhari-hari dengan luka dan borok yang busuk dan penuh belatung.
claims.quote: His office is to build high Towers, Castles and Cities, and to furnish them with Armour, etc. Also he can afflict Men for many days with Wounds and with Sores rotten and full of Worms.

claims.statement: At the request of the Exorcist he gives good familiars, and he commands 50 legions of spirits.
claims.statement_id: Atas permintaan sang pemanggil (exorcist), ia memberikan familiar yang baik, dan ia memimpin 50 legiun roh.
claims.quote: He giveth Good Familiars at the request of the Exorcist. He commandeth 50 Legions of Spirits

claims.statement: Wikipedia lists other spellings of Sabnock (Sab Nac, Sabnac, Sabnach, Sabnack, Sabnacke, Salmac, Savnock) and calls him a mighty Great Marquis of Hell commanding 50 legions of demons.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat ejaan lain Sabnock: Sab Nac, Sabnac, Sabnach, Sabnack, Sabnacke, Salmac, dan Savnock; ia disebut Markis Agung Neraka yang memimpin 50 legiun iblis.
claims.quote: Sabnock (also Sab Nac, Sabnac, Sabnach, Sabnack, Sabnacke, Salmac, and Savnock) is a mighty Great Marquis of Hell, having 50 legions of demons under his command.

claims.statement: Shiryō are spirits of dead people in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Shiryō adalah arwah orang mati dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Shiryō (死霊) are the souls of the dead in Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: The contrasting term ikiryō refers to spirits of living people.
claims.statement_id: Istilah ikiryō sebaliknya menunjuk roh orang yang masih hidup.
claims.quote: This contrasts with ikiryō, which are souls of the living.

claims.statement: Classical writings describe different behaviors for shiryō.
claims.statement_id: Tulisan klasik menggambarkan beragam perilaku shiryō.
claims.quote: Classical literature and folklore material has left many mentions of shiryō, and they have various behaviors.

claims.statement: A story in Tōno Monogatari has a dead father return to his daughter.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Tōno Monogatari, arwah seorang ayah mendatangi putrinya.
claims.quote: In the Tōno Monogatari, there was a story in which a man died, and afterward, his shiryō appeared before his daughter and tried to take her away.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the word shiryō is almost exclusively used for unpleasant, malevolent spirits, unlike yūrei, which can at times be beautifully mysterious.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, istilah shiryō hampir selalu dipakai untuk roh yang tidak menyenangkan dan jahat, berbeda dengan yūrei yang kadang indah dan misterius.
claims.quote: while yūrei can be creepy sometimes and beautifully mysterious at other times, shiryō is almost exclusively used to refer to unpleasant, malevolent spirits.

claims.statement: Yokai.com says shiryō act like ikiryō, appearing to relatives or close friends of the deceased; ikiryō usually appear just before death, while a shiryō appears just after.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: shiryō bertindak mirip ikiryō dan menampakkan diri kepada kerabat atau sahabat dekat orang yang meninggal; ikiryō biasanya muncul sesaat sebelum kematian, sedangkan shiryō sesaat sesudahnya.
claims.quote: Shiryō act in similar ways to ikiryō, appearing to relatives or close friends of the deceased. While ikiryō usually appear in the moments just before death, a shiryō appears in the moments just after death.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, shiryō do not always appear to say goodbye; sometimes they come to take loved ones away with them into the world of the dead.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, shiryō tidak selalu datang untuk berpamitan; kadang mereka datang untuk membawa orang yang dikasihi ke dunia orang mati.
claims.quote: shiryō do not always appear in order to say goodbye; sometimes they come to take their loved ones away with them into the world of the dead.

claims.statement: Yokai.com states that belief in shiryō goes back to before recorded history and has long been a staple of Japanese folk superstition.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyatakan kepercayaan pada shiryō sudah ada sebelum zaman tercatat dan lama menjadi bagian takhayul rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Belief in shiryō goes back to before recorded history, and has long been a staple of Japanese folk superstition.

claims.statement: In a story as told by Yokai.com, after her father died his shiryō appeared before his daughter and tried to take her into the world of the dead; she narrowly escaped and fled to ask for help.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebuah kisah menurut Yokai.com, setelah ayahnya meninggal, shiryō sang ayah mendatangi putrinya dan berusaha membawanya ke dunia orang mati; sang gadis nyaris lolos dan lari meminta pertolongan.
claims.quote: After her father died, his shiryō appeared before the young girl and tried to take her with him into the world of the dead. The girl narrowly escaped and fled from the house to ask for help.

claims.statement: In that story the ghost stopped appearing only after a whole month of sleepless, terrifying nights.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu, hantu sang ayah baru berhenti muncul setelah sebulan penuh malam tanpa tidur yang menakutkan.
claims.quote: Only after a whole month of sleepless, terrifying nights did the ghost stop appearing, and finally the girl was left in peace.

claims.statement: Yokai.com gives 死霊 (しりょう) with the translation "dead ghost" and the alternate name shirei.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis 死霊 (しりょう) dengan terjemahan "hantu mati" dan nama lain shirei.
claims.quote: Shiryō 死霊 しりょう Translation: dead ghost Alternate names: shirei

claims.statement: Shuten-dōji is an oni leader killed by Minamoto no Raikō in Japanese legend.
claims.statement_id: Shuten-dōji adalah pemimpin oni yang dibunuh Minamoto no Raikō dalam legenda Jepang.
claims.quote: Shuten-dōji (酒呑童子, also sometimes called 酒顛童子, 酒天童子, or 朱点童子) is a mythical oni or demon leader of Japan, who according to legend was killed by the hero Minamoto no Raikō.

claims.statement: One story says his severed head still bit at Raikō.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kisah menyebut kepalanya yang terpenggal masih menggigit Raikō.
claims.quote: Although decapitated, the demon's detached head still took a bite at the hero, who avoided death by wearing multiple helmets stacked on his head.

claims.statement: Accounts place his dwelling on Mount Ōe or Mount Ibuki.
claims.statement_id: Berbagai versi menempatkan sarangnya di Gunung Ōe atau Gunung Ibuki.
claims.quote: Shuten-dōji had his lair at Mount Ōe (大江山) northwest of the city of Kyoto, or Mount Ibuki, depending on the version.

claims.statement: The fourteenth-century Ōeyama Ekotoba preserves an early form of the legend.
claims.statement_id: Naskah Ōeyama Ekotoba dari abad ke-14 menyimpan versi awal legenda itu.
claims.quote: The oldest surviving text of the legend is recorded in the 14th century Ōeyama Ekotoba (大江山絵詞 "Tale of Mount Ōe in Pictures and Words"), a picture scroll held by the Itsuō Art Museum.

claims.statement: The Digital Daijisen dictionary describes Shuten-dōji as a legendary leader of the oni said to live on Ōeyama in Tanba, who plundered women and treasure in the capital and was said to have been destroyed by Minamoto no Raikō leading his Four Guardian Kings under imperial command.
claims.statement_id: デジタル大辞泉は、酒呑童子を丹波の大江山に住んだという伝説上の鬼の頭目とし、都で婦女や財宝を奪ったため、勅命により源頼光が四天王を率いて退治したと記す。
claims.quote: 丹波の大江山に住んでいたという伝説上の鬼の頭目。都に出ては婦女・財宝を奪ったので、勅命により、源頼光が四天王を率いて退治したという。

claims.statement: According to the Heibonsha World Encyclopedia, in the Ōeyama Ekotoba the name Shuten-dōji comes from his being someone who deeply loves sake.
claims.statement_id: 世界大百科事典によれば、『大江山絵詞』では酒呑童子の名は「酒を深く愛する者」であることに由来する。
claims.quote: 酒呑童子の名称は,《大江山絵詞》では〈酒を深く愛する者〉ゆえの名となっている

claims.statement: The Heibonsha World Encyclopedia says Ōeyama was apparently originally Oi-no-saka near the capital, but is the Ōeyama of Senjōgatake in Tanba and Tango in the Ōeyama Ekotoba and Mount Ibuki in Ōmi in the Shuten-dōji Emaki.
claims.statement_id: 世界大百科事典は、大江山はもともと都の近くの老ノ坂だったらしいが、『大江山絵詞』では丹波・丹後の千丈ヶ嶽の大江山、『酒伝童子絵巻』では近江の伊吹山になっていると述べる。
claims.quote: 大江山は元来は都のあたりにほど近い老ノ坂であったらしいが,《大江山絵詞》では丹波・丹後の千丈ヶ嶽の大江山,《酒伝童子絵巻》では近江伊吹山となっている。

claims.statement: The Heibonsha encyclopedia author says the idea of an oni deity holed up on Ōeyama should be analysed against the background of Oi-no-saka being a boundary between the capital and the outside world, the stage of the Shikyō-sai rite that kept plague deities out, and a haunt of bandits.
claims.statement_id: 世界大百科事典の筆者は、大江山に鬼神がこもるという観念を、老ノ坂が都と外界を隔てる境界であったこと、疫神を防ぐ四境祭の舞台であったこと、盗賊の出没する場所であったことなどを背景に分析すべきだとする。
claims.quote: 大江山に鬼神がこもるとする観念は,老ノ坂が都(山城国)と外界を隔てる境界の性格をもった場所であったこと,疫神の侵入をさえぎり都の安寧と清浄を確保する四境祭の舞台であったこと,多くの盗賊・強盗が出没し,そのすみかとなったこと,などを背景として分析されるべきであろう。

claims.statement: In the Otogi-zōshi Shuten-dōji, Raikō strikes the sleeping Shuten-dōji, who has become an oni about two jō tall, with the three gods appearing to lend their strength; the severed head flies up into the sky and aims at Raikō, who is protected by his star helmet (星甲).
claims.statement_id: 御伽草子の『酒呑童子』では、頼光は二丈ほどの鬼となって伏す酒呑童子に斬りかかり、三神も現れて力を貸す。斬られた首は天に舞い上がって頼光を狙うが、頼光は星甲に守られる。
claims.quote: 御伽草子。江戸時代に〈御伽文庫〉として刊行された渋川版の一つ。 ... 頼光は2丈ばかりの鬼となって臥している酒呑童子に切りかかり,3神も現じて力を貸す。切られた童子の首は天に舞いあがり頼光をねらうが,頼光は星甲に守られる。

claims.statement: In the Otogi-zōshi plot, Raikō's party is hosted by three old men in whom the gods of three shrines have appeared and is given the Jinben kidoku sake and a hoshi kabuto helmet.
claims.statement_id: 御伽草子の筋では、頼光一行は三社の神が姿を現した三人の翁にもてなされ、神便鬼毒酒と星甲を授けられる。
claims.quote: 御伽草子。江戸時代に〈御伽文庫〉として刊行された渋川版の一つ。 ... 三社の神の現じた3人の翁からもてなされ,神便鬼毒(じんべんきどく)酒と星甲(ほしかぶと)とを授けられ

claims.statement: In the oldest version Raikō offers Shuten-dōji the sake given to him by one of the deities, which renders him incapacitated.
claims.statement_id: Dalam versi tertua, Raikō menawarkan sake pemberian salah satu dewa kepada Shuten-dōji, yang membuatnya tak berdaya.
claims.quote: Raikō then offered Shuten-dōji the sake given to him by one of the deities, which rendered him incapacitated.

claims.statement: In the oldest version, many people were reported missing in the capital city of Kyoto, most of the victims being young women.
claims.statement_id: Dalam versi tertua, banyak orang dilaporkan hilang di ibu kota Kyoto, kebanyakan korbannya perempuan muda.
claims.quote: a large number of missing people were being reported in the capital city of Kyoto, most of the victims being young women.

claims.statement: According to the Ōeyama Ekotoba version, Shuten-dōji returned to his true form when he slept: 50 feet tall, with a red body and a five-horned head with fifteen eyes.
claims.statement_id: Menurut versi Ōeyama Ekotoba, Shuten-dōji kembali ke wujud aslinya saat tidur: setinggi 50 kaki, bertubuh merah, berkepala bertanduk lima, dan bermata lima belas.
claims.quote: According to the Ōeyama Ekotoba version, Shuten-dōji returned to his true form when he slept. He was 50 feet in height, had a red body and a five-horned head, with fifteen eyes

claims.statement: Wikipedia summarises the oldest text version (Ōeyama Ekotoba or Ōeyama Emaki) as a story set in the reign of Emperor Ichijō (r. 986-1011).
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia meringkas versi teks tertua (Ōeyama Ekotoba atau Ōeyama Emaki) sebagai kisah pada masa pemerintahan Kaisar Ichijō (986–1011).
claims.quote: The oldest text (Ōeyama Ekotoba or Ōeyama Emaki) version the legend can be summarized as follows: During the reign of Emperor Ichijō (r. 986-1011)

claims.statement: Wanyūdō is a wheel-shaped yōkai portrayed in an illustrated collection by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Wanyūdō adalah yōkai berbentuk roda yang digambar Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Wanyūdō (Japanese: 輪入道, literally "wheel (輪) monk (入道)"), also known as "Firewheel" or "Soultaker", is a yōkai depicted in Toriyama Sekien's collection of yōkai illustrations, Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki.

claims.statement: The image gives the burning wheel a human face.
claims.statement_id: Gambar itu menampilkan wajah manusia pada roda yang menyala.
claims.quote: In Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki, Toriyama Sekien depicts Wanyūdō as a figure with a male face attached to the center of an ox cart wheel wrapped in flames.

claims.statement: Its explanatory text says witnesses may lose their souls.
claims.statement_id: Menurut keterangannya, orang yang melihatnya dapat kehilangan jiwa.
claims.quote: Those who see this lose their souls.

claims.statement: The same text recommends placing a written charm on a house door.
claims.statement_id: Teks yang sama menyarankan tulisan pelindung ditempel di pintu rumah.
claims.quote: If you write "This place is the village of Shōbo" on a piece of paper and stamp it on the door of your house, it will not dare to approach.

claims.statement: Various folklore also presents him as the condemned soul of a tyrannical daimyō who in life was known for having his victims drawn on the back of an ox cart.
claims.statement_id: Berbagai cerita rakyat juga menganggapnya jiwa terkutuk seorang daimyō lalim yang semasa hidup dikenal membuat korbannya diseret di belakang kereta sapi.
claims.quote: Various folklore also purports him as the condemned soul of a tyrannical daimyō who, in life, was known for having his victims drawn on the back of an ox cart.

claims.statement: He is said to guard the gates of Hell and wander along the road between this world and the underworld, scaring townsfolk and stealing the souls of anyone who gets too close in order to take them to Hell.
claims.statement_id: Ia dikatakan menjaga gerbang Neraka dan mondar-mandir di jalan antara dunia ini dan dunia bawah, menakuti penduduk dan mencuri jiwa siapa pun yang terlalu dekat untuk dibawa ke Neraka.
claims.quote: He is said to guard the gates of Hell, and to wander back and forth along the road between this world and the underworld, scaring townsfolk as he passes and stealing the souls of anyone who gets too close in order to bring them to Hell with him.

claims.statement: Sekien's Wanyūdō is considered to be based on the "Katawaguruma" (wheel) yōkai recorded in Shokoku Hyakumonogatari, published in 1677 (Enpō 5), because of its shape and content.
claims.statement_id: Wanyūdō karya Sekien dianggap digambar berdasarkan yōkai "Katawaguruma" (Roda) yang dicatat dalam Shokoku Hyakumonogatari yang terbit tahun 1677 (Enpō 5), karena bentuk dan isinya.
claims.quote: Sekien's Wanyūdō is considered to be drawn based on the "Katawaguruma" (Wheel) yōkai (Volume 1, "The Matter of the Katawaguruma of Higashinotoin, Kyoto") recorded in Shokoku Hyakumonogatari (One Hundred Tales from Various Provinces) published in 1677 (Enpō 5), due to its shape and content.

claims.statement: Wanyūdō is depicted as male and Katawaguruma as female, and so they are read today; but depicting Katawaguruma as female began with the Shokoku Rijindan, published in 1743 (Kanpō 3).
claims.statement_id: Wanyūdō digambarkan laki-laki dan Katawaguruma perempuan, dan begitulah keduanya ditafsirkan kini; namun penggambaran Katawaguruma sebagai perempuan dimulai dengan Shokoku Rijindan yang terbit tahun 1743 (Kanpō 3).
claims.quote: Wanyūdō is depicted as male and Katawaguruma as female, and they are interpreted as such today; however, the depiction of Katawaguruma as a female began with the Shokoku Rijindan (Tales of Country Folk from Various Provinces) published in 1743 (Kanpō 3).

claims.statement: One of the most famous legends comes from Kyoto: as Wanyūdō rolled through the town, a woman peeked out her window at him, and he told her to look at her own child instead of at him.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu legenda paling terkenal berasal dari Kyoto: ketika Wanyūdō bergulir melewati kota, seorang perempuan mengintipnya dari jendela, dan Wanyūdō berkata kepadanya agar melihat anaknya sendiri alih-alih melihat dirinya.
claims.quote: One of the most famous legends comes from Kyoto, Japan. As Wanyūdō rolled through the town, a woman peeked out her window at him. Wanyūdō told her "Instead of looking at me, have a look at your own child!"

claims.statement: She looked down to find her baby lying on the floor in a pool of blood with his legs missing; looking back at the demon, she saw the baby's legs in his mouth as he ate them.
claims.statement_id: Perempuan itu menunduk dan mendapati bayinya terbaring di lantai dalam genangan darah dengan kaki hilang; ketika menoleh kembali, ia melihat kaki bayinya di mulut sang iblis yang memakannya.
claims.quote: She looked down at her baby to find him lying on the floor in a pool of blood with his legs missing. When she looked back outside at the demon, she saw her baby's legs in his mouth as he ate them.

claims.statement: The phrase "This place is the village of Shōbo" derives from an anecdote in the "Biographies of Zou Yang" in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji).
claims.statement_id: Ungkapan "Tempat ini adalah desa Shōbo" berasal dari sebuah anekdot dalam "Biografi Zou Yang" di Catatan Sejarawan Agung (Shiji).
claims.quote: The phrase "This place is the village of Shōbo" is derived from an anecdote in the "Biographies of Zou Yang" from the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji).

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: 輪入道 (わにゅうどう) is a Japanese yōkai drawn in Toriyama Sekien's yōkai picture collection Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: 輪入道 (わにゅうどう) adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambar dalam kumpulan gambar yōkai Toriyama Sekien, Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki.
claims.quote: 輪入道（わにゅうどう）は、鳥山石燕の妖怪画集『今昔画図続百鬼』に描かれている日本の妖怪。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, wa nyūdō appear as giant, fearsome men's heads trapped within flaming ox-cart wheels, shaved like monks' in penance for sins in life.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, wa nyūdō tampak sebagai kepala pria raksasa yang menakutkan terperangkap dalam roda kereta sapi yang menyala; kepala mereka dicukur seperti biksu sebagai penebusan dosa semasa hidup.
claims.quote: Wa nyūdō appear as giant, fearsome men’s heads trapped within flaming ox-cart wheels. Their heads are shaved like monks’ in penance for sins during life.

claims.statement: Wa nyūdō are servants of hell but spend most of their time on earth patrolling for the wicked.
claims.statement_id: Wa nyūdō adalah pelayan neraka, tetapi sebagian besar waktunya di bumi dipakai berpatroli mencari orang jahat.
claims.quote: Wa nyūdō are servants of hell, but spend most of their time on earth patrolling for the wicked.

claims.statement: When a wa nyūdō is sighted, smart townspeople keep off the roads and away from all doors and windows to avoid its notice.
claims.statement_id: Ketika wa nyūdō terlihat, penduduk yang cerdik menjauhi jalan dan semua pintu serta jendela agar tidak diperhatikan iblis ini.
claims.quote: When a wa nyūdō is sighted, smart townspeople keep off the roads and stay away from all doors and windows to avoid any notice by this demon.

claims.statement: The extra-cautious decorate their homes with prayer charms hoping the monster will be repulsed; merely witnessing a wa nyūdō is enough to bring calamity upon a whole family.
claims.statement_id: Mereka yang ekstra hati-hati menghias rumah dengan jimat doa agar monster itu tertolak; sekadar melihat wa nyūdō sudah cukup mendatangkan malapetaka bagi seluruh keluarga.
claims.quote: The extra-cautious decorate their homes with prayer charms in hopes that the monster will be repulsed and stay away. Merely witnessing the wa nyūdō is enough to bring calamity upon a whole family.

claims.statement: Wikipedia lists Ōkami, an action-adventure game for PlayStation 2 (2006), among Wanyūdō's modern appearances.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencantumkan Ōkami, gim aksi-petualangan untuk PlayStation 2 (2006), di antara penampilan modern Wanyūdō.
claims.quote: Ōkami – action-adventure game for PlayStation 2 (2006)

claims.statement: Yamabiko is a mountain spirit linked with echoes in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Yamabiko adalah roh gunung yang dikaitkan dengan gema dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Yamabiko (山彦; also yamahiko) is a mountain god, spirit, and yōkai in Japanese folklore; the term "yamabiko" also refers to the echo that occurs in mountains, after which the yōkai is named.

claims.statement: Its name literally means mountain boy.
claims.statement_id: Namanya secara harfiah berarti anak gunung.
claims.quote: Literally translated, the term means "mountain boy".

claims.statement: Stories place it deep in mountain country.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menempatkannya jauh di pegunungan.
claims.quote: Living deep in the mountains, direct encounters with the yamabiko are rare.

claims.statement: People are said to hear it more often than they see it.
claims.statement_id: Orang konon lebih sering mendengar daripada melihatnya.
claims.quote: Often they are heard, but never seen.

claims.statement: The yamabiko is a small creature that resembles a cross between a dog and a monkey.
claims.statement_id: Yamabiko adalah makhluk kecil yang menyerupai persilangan antara anjing dan monyet.
claims.quote: The yamabiko is a small creature that resembles a cross between a dog and a monkey.

claims.statement: The term "yamabiko" is also used for the phenomenon of a delayed echo in mountains and valleys, thought to be the spirit answering.
claims.statement_id: Istilah yamabiko juga dipakai untuk gema tertunda di gunung dan lembah, yang dianggap sebagai jawaban sang roh.
claims.quote: The term "yamabiko" is also used to describe the phenomenon of a delayed echo in mountains and valleys, and is thought to be the spirit answering.

claims.statement: This anomaly is sometimes called "kodama" when it is thought to be the answering voice of a tree spirit.
claims.statement_id: Gejala gema ini kadang disebut "kodama" bila dianggap sebagai suara jawaban roh pohon.
claims.quote: This anomaly is also sometimes called "kodama", when it is thought to be the answering voice of a tree spirit

claims.statement: In Tottori, Tottori Prefecture, a yobuko ("calling child") or yobukodori ("small calling bird") living in the mountain is thought to give out the yamabiko's voice.
claims.statement_id: Di Tottori, Prefektur Tottori, yobuko ("anak pemanggil") atau yobukodori ("burung pemanggil kecil") yang hidup di gunung dianggap yang mengeluarkan suara yamabiko.
claims.quote: In Tottori, Tottori Prefecture, a yobuko (呼子 ; "calling child") or a yobukodori (呼子鳥 ; "small calling bird") that lives in the mountain is thought to give out the yamabiko's voice.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes a small rock mountain in Kitaazumi District, Nagano Prefecture called the "yamabiko rock" that returns people's words, and concludes that yamabiko as yōkai are not uniform in origin or in what kind of yōkai they are.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat sebuah gunung batu kecil di Distrik Kitaazumi, Prefektur Nagano, bernama "batu yamabiko" yang mengembalikan kata-kata orang, dan menyimpulkan bahwa yamabiko sebagai yōkai tidak seragam asal-usul maupun jenisnya.
claims.quote: there is also a small rock mountain in Kitaazumi District, Nagano Prefecture called the "yamabiko rock" (山彦岩 ) that return people's words, among other appearances of the word "yamabiko", and thus it can be seen that the yamabiko as yōkai are not uniform in either origin or what kind of yōkai they are.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, yamabiko are known almost exclusively by their voices and are skilled at mimicking any sound, including natural sounds, human language, and trains and cars.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, yamabiko hampir hanya dikenal lewat suaranya dan pandai menirukan bunyi apa pun, termasuk suara alam, bahasa manusia, serta kereta dan mobil.
claims.quote: Yamabiko are known almost exclusively by their voices. They are skilled at mimicking any sound, including natural sounds, human language, and trains and cars.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, yamabiko live deep in the mountains and make their homes in camphor trees.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, yamabiko hidup jauh di dalam pegunungan dan bersarang di pohon kamper.
claims.quote: They live deep in the mountains and make their homes in camphor trees

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the creature's form was only decided in the Edo period, when yōkai researchers such as Sawaki Sūshi and Toriyama Sekien began making illustrated yokai bestiaries.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, bentuk makhluk ini baru ditetapkan pada zaman Edo, ketika peneliti yōkai seperti Sawaki Sūshi dan Toriyama Sekien membuat bestiari bergambar.
claims.quote: It wasn't until the Edo period-when determined yōkai researchers like Sawaki Sūshi and Toriyama Sekien began making illustrated yokai bestiaries-that this creature's form was decided.

claims.statement: Amatsu-Mikaboshi is a star deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Amatsu-Mikaboshi adalah dewa bintang dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Amatsu-Mikaboshi (天津甕星), also called Ame-no-Kagaseo (天香香背男) or Hoshi-no-Kami Kagaseo (星神香香背男), is a god of stars who appears in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki mentions him, while the Kojiki does not.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut dalam Nihon Shoki, tetapi tidak dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: No reference to Mikaboshi is made in the Kojiki; however, he plays a minor role in the Nihon Shoki as a deity insubordinate to the amatsukami during the latter's subjugation of the land.

claims.statement: In the Nihon Shoki conquest account, Mikaboshi (called Kagaseo) is mentioned only in passing as a rebellious kunitsukami.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah penaklukan di Nihon Shoki, Mikaboshi (disebut Kagaseo) hanya disebut sekilas sebagai kunitsukami pemberontak.
claims.quote: Mikaboshi (referred to as Kagaseo) is mentioned in passing as a rebellious kunitsukami

claims.statement: Takehazuchi is sent to bring about his submission.
claims.statement_id: Dewa Penenun (Weaver-God) Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto dikirim sehingga Mikaboshi menyatakan tunduk.
claims.quote: Therefore they sent the Weaver-God Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto (倭文神建葉槌命, Shitorigami Take-ha-dzuchi-no-Mikoto) also, upon which he rendered submission.

claims.statement: The deity is called both Ama-tsu-mika-hoshi (天津甕星; "August Star of Heaven" or "Dread Star of Heaven") and Ama-no-kagase-o (天香香背男; "Brilliant Male of Heaven" or "Scarecrow Male of Heaven") in the Nihon Shoki.
claims.statement_id: Dewa ini disebut Ama-tsu-mika-hoshi (天津甕星; "Bintang Agung dari Surga" atau "Bintang Menakutkan dari Surga") dan Ama-no-kagase-o (天香香背男; "Lelaki Gemilang dari Surga" atau "Lelaki Orang-orangan Sawah dari Surga") dalam Nihon Shoki.
claims.quote: The deity is referred to as both Ama-tsu-mika-hoshi (天津甕星; "August Star of Heaven" or "Dread Star of Heaven") and Ama-no-kagase-o (天香香背男; "Brilliant Male of Heaven" or "Scarecrow Male of Heaven") in the Nihon Shoki.

claims.statement: The name Kagaseo is theorized to come from the word kagayaku (輝く; "to shine").
claims.statement_id: Nama Kagaseo diduga berasal dari kata kagayaku (輝く; "bersinar").
claims.quote: With the name Kagaseo theorized to come from the word kagayaku (輝く; "to shine").

claims.statement: The component mika (kanji 甕, "earthenware pot") of Mikaboshi is interpreted as derived from ika (厳, "imposing" or "austere"), which led the kokugaku scholar Hirata Atsutane to identify Amatsu-Mikaboshi with the planet Venus.
claims.statement_id: Unsur mika (ditulis dengan kanji 甕; "periuk tanah liat") pada Mikaboshi ditafsirkan berasal dari ika (厳; "agung" atau "keras"), yang mendorong sarjana kokugaku Hirata Atsutane mengidentifikasi Amatsu-Mikaboshi dengan planet Venus.
claims.quote: the component mika (written using the kanji 甕; "earthenware pot"), from Mikaboshi, is interpreted as being derived from ika (厳; "imposing" or "austere"), which prompted the kokugaku scholar Hirata Atsutane to identify Amatsu-Mikaboshi with the planet Venus.

claims.statement: A second account in the Nihon Shoki instead presents Mikaboshi as an amatsukami who is slain by Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi before their descent to earth.
claims.statement_id: Catatan kedua dalam Nihon Shoki justru menampilkan Mikaboshi sebagai amatsukami yang dibunuh oleh Takemikazuchi dan Futsunushi sebelum mereka turun ke bumi.
claims.quote: A second account provided in the Nihon Shoki instead presents Mikaboshi as an amatsukami, who is slain by Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi before their descent to earth

claims.statement: These are virtually the only passages in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki that deal with a star kami and, uniquely, present the deity as antagonistic toward the amatsukami.
claims.statement_id: Bagian-bagian ini hampir satu-satunya dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki yang membahas kami bintang, dan secara unik menampilkan dewa itu sebagai penentang para amatsukami.
claims.quote: These are virtually the only passages in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki that deal with a kami of stars, and, uniquely, present the deity as antagonistic towards the amatsukami.

claims.statement: The Ōmika Shrine in Hitachi (Ibaraki Prefecture) enshrines Mikaboshi-Kagaseo (甕星香々背男) as a jinushigami alongside Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto (武葉槌命); a "spirit-housing stone" (宿魂石) in its precincts is believed to contain Mikaboshi's ara-mitama.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Ōmika di Hitachi (Prefektur Ibaraki) memuliakan Mikaboshi-Kagaseo (甕星香々背男) sebagai jinushigami bersama Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto (武葉槌命); sebuah "batu penampung roh" (宿魂石) di pelataran kuil diyakini berisi ara-mitama Mikaboshi.
claims.quote: in Hitachi (Ibaraki Prefecture) enshrines Mikaboshi-Kagaseo (甕星香々背男) as a jinushigami alongside Takehazuchi-no-Mikoto (武葉槌命). Additionally, a "spirit-housing stone" (宿魂石, Shukukonseki) within the shrine's precincts is believed to contain Mikaboshi's ara-mitama.

claims.statement: Mikaboshi is also enshrined at various Hoshi-Jinja (星神社, "star shrine") and Hoshimiya-Jinja (星宮神社, "star palace shrine") throughout Japan.
claims.statement_id: Mikaboshi juga dimuliakan di berbagai Hoshi-Jinja (星神社; "kuil bintang") dan Hoshimiya-Jinja (星宮神社; "kuil istana bintang") di seluruh Jepang.
claims.quote: Mikaboshi is also enshrined at various Hoshi-Jinja ... (星神社; "star shrine") and Hoshimiya-Jinja ... (星宮神社; "star palace shrine") throughout Japan.

claims.statement: Amatsu-Mikaboshi, the Chaos King, is a fictional character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.
claims.statement_id: Amatsu-Mikaboshi, sang Raja Kekacauan, adalah tokoh fiksi dalam komik Amerika terbitan Marvel Comics.
claims.quote: Amatsu-Mikaboshi, the Chaos King,  is a fictional character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: 天津甕星 (Amatsu-Mikaboshi) is a star god in Japanese mythology, with the other names 天香香背男 (Ame-no-Kagaseo) and 香香背男 (Kagaseo).
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: 天津甕星 (Amatsu-Mikaboshi) adalah dewa bintang dalam mitologi Jepang, dengan nama lain 天香香背男 (Ame-no-Kagaseo) dan 香香背男 (Kagaseo).
claims.quote: 天津甕星（あまつみかぼし）は、日本神話に登場する星の神である。別名は天香香背男（あめのかがせお）、香香背男（かがせお）。

claims.statement: In Japanese mythology the star god is portrayed as a god to be subdued, a "disobedient god"; one theory holds this reflects a tribe that worshipped a star god and was slow to submit to the Yamato court.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Jepang, dewa bintang digambarkan sebagai dewa yang harus ditundukkan, yakni "dewa yang tak patuh"; ada teori bahwa ini mencerminkan adanya suku pemuja dewa bintang yang lama tidak tunduk kepada kekuasaan Yamato.
claims.quote: しかし、日本神話においては星神は服従させるべき神、すなわち「まつろわぬ神」として描かれている。これについては、星神を信仰していた部族があり、それが大和王権になかなか服従しなかったことを表しているとする説がある。

claims.statement: Because he resisted the pacification of the Central Land of Reed-Plains to the end, he is sometimes treated as the same god as Takeminakata, and in Shinto-Buddhist syncretism sometimes as an incarnation of Bodhisattva Myōken, the deified Pole Star.
claims.statement_id: Karena dikisahkan melawan penaklukan Ashihara no Nakatsukuni sampai akhir, ia kadang disamakan dengan Takeminakata, dan dalam gagasan sinkretisme Shinto-Buddha kadang dianggap penjelmaan Bodhisattwa Myōken, personifikasi Bintang Utara.
claims.quote: 葦原中国平定に最後まで抵抗した神ということで建御名方神と同一神とされることもあり、また、神仏習合の発想では北極星を神格化した妙見菩薩の化身とされることもある。

claims.statement: According to that shrine's tradition, Mikaboshi-Kagaseo (Amatsu-Mikaboshi) made his seat at Mount Ōmika in Hitachi Province and ruled the eastern lands.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi kuil itu, Mikaboshi-Kagaseo (Amatsu-Mikaboshi) bermarkas di Gunung Ōmika di Provinsi Hitachi dan menguasai Jepang timur.
claims.quote: 同神社伝では、甕星香々背男（天津甕星）は常陸国の大甕山に居を構えて東国を支配していたとしている。

claims.statement: Aston's note: this is the only Star-God mentioned in Japanese myth, and it may be noted that little honour is shown him.
claims.statement_id: Catatan penerjemah Aston: ini satu-satunya Dewa Bintang yang disebut dalam mitos Jepang, dan perlu dicatat bahwa kehormatan yang diberikan kepadanya sedikit.
claims.quote: This is the only Star-God mentioned in Japanese myth, and it may be noted that little honour is shown him.

claims.statement: Aston's note says he is described as a conquered rebel and has neither Kami nor Mikoto affixed to his name.
claims.statement_id: Menurut catatan Aston, ia digambarkan sebagai pemberontak yang ditaklukkan dan namanya tidak diberi imbuhan Kami maupun Mikoto.
claims.quote: He is described as a conquered rebel, and has neither Kami nor Mikoto affixed to his name.

claims.statement: In one Nihongi version two gods say that in Heaven there is an Evil Deity called Ama-tsu-mika-hoshi or Ame no Kagase-wo, and pray that he be executed before they go down to make clear the Central Land of Reed-Plains.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu catatan Nihongi, dua dewa berkata bahwa di Surga ada Dewa Jahat bernama Ama-tsu-mika-hoshi atau Ame no Kagase-wo, dan memohon agar ia dihukum mati sebelum mereka turun menjernihkan Negeri Dataran Alang-Alang Tengah.
claims.quote: In Heaven there is an Evil Deity called Ama-tsu-mika-hoshi, or Ame no Kagase-wo. We pray that this Deity may be executed before we go down to make clear the Central Land of Reed-Plains.

claims.statement: Aston's note: Kaga is obviously connected with kagayaku, to shine.
claims.statement_id: Catatan Aston: Kaga jelas berkaitan dengan kagayaku, "bersinar".
claims.quote: Kaga is obviously connected with kagayaku, to shine.

claims.statement: Ame no Wakahiko is a grain deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Ame no Wakahiko adalah dewa padi-padian dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Ame no Wakahiko (天稚彦 or 天若日子) is a god of grains and an Amatsukami in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: He is named as a son of Amatsukunitama.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut sebagai putra Amatsukunitama.
claims.quote: He is the son of Amatsukunitama.

claims.statement: Some versions send him to govern the earth after another envoy fails to report.
claims.statement_id: Dalam beberapa versi, ia diutus menguasai bumi setelah utusan lain tak memberi kabar.
claims.quote: In many versions, when Ame no Hohi did not send word for three years, all the gods gathered up, and Ame no Wakahiko was the one who was chosen to rule the earth.

claims.statement: Some versions say he fell in love with Shitateruhime.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa versi menyebut ia jatuh cinta kepada Shitateruhime.
claims.quote: In some versions, Ame no Wakahiko fell in love with Shitateruhime.

claims.statement: The name Ame no Wakahiko means "a young boy in heaven," and he is thought to be an exceptionally handsome youth.
claims.statement_id: Nama Ame no Wakahiko berarti "anak muda di surga", dan ia dianggap pemuda yang sangat tampan.
claims.quote: The name Ame no Wakahiko means "a young boy in heaven," and he is thought to be an exceptionally handsome youth.

claims.statement: In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and was sent to earth to look for him.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebagian versi, Ame no Wakahiko adalah putra Ame no Hohi dan dikirim ke bumi untuk mencarinya.
claims.quote: In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.

claims.statement: Eight years later, with no report, the gods sent a bird named Nakime to earth to check on him. On a wise woman's advice Ame no Wakahiko shot the bird with his bow; the bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven.
claims.statement_id: Delapan tahun kemudian, karena tak ada kabar, para dewa mengirim burung bernama Nakime ke bumi untuk menengoknya. Atas saran seorang perempuan bijak, Ame no Wakahiko memanah burung itu; burung itu mati, tetapi anak panahnya melesat hingga ke surga.
claims.quote: Eight years later, after receiving no report back, the gods sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird. The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven.

claims.statement: Takamimusubi saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth, where it hit Ame no Wakahiko as he lay in bed and killed him. Other versions say Amaterasu shot the arrow back at him.
claims.statement_id: Takamimusubi melihat anak panah itu dan melemparkannya kembali ke bumi hingga mengenai Ame no Wakahiko yang sedang berbaring di tempat tidur dan membunuhnya. Versi lain menyebut Amaterasu yang menembakkan panah itu kembali.
claims.quote: Takamimusubi saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was lying in bed, killing him. Other versions state that Amaterasu was the one who shot the arrow back at him.

claims.statement: This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow.
claims.statement_id: Mitos ini adalah asal ungkapan Jepang tentang anak panah yang kembali.
claims.quote: This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow.

claims.statement: It is likely also a mythicisation of attempts by the Yamato state to impose its authority over neighbouring states.
claims.statement_id: Mitos ini kemungkinan juga merupakan mitologisasi upaya negara Yamato menegakkan kekuasaannya atas negara-negara tetangga.
claims.quote: It is likely also a mythicisation of attempts made by the Yamato state to impose its authority over neighbouring states.

claims.statement: After Ame no Wakahiko's death his parents built a mourning hut (喪屋 moya) for him. Ajisukitakahikone went down to pay respects, but because he looked like Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken for Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life.
claims.statement_id: Setelah Ame no Wakahiko meninggal, orang tuanya membangun gubuk (喪屋 moya) untuknya. Ajisukitakahikone turun memberi penghormatan, tetapi karena mirip Ame no Wakahiko ia disangka Ame no Wakahiko yang dihidupkan kembali.
claims.quote: After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. Ajisukitakahikone went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life.

claims.statement: Ajisukitakahikone was offended, destroyed the hut and kicked it; the hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.
claims.statement_id: Ajisukitakahikone tersinggung, menghancurkan gubuk itu dan menendangnya; gubuk itu jatuh di tanah Mino dan menjadi gunung bernama Moyama.
claims.quote: Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.

claims.statement: Ame no Wakahiko is enshrined at Abiko Shrine in Aishō, Shiga, and Iwakura Shrine in Shinshiro, Aichi.
claims.statement_id: Ame no Wakahiko dimuliakan di Kuil Abiko di Aishō, Shiga, dan Kuil Iwakura di Shinshiro, Aichi.
claims.quote: Ame no Wakahiko is enshrined at Abiko Shrine in Aishō, Shiga and Iwakura Shrine in Shinshiro, Aichi.

claims.statement: Another story of Ame no Wakahiko appears in medieval Japanese literature of the Muromachi period (Otogi-zōshi), in a narrative very similar to tale type ATU 425, "The Search for the Lost Husband", or to the Graeco-Roman story of Cupid and Psyche by Apuleius.
claims.statement_id: Kisah lain tentang Ame no Wakahiko muncul dalam sastra Jepang abad pertengahan zaman Muromachi (Otogi-zōshi), dengan alur yang sangat mirip tipe dongeng ATU 425 "Pencarian Suami yang Hilang" atau kisah Yunani-Romawi Cupid dan Psyche karya Apuleius.
claims.quote: Another story of Ame no Wakahiko appears in Japanese medieval literature of the Muromachi period (Otogi-zōshi), in a narrative very similar to the Aarne-Thompson-Uther tale type ATU 425, "The Search for the Lost Husband", or to the Graeco-Roman story of Cupid and Psyche, by writer Apuleius.

claims.statement: The story is also known as Ame no Wakahiko sōshi or Ame no Wakahiko monogatari (The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko), and serves as another etiological tale for the Tanabata festival.
claims.statement_id: Kisah ini juga dikenal sebagai Ame no Wakahiko sōshi atau Ame no Wakahiko monogatari (Kisah Ame no Wakahiko), dan menjadi kisah asal-usul lain bagi festival Tanabata.
claims.quote: The story is alternatively known as Ame no Wakahiko sōshi or Ame no Wakahiko monogatari (The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko), and serves as another etiological tale for the Tanabata festival.

claims.statement: In this tale, Prince Ame no Wakahiko takes the form of a serpent.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah ini, Pangeran Ame no Wakahiko menjelma menjadi ular.
claims.quote: In this tale, Prince Ame no Wakahiko takes the form of a serpent.

claims.statement: At the end of the tale the oni father lets his son and the wife meet once a month, but she mistakes it for "once a year", so the lovers can only reunite at Tanabata.
claims.statement_id: Di akhir kisah, ayah oni mengizinkan putranya dan sang istri bertemu sebulan sekali, tetapi sang istri salah mengira "setahun sekali", sehingga sepasang kekasih itu hanya bisa bersatu saat Tanabata.
claims.quote: At the end of this tale, the oni father  lets his son and the wife meet once a month, but she mistakes it for "once a year" and thus, the lovers can only reunite during the Tanabata.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: アメノワカヒコ (天若日子, 天稚彦) is a deity in Japanese mythology, also written アメワカヒコ and アマノワカヒコ.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: アメノワカヒコ (天若日子, 天稚彦) adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang, juga ditulis アメワカヒコ dan アマノワカヒコ.
claims.quote: アメノワカヒコ（天若日子、天稚彦）は、日本神話に登場する神。アメワカヒコ、アマノワカヒコともする。

claims.statement: "Wakahiko" in his name means a young man; one theory says that because it was a common noun rather than a divine name he carries no honorific such as 神, 命 or 尊, while another says it is because he rebelled against the amatsukami.
claims.statement_id: "Wakahiko" dalam namanya berarti pemuda; ada teori bahwa karena itu kata benda umum, bukan nama dewa, ia tidak diberi gelar kehormatan seperti 神, 命, atau 尊, dan teori lain karena ia memberontak kepada para amatsukami.
claims.quote: 名前の「ワカヒコ」は若い男の意味である。これが神名ではなく普通名詞だったため、「神」「命」「尊」の尊称が付かないとする説がある。また、天津神に反逆したためであるとする説もある。

claims.statement: In the Kojiki the mourning hut of Ame no Wakahiko was built on earth, whereas in the Nihon Shoki a gale lifted the body and the hut was built in heaven.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kojiki, gubuk duka Ame no Wakahiko dibuat di bumi, sedangkan Nihon Shoki menyebut jenazah dinaikkan oleh angin kencang dan gubuk duka dibuat di surga.
claims.quote: 天若日子の喪屋は『古事記』では地上に作ったとあるが、『日本書紀』では疾風（はやち）に遺体を上げさせて、喪屋は天に作ったとある。

claims.statement: Because Ame no Wakahiko and Ajisukitakahikone looked so alike, one theory holds they were originally the same god: Ame no Wakahiko's death and his revival as Ajisukitakahikone, representing grain withering in autumn and reviving in spring, or the sun weakening in winter and reviving in spring.
claims.statement_id: Karena Ame no Wakahiko dan Ajisukitakahikone sangat mirip, ada teori bahwa mereka pada mulanya dewa yang sama: kematian Ame no Wakahiko dan kebangkitannya sebagai Ajisukitakahikone, yang melambangkan padi-padian yang layu di musim gugur lalu tumbuh kembali di musim semi, atau matahari yang melemah di musim dingin lalu bangkit di musim semi.
claims.quote: 天若日子と阿遅鉏高日子根神がそっくりだったということで、本来同一の神であったとする説もある。すなわち、アメノワカヒコの死とアヂスキタカヒコネとしての復活であり、これは穀物が秋に枯れて春に再生する、または太陽が冬に力が弱まり春に復活する様子を表したものであるとする。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi, the gods say: "Ame-waka-hiko, son of Ame no Kuni-dama. He is a valorous person. Let him be tried."
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi, para dewa berkata: "Ame-waka-hiko, putra Ame no Kuni-dama. Ia orang yang gagah berani. Biarlah ia dicoba."
claims.quote: Ame-waka-hiko, son of Ame no Kuni-dama. He is a valorous person. Let him be tried.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi this god too was disloyal and as soon as he arrived took Shita-teru-hime to wife.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, dewa ini juga tidak setia dan begitu tiba ia mengambil Shita-teru-hime sebagai istri.
claims.quote: This God also was disloyal, and as soon as he arrived took to wife Shita-teru-hime

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, Ame-waka-hiko took the heavenly deer-bow and heavenly feathered arrows given him by Taka-mi-musubi no Mikoto and shot the pheasant so that it died.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, Ame-waka-hiko mengambil busur rusa surgawi dan anak panah berbulu surgawi pemberian Taka-mi-musubi no Mikoto, lalu memanah burung pegar itu hingga mati.
claims.quote: Then Ame-waka-hiko took the heavenly deer-bow and the heavenly feathered arrows which had been given him by Taka-mi-musubi no Mikoto, and shot the pheasant, so that it died.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, Ame-waka-hiko was lying down after the feast of first-fruits and died immediately when hit by the arrow.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, Ame-waka-hiko sedang berbaring setelah pesta buah pertama, dan ketika terkena anak panah itu ia langsung meninggal.
claims.quote: Ame-waka-hiko was lying down after the feast of first-fruits, and when hit by the arrow died immediately.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi a swift wind was sent down to bring the body up to Heaven, and a mortuary house was promptly made.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, angin kencang dikirim turun untuk membawa jenazah naik ke Surga, lalu segera dibuat rumah duka.
claims.quote: and sent down a swift wind. to bring the body up to Heaven. Forthwith a mortuary house was made

claims.statement: Andrealphus is a demon in European demonology.
claims.statement_id: Andrealphus adalah iblis dalam demonologi Eropa.
claims.quote: アンドレアルフス（Andrealphus）またはアンドロアルフス（Androalphus）は、悪魔学における悪魔の一人。

claims.statement: According to the Goetia he is a great marquis, leading 30 legions, in the 65th position.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Goetia, ia adalah markis agung yang memimpin 30 legiun dan menempati urutan ke-65.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の30の軍団を率いる序列65番の大侯爵。

claims.statement: In this demonology list he has the appearance of a peacock who raises great noises and teaches cunning in astronomy, and in human form also teaches geometry perfectly.
claims.statement_id: Menurut daftar demonologi ini, ia tampil dengan wujud merak yang menimbulkan bunyi gaduh, mengajarkan kecerdikan dalam astronomi, dan dalam wujud manusia mengajarkan geometri secara sempurna.
claims.quote: with the appearance of a peacock who raises great noises and teaches cunning in astronomy, and when in human form also teaches geometry in a perfect manner.

claims.statement: The Goetia says he teaches geometry.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menyebut ia mengajarkan geometri.
claims.quote: when in human form also teaches geometry in a perfect manner.

claims.statement: According to Japanese Wikipedia he appears first as a peacock accompanied by noise and after a while takes human form; he teaches geometry perfectly, together with all techniques of measurement and skilled argument.
claims.statement_id: Ia mula-mula muncul dalam wujud merak disertai kebisingan, lalu mengambil wujud manusia; ia mengajarkan geometri dengan sempurna beserta semua teknik pengukuran dan kepandaian berargumentasi.
claims.quote: 最初は騒音と共に孔雀の姿で現れるが、しばらくすると人間の姿を採る。幾何学を完璧に教え、測量に関わるあらゆる技術や巧みな弁論術も教えてくれる。

claims.statement: He also makes people well versed in astronomy, and this source says he can change a person into a bird when given a human sacrifice.
claims.statement_id: Ia membuat orang mahir dalam astronomi, dan menurut sumber ini ia memiliki kuasa mengubah orang menjadi burung bila diberi korban manusia.
claims.quote: 天文学にも精通させてくれる。また、人間の生け贄を与える事で人を鳥の姿に変える力も持つ。

claims.statement: According to Collin de Plancy, Andrealphus is a preacher of sophistry who sometimes changes only a person's face into a bird so that he escapes the reach of justice.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Collin de Plancy, Andrealphus adalah penyebar dalih yang berbelit, dan kadang hanya mengubah wajah seseorang menjadi burung agar lolos dari kejaran hukum.
claims.quote: コラン・ド・プランシーによればアンドレアルフスは屁理屈の伝道者であり、人の顔だけを鳥に変えて司法の追及の手から逃がすことがあるという。

claims.statement: The Japanese occult writer 江口之隆 added in his book that in human form Andrealphus takes the shape of a cowherd accompanied by a monkey and a bear.
claims.statement_id: Penulis okultisme Jepang 江口之隆 menambahkan dalam bukunya bahwa dalam wujud manusia Andrealphus berupa penggembala sapi yang membawa kera dan beruang.
claims.quote: 伝統的な悪魔に独自設定を付け加えたことで知られる江口之隆は、『西洋魔物図鑑』でアンドレアルフスに人間の姿を取るときには猿と熊を連れた牛飼いの姿をとるという設定を付け加えている。

claims.statement: In the Goetia the 65th spirit is called Andrealphus, a mighty great marquis who appears at first as a peacock with great noises but afterward puts on human shape.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Goetia, roh ke-65 itu disebut Andrealphus, markis agung yang mula-mula tampil sebagai merak disertai bunyi gaduh, tetapi kemudian mengenakan wujud manusia.
claims.quote: The 65 spirit is called Andrealphus,75 he is a Mighty great Marquiz appearing at first in ye forme of [a] Peacock, with great Noises but afterward he putteth on humane shape

claims.statement: The Goetia says he can teach geometry and everything belonging to measuring, also astronomy, makes men subtle and cunning in them, can transform a man into the likeness of a bird, and governs 30 legions of spirits.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menyebut ia dapat mengajarkan geometri dan segala hal tentang pengukuran serta astronomi, membuat orang cerdik di dalamnya, dapat mengubah manusia menjadi rupa burung, dan memerintah 30 legiun roh.
claims.quote: he can teach perfectly geomitry, & all Things belonging to measuring, also Astronomy, he maketh men very subtile and cunning therin, he can Transforme a Man into ... likness of a Bird & he governeth 30 Legions of spirits

claims.statement: The editor's note says that Weyer's catalogue gives the name as Androalphus and Scot's translation as Andrealphus, and that he is number 55 in both.
claims.statement_id: Catatan penyunting menyebut bahwa dalam katalog Weyer namanya tertulis Androalphus, sedangkan dalam terjemahan Scot tertulis Andrealphus; ia adalah nomor 55 di keduanya.
claims.quote: 75. Andrealphus (Marquis): #55 in W and Scot. W: Androalphus; Scot: Andrealphus.

claims.statement: In the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (Scot's translation) Andrealphus is a great marquis who appears as a peacock, raises great heavy noises, and in human shape perfectly teaches geometry.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (terjemahan Scot), Andrealphus adalah markis agung yang tampil sebagai merak, menimbulkan bunyi berat, dan dalam wujud manusia mengajarkan geometri dengan sempurna.
claims.quote: Andrealphus [*Androalphus] is a great marquesse, appearing as a pecocke, he raiseth great [*bass, heavy] noises, and in humane shape perfectlie teacheth geometrie

claims.statement: The Weyer-Scot text adds that he makes a man a subtle disputer and cunning in astronomy, transforms a man into the likeness of a bird, and has thirty legions under him.
claims.statement_id: Teks Weyer-Scot menambahkan bahwa ia membuat orang menjadi pendebat yang halus dan cerdik dalam astronomi, mengubah manusia menjadi rupa burung, dan memiliki tiga puluh legiun di bawahnya.
claims.quote: he maketh a man to be a subtill disputer, and cunning in astronomie, and transformeth a man into the likenes of a bird, and there are under him thirtie legions.

claims.statement: Andromalius is a demon in European demonology.
claims.statement_id: Andromalius adalah iblis dalam demonologi Eropa.
claims.quote: アンドロマリウス（Andromalius）は、悪魔学における悪魔の一人。

claims.statement: The Goetia calls him its seventy-second spirit and an earl.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu memberinya gelar earl.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の36の軍団を率いる序列72番の大いなる伯爵。

claims.statement: He appears as a man holding a large serpent.
claims.statement_id: Ia tampil sebagai pria yang memegang ular besar.
claims.quote: 巨大な蛇を手にした人間の姿で現れるとされる。 ... 盗人を捕らえ盗品を取り戻し、悪と不正を発見し、あらゆる盗人やその他の邪悪な人間を罰し、隠された財宝を発見する事に力を発揮するという。

claims.statement: The Goetia credits him with recovering thieves and stolen goods.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menyebut ia dapat menangkap pencuri dan mengembalikan barang curian.
claims.quote: 盗人を捕らえ盗品を取り戻し、悪と不正を発見し、あらゆる盗人やその他の邪悪な人間を罰し、隠された財宝を発見する事に力を発揮するという。

claims.statement: In the Goetia the 72nd spirit in order is called Andromalius, a great and mighty earl who appears in the form of a man holding a serpent in his hand; his office is to bring back a thief and the stolen goods.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Goetia, roh urutan ke-72 bernama Andromalius, seorang earl (bangsawan) yang besar dan perkasa, tampil dalam bentuk manusia yang memegang ular; tugasnya membawa kembali pencuri dan barang curian.
claims.quote: The 72d spirit in order is called Andromalius82 he is a great and Mighty Earle appearing in ye form of a Man, holding a serpent in his hand, his office is to bring a Theefe & goods

claims.statement: The Goetia also says he punishes thieves and other wicked people, discovers hidden treasure, and rules 36 legions of spirits.
claims.statement_id: Goetia juga menyebut ia menghukum pencuri dan orang jahat lain, menemukan harta yang tersembunyi, dan memerintah 36 legiun roh.
claims.quote: to punish Theives & other wicked people, & to discover Treasure that is hidd, &c, he ruleth 36 Legions of spirits

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia says he does not appear in the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum and is not covered in Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire infernal.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Jepang, ia tidak muncul dalam Pseudomonarchia Daemonum dan juga tidak dibahas dalam Dictionnaire infernal karya Collin de Plancy.
claims.quote: 『悪魔の偽王国』には登場しておらず、コラン・ド・プランシーの『地獄の辞典』にも取り上げられていない。

claims.statement: The Goetia editor's note says he is not in W or Scot, is often seen in stand-alone spells in magic manuscripts for detecting a thief or discovering treasure, and his name is usually spelled Andromalcus, with many variants.
claims.statement_id: Catatan penyunting Goetia: ia tidak ada dalam katalog W maupun Scot, sering muncul dalam mantra mandiri di naskah sihir untuk menemukan pencuri atau harta, dan namanya biasanya ditulis Andromalcus dengan banyak ragam ejaan.
claims.quote: Not in W or Scot. Often seen in stand-alone spells in magic mss., where he is employed for detecting a thief or discovering treasure. The name is usually spelled Andromalcus, with many variants

claims.statement: Spelling variants recorded by the editor: Andromalce, Andromalcum, Andrewemalcus and Andrea Malchus.
claims.statement_id: Ragam ejaan yang dicatat penyunting: Andromalce, Andromalcum, Andrewemalcus, dan Andrea Malchus.
claims.quote: (e.g. Andromalce, Andromalcum, Andrewemalcus, Andrea Malchus)

claims.statement: The Japanese occult writer 江口之隆 speculates in his book that Andromalius may have been a god of thieves in Canaanite mythology.
claims.statement_id: Penulis okultisme Jepang 江口之隆 menduga dalam bukunya bahwa Andromalius dahulu adalah dewa pencuri dalam mitologi Kanaan.
claims.quote: 伝統的な悪魔に独自設定を付け加えて考察することで知られる江口之隆は、『西洋魔物図鑑』でアンドロマリウスはカナン神話の盗賊の神だったのではないかと推測している。

claims.statement: English Wikipedia likewise describes him as a Great Earl of Hell with 36 legions of demons who can bring back both a thief and the stolen goods.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Inggris juga menggambarkannya sebagai Earl Agung Neraka yang memiliki 36 legiun iblis dan dapat membawa kembali pencuri beserta barang curiannya.
claims.quote: Andromalius is a mighty Great Earl of Hell, having 36 legions of demons at his service. He can bring back both a thief and the stolen goods

claims.statement: Ayakashi names a group of supernatural beings associated with water.
claims.statement_id: Ayakashi adalah sebutan bagi kelompok makhluk gaib yang berkaitan dengan air.
claims.quote: Ayakashi (アヤカシ) is the collective name for yōkai that appear above the surface of a body of water.

claims.statement: Some regional traditions use the name for lights or ghosts seen over water.
claims.statement_id: Di beberapa daerah, namanya dipakai untuk cahaya atau hantu di atas air.
claims.quote: In Nagasaki Prefecture, the atmospheric ghost lights that appear above water are called ayakashi, and so are the funayūrei in Yamaguchi Prefecture and Saga Prefecture.

claims.statement: In western Japan, some accounts connect them with those who died at sea.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang barat, sebagian kisah menghubungkannya dengan orang yang mati di laut.
claims.quote: In western Japan, ayakashi are said to be the vengeful spirits of those who died at sea and that they are attempting to capture more people to join them.

claims.statement: Toriyama Sekien illustrated an ayakashi as a large sea serpent.
claims.statement_id: Toriyama Sekien menggambar ayakashi sebagai ular laut besar.
claims.quote: In the Konjaku Hyakki Shūi by Sekien Toriyama, the ayakashi are represented by a large sea snake, but this may actually be an ikuchi.

claims.statement: There is also a folk belief that if a live sharksucker sticks to the bottom of a boat the boat cannot move, so ayakashi is used as a synonym for this fish.
claims.statement_id: Ada pula kepercayaan rakyat bahwa jika ikan remora hidup menempel di dasar perahu, perahu itu tak bisa bergerak, sehingga ayakashi dipakai sebagai sinonim ikan jenis ini.
claims.quote: There is also the folk belief that if a live sharksucker were to get stuck to the bottom of a boat, it would not be able to move, so ayakashi is used as a synonym for this type of fish.

claims.statement: On Tsushima Island they are also called "atmospheric ghost lights of ayakashi (ayakashi no kaika)", appear on beaches in the evening, and are said to look like a child walking in the middle of a fire.
claims.statement_id: Di Pulau Tsushima, mereka juga disebut "cahaya hantu atmosferik ayakashi (ayakashi no kaika)", muncul di pantai pada petang, dan konon tampak seperti anak kecil berjalan di tengah api.
claims.quote: On Tsushima Island, they are also called "atmospheric ghost lights of ayakashi (ayakashi no kaika)", and appear on beaches in the evening, and are said to look like a child walking in the middle of a fire.

claims.statement: According to Zack Davisson, in its most basic usage ayakashi is a general term for yōkai that appear above the surface of the water, and can be translated as "strange phenomenon of the sea."
claims.statement_id: Menurut Zack Davisson, dalam pemakaian paling dasar ayakashi adalah istilah umum bagi yōkai yang muncul di atas permukaan air, dan dapat diterjemahkan sebagai "fenomena aneh di laut".
claims.quote: In its most basic usage, ayakashi is a general term for yokai that appear above the surface of the water, and can be translated as “strange phenomenon of the sea.”

claims.statement: Ayakashi is written in hiragana (あやかし) or katakana (アヤカシ), neither of which gives any hint of its meaning.
claims.statement_id: Ayakashi ditulis dalam hiragana (あやかし) atau katakana (アヤカシ), yang keduanya tidak memberi petunjuk tentang maknanya.
claims.quote: But ayakashi is written either in hiragana (あやかし) or katakana (アヤカシ), neither of which give any hints as to the meaning.

claims.statement: In Yamaguchi and Saga prefectures ayakashi refers to funa yūrei, a group of yūrei who drowned at sea and now try to sink boats to increase their numbers.
claims.statement_id: Di Prefektur Yamaguchi dan Saga, ayakashi merujuk pada funa yūrei, sekelompok yūrei yang tenggelam di laut dan kini berusaha menenggelamkan perahu untuk menambah jumlah mereka.
claims.quote: In Yamaguchi and Saga prefectures ayakashi refers to funa yurei, a group of yurei who drowned at sea and now try to sink boats to increase their numbers.

claims.statement: By far the most famous depiction of ayakashi is the massive sea serpent Ikuchi.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran ayakashi yang paling terkenal adalah ular laut raksasa Ikuchi.
claims.quote: By far the most famous depiction of ayakashi is the massive sea serpent Ikuchi.
