claims.statement: In Toriyama Sekien's quoted text, boats in the seas of Western Japan meet a beast so large it takes 2-3 days to sail past; its body drips oil, and if the sailors work together to clear the oil from the boat no harm will come to them.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kutipan keterangan Toriyama Sekien, perahu di laut Jepang barat bertemu binatang yang begitu besar sehingga butuh 2-3 hari untuk melewatinya; tubuhnya meneteskan minyak, dan jika para pelaut bekerja sama membersihkan perahu dari minyak itu, mereka tak akan celaka.
claims.quote: When boats sail the seas of Western Japan, they encounter a beast so large it takes 2-3 days just to sail past. The body of the beast drips oil, but if the sailors work together to clear the boat of the oil no harm will come to them.

claims.statement: In Noh theater, the name for a male mask of a ghost or violent god is ayakashi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam teater Noh, nama topeng laki-laki untuk hantu atau dewa yang ganas adalah ayakashi.
claims.quote: the name for a male mask of a ghost or violent god is called ayakashi.

claims.statement: In Taidozaki, in the Chosei district of Chiba Prefecture, a group of sailors put ashore to restock their fresh water.
claims.statement_id: Di Taidozaki, distrik Chosei, Prefektur Chiba, sekelompok pelaut berlabuh untuk mengisi ulang persediaan air tawar.
claims.quote: In Taidozaki, in the Chosei district of Chiba prefecture, a group of sailors put to show in order to re-stock their fresh water holds.

claims.statement: The captain said there was no well nearby and called the beautiful woman offering water an ayakashi.
claims.statement_id: Sang kapten berkata tidak ada sumur di dekat situ dan menyebut perempuan cantik yang menawarkan air itu sebagai ayakashi.
claims.quote: Hearing this, the Captain said “There’s no well nearby. I’ve heard similar stories of thirsty sailors beguiled by a beautiful woman offering them water, never to be seen again. That woman is an ayakashi!”

claims.statement: The woman ran toward the ship in a rage, leapt into the ocean, bit the hull of the ship and held on tight.
claims.statement_id: Perempuan itu berlari ke arah kapal dengan marah, melompat ke laut, menggigit lambung kapal, dan bergantung erat.
claims.quote: the woman came running towards the ship in a rage, and leapt into the ocean biting the hull of the ship and holding on tight.

claims.statement: This ayakashi story appears only once, in the Edo-period kaidanshu Kaidanro no Sue (怪談老の杖; A Cane for an Old Man of Kaidan).
claims.statement_id: Kisah ayakashi ini hanya muncul sekali, dalam kumpulan kisah ganjil zaman Edo Kaidanro no Sue (怪談老の杖).
claims.quote: This story of the ayakashi appears only once, in the Edo period Kaidanshu Kaidanro no Sue (怪談老の杖; A Cane for an Old Man of Kaidan).

claims.statement: The 1918 book Dozoku to Densetsu describes the ayakashi as a mystery of the sea that haunts boats, looking like an enormous octopus that wraps around a boat and lets go only when given gold coins.
claims.statement_id: Buku Dozoku to Densetsu (1918) menggambarkan ayakashi sebagai misteri laut yang menghantui perahu, berwujud seperti gurita raksasa yang melilit perahu dan baru melepaskannya bila diberi koin emas.
claims.quote: The 1918 book Dozoku to Densetsu (土俗と伝説; Local Customs and Legends) describes the ayakashi like this: “The ayakashi is a mystery of the sea. They haunt boats on the open waters. Their appearance is like an enormous octopus. It will wrap itself around a boat, and only let go when gold coins are given to it.”

claims.statement: Betobeto-san is a Japanese yōkai said to follow night travelers.
claims.statement_id: Betobeto-san adalah yōkai yang konon mengikuti pejalan pada malam hari.
claims.quote: Betobeto-san (べとべとさん) is a kind of Japanese yōkai said to follow people walking at night.

claims.statement: In Shizuoka it is said that one meets Betobeto-san when descending from a small hill.
claims.statement_id: Di Shizuoka dikatakan orang bertemu Betobeto-san ketika menuruni sebuah bukit kecil.
claims.quote: In Shizuoka, it is said that one will encounter Betobeto-san when descending from a small mountain.

claims.statement: Betobeto-san is said not to harm people; a person who hears its footsteps should stop at one side of the road and say "Go ahead, Betobeto-san" (Nara Prefecture).
claims.statement_id: Betobeto-san dikatakan tidak mencelakai orang; bila seseorang mendengar langkah kakinya, ia sebaiknya berhenti di tepi jalan dan berkata "Silakan lebih dulu, Betobeto-san" (Prefektur Nara).
claims.quote: Although it is said that Betobeto-san does not cause harm to people, if one hears footsteps, they should stop by one side of the road and say "Go ahead, Betobeto-san" (Nara Prefecture).

claims.statement: The manga artist Shigeru Mizuki reported a similar experience.
claims.statement_id: Mangaka Shigeru Mizuki pernah mengaku mengalami hal serupa.
claims.quote: Manga artist Shigeru Mizuki said that he has encountered something that seems to be akin to this yōkai.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: Betobeto-san is a kind of yōkai said to follow people walking on night roads; in Uda District, Nara, it is met on dark night roads, and in Shizuoka when coming down from a small hill.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Betobeto-san adalah sejenis yōkai yang konon mengikuti orang di jalan malam; di Kabupaten Uda, Nara, ia ditemui di jalan malam yang gelap, dan di Shizuoka ketika turun dari bukit kecil.
claims.quote: べとべとさんは、日本の妖怪の一種。夜道を歩く人間の後をつけてくるといわれる。奈良県宇陀郡では暗い夜道で遭うといい、静岡県では小山を降りてくるときに遭うという。

claims.statement: It is said to make only the sound of footsteps and not harm people; if the footsteps feel eerie, one steps to the side of the road and says 「べとべとさん、お先にお越し」 (Nara) or 「お先にお越し」 / 「お先にどうぞ」 (Shizuoka), and it leaves the person it was following.
claims.statement_id: Hanya terdengar langkah kaki dan ia tidak membahayakan orang; bila langkah itu terasa menyeramkan, orang menepi dan mengucapkan 「べとべとさん、お先にお越し」 (Nara) atau 「お先にお越し」 / 「お先にどうぞ」 (Shizuoka), maka ia konon meninggalkan orang yang diikutinya.
claims.quote: 足音がするのみで人に危害を加えることはないとされるが、足音を不気味に感じるときには道の片側に寄って、「べとべとさん、お先にお越し」（奈良県）「お先にお越し」（静岡県）「お先にどうぞ」（同県）などと唱えれば、ついてきた人間から離れるという。

claims.statement: In Sakai District, Fukui (now Sakai City), a phenomenon called 「びしゃがつく」 is told: on a dark night in winter sleet, something unseen follows a walker with a squelching bisha-bisha sound on the sleet-covered road; it is regarded as the same kind of yōkai as Betobeto-san.
claims.statement_id: Di Kabupaten Sakai, Fukui (kini Kota Sakai), dikisahkan 「びしゃがつく」: pada malam bersalju basah, sesuatu yang tak terlihat mengikuti orang dengan bunyi 「びしゃ、びしゃ」 di jalan berlumpur salju; ia dianggap yōkai sejenis Betobeto-san.
claims.quote: 福井県坂井郡（現・坂井市）に伝わる「びしゃがつく」は、冬のみぞれの降る中、暗い夜道を歩く人間の後を、姿の見えないものがびしゃ、びしゃとみぞれ混じりの道を歩くような音を立ててつけてくるという怪異が伝わっており、べとべとさんと同類の妖怪とされる。

claims.statement: Yokai.com: Betobetosan are formless specters, recognizable only by their telltale sound, the "beto beto" clacking of wooden clogs.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: Betobetosan adalah hantu tanpa wujud yang hanya dikenali dari bunyi khasnya, bunyi "beto beto" sandal kayu.
claims.quote: Betobetosan are formless specters, and are recognizable only by their telltale sound—the “beto beto” clacking of wooden clogs.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: they synchronize their pace with walkers and follow them as long as they can, getting closer with every step.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: mereka menyamakan langkah dengan pejalan kaki dan mengikutinya selama mungkin, semakin mendekat pada tiap langkah.
claims.quote: They synchronize their pace with walkers and follow them as long as they can, getting closer and closer with every step.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: the name is onomatopoeic, from the sound of footsteps; an alternate name is bishagatsuku.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: namanya bersifat onomatope, berasal dari bunyi langkah kaki; nama lainnya adalah bishagatsuku.
claims.quote: Translation: onomatopoeic; from the sound of footsteps Alternate names: bishagatsuku

claims.statement: Yokai.com: in Matsuoka in northern Fukui Prefecture, a betobetosan that appears during cold winter sleet storms is known as bishagatsuku.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: di Matsuoka, Prefektur Fukui bagian utara, Betobetosan yang muncul saat badai salju basah musim dingin dikenal sebagai bishagatsuku.
claims.quote: In Matsuoka in northern Fukui Prefecture, a betobetosan which appears during cold winter sleet storms is known as bishagatsuku.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: betobetosan can be disconcerting but are not dangerous; once you realize you are being followed, simply step to the side of the road and say "After you, betobetosan."
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: Betobetosan bisa mengganggu tetapi tidak berbahaya; bila sadar diikuti, cukup menepi dan berkata "Silakan lebih dulu, betobetosan".
claims.quote: Though betobetosan can be disconcerting, they are not dangerous. Once you realize you are being followed by a betobetosan, simply step to the side of the road and say “After you, betobetosan.”

claims.statement: Yokai.com: habitat is alleys and narrow, sloped roads; it only appears at night.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: habitatnya gang dan jalan sempit yang miring, dan ia hanya muncul pada malam hari.
claims.quote: Habitat: alleys and narrow, sloped roads; only appears at night

claims.statement: According to Japanese Wikipedia, Betobeto-san is essentially a sound without a visible form, yet appears in Shigeru Mizuki's manga such as GeGeGe no Kitarō (『ゲゲゲの鬼太郎』), 『のんのんばあとオレ』 and 『コミック昭和史』.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Jepang, Betobeto-san pada dasarnya hanya berupa bunyi tanpa wujud terlihat, tetapi muncul dalam manga Mizuki Shigeru seperti GeGeGe no Kitarō (『ゲゲゲの鬼太郎』), 『のんのんばあとオレ』, dan 『コミック昭和史』.
claims.quote: べとべとさんは、本来音だけで姿が見えない存在だが、水木しげるの漫画『ゲゲゲの鬼太郎』・『のんのんばあとオレ』・『コミック昭和史』などにも登場する。

claims.statement: Yonago Airport Station on the JR West Sakai Line, near Mizuki's home area, has the nickname 「べとべとさん」 station.
claims.statement_id: Stasiun Yonago Airport di Jalur Sakai milik JR West, kampung halaman Mizuki, memiliki nama julukan 「べとべとさん」.
claims.quote: 水木の地元、西日本旅客鉄道（JR西日本）境線・米子空港駅の愛称が「べとべとさん」駅である。

claims.statement: Boroboroton is a yōkai belonging to the animated-object group called tsukumogami.
claims.statement_id: Boroboroton adalah yōkai dari kelompok benda hidup yang disebut tsukumogami.
claims.quote: The Boroboroton (Japanese: 暮露暮露団 [bo̞ɺo̞bo̞ɺo̞to̞ɴ]; meaning "boroboro (tattered) futon") is a tsukumogami yōkai, and is believed to be evil and dangerous to humans.

claims.statement: It resembles an old, tattered futon that moves at night.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya futon usang yang bergerak pada malam hari.
claims.quote: The Boroboroton is described as a tattered futon (a Japanese sleeping mat) who comes to life at night.

claims.statement: Stories describe it wrapping around a sleeper to strangle them.
claims.statement_id: Menurut cerita, ia melilit orang tidur untuk mencekiknya.
claims.quote: It rises up into the air and throws its (former) owner out of bed, then begins to twine around the head and neck of the sleeper with the intent of strangling him.

claims.statement: One account says the futon comes alive after being neglected.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kisah menyebut futon itu hidup setelah diabaikan.
claims.quote: Boroboroton will come to life when feeling ignored or unneeded.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: Boroboroton is a kind of Japanese yōkai, one of the tsukumogami, drawn in the yōkai picture collection 『百器徒然袋』 by the Edo-period painter Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Boroboroton adalah sejenis yōkai Jepang, salah satu tsukumogami, yang digambar dalam kumpulan gambar yōkai 『百器徒然袋』 karya pelukis zaman Edo Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: 暮露暮露団（ぼろぼろとん）は、日本の妖怪の一種。付喪神（つくもがみ）の一つ。江戸時代の画家・鳥山石燕の妖怪画集『百器徒然袋』に描かれている。

claims.statement: A futon that has grown old and tattered yet been kept for various reasons is said to become a Boroboroton; no records of it remain as folk tradition and it is presumed to be Sekien's creation.
claims.statement_id: Futon yang sudah tua dan compang-camping tetapi tetap disimpan karena berbagai alasan konon menjadi Boroboroton; tidak ada catatan tentangnya sebagai cerita rakyat dan ia diduga ciptaan Sekien.
claims.quote: 古くなってボロボロになりながらも、様々な理由で残された布団が暮露暮露団となるという。この妖怪にまつわる記録は民間伝承としては残っておらず、石燕による創作と推測されている。

claims.statement: Many yōkai in 『百器徒然袋』 are based on 『徒然草』; the Boroboroton caption mentions 「ぼろぼろ」 meaning monks of the Fuke Zen school, so one theory is that the yōkai was invented as wordplay between the boroboro story in section 115 of 『徒然草』 and a tattered futon.
claims.statement_id: Banyak yōkai dalam 『百器徒然袋』 bersumber dari 『徒然草』; keterangan Boroboroton menyebut 「ぼろぼろ」 yang berarti biksu aliran Fuke Zen, sehingga ada teori bahwa yōkai ini dibuat sebagai permainan kata antara kisah boroboro dalam bagian ke-115 『徒然草』 dan futon yang compang-camping.
claims.quote: また『百器徒然袋』では『徒然草』をもとにした妖怪が多いが、この暮露暮露団の解説にも普化禅宗の僧を意味する「ぼろぼろ」のことが述べられていることから、『徒然草』の第百十五段にあるぼろぼろの話と、ぼろぼろに破れた布団との言葉遊びで暮露暮露団という妖怪が創作されたとの説もある。

claims.statement: Daijisen: a tsukumogami is a spirit said to dwell in an implement that has passed 100 years, and to transform or harm people.
claims.statement_id: Daijisen: tsukumogami adalah roh yang konon menghuni perkakas yang telah berusia 100 tahun, lalu berubah wujud atau mencelakai orang.
claims.quote: つくも‐がみ【付喪神】 100年を経過した器物に宿り、化けたり人に害をなしたりするとされる精霊。

claims.statement: Heibonsha: an old woman is said to become a female oni, and a shabby discarded tool is said to become an oni called tsukumogami, according to the 《付喪神記》.
claims.statement_id: Heibonsha: dikatakan bahwa perempuan tua menjadi oni perempuan, dan perkakas tua yang dibuang menjadi oni yang disebut tsukumogami menurut 《付喪神記》.
claims.quote: 年老いた女は鬼女になるといい(《今昔物語集》)，古ぼけて捨てられた道具は〈付喪神（つくもがみ）〉という鬼になるという(《付喪神記》)。

claims.statement: Itsumade is a strange bird pictured by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Itsumade adalah burung aneh yang digambar Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Itsumade (Japanese: 以津真天) is an eerie bird featured in the Japanese collection of Yōkai pictures, the Konjaku Gazu Zoku Hyakki by Toriyama Sekien published in 1779.

claims.statement: A Taiheiki episode places its cries during a deadly epidemic.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Taiheiki, jeritannya terdengar saat wabah mematikan.
claims.quote: According to the Taiheiki, around the fall of 1334 (in the Kenmu years), an epidemic illness was causing many deaths and almost every night, an eerie bird appeared on top of the Shishinden (ja:紫宸殿) crying "itsumade itsumade" (until when?

claims.statement: In that account an archer named Hiroari shoots the bird.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu, pemanah bernama Hiroari menembaknya.
claims.quote: The nobility thought back to how the master of arrows Minamoto no Yorimasa slew the nue and made a request to Oki Jirōzaemon Hiroari (ja:真弓広有) who splendidly shot down the eerie bird with a kabura-ya.

claims.statement: The Taiheiki describes a strange bird without calling it Itsumade.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki hanya menyebut burung aneh tanpa nama Itsumade.
claims.quote: In the Taiheiki, the bird is merely written to be the "eerie bird" with no distinctive name.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: Itsumade (以津真天) is an eerie bird in Toriyama Sekien's Edo-period yōkai picture collection 『今昔画図続百鬼』; its caption shows it was created from the eerie bird in 「広有射怪鳥事」 in scroll 12 of the 『太平記』.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Itsumade (以津真天) adalah burung aneh dalam kumpulan gambar yōkai zaman Edo 『今昔画図続百鬼』 karya Toriyama Sekien; keterangan gambarnya menunjukkan bahwa ia dibuat dari burung aneh dalam 「広有射怪鳥事」 di jilid 12 『太平記』.
claims.quote: 以津真天（いつまで）は、鳥山石燕による江戸時代の日本の妖怪画集『今昔画図続百鬼』にある怪鳥。解説文に「広有 いつまでいつまでと鳴し怪鳥を射し事 太平記に委し」とあるように、『太平記』巻12の「広有射怪鳥事」に登場する怪鳥を題材に創られた妖怪であることがわかる。

claims.statement: The bird had a human-like face, a curved beak lined with saw-like teeth, a snake-like body, claws on both feet sharp as swords, and a wingspan of 1 jō 6 shaku (about 4.8 meters).
claims.statement_id: Burung itu berwajah seperti manusia, berparuh bengkok dengan gigi seperti gergaji, bertubuh seperti ular, bercakar tajam seperti pedang di kedua kakinya, dan berbentang sayap 1 jō 6 shaku (sekitar 4,8 meter).
claims.quote: その怪鳥は顔が人間のようで、曲がったくちばしに鋸のような歯が並び、体はヘビのようで、両足の爪は剣のように鋭く、翼長は1丈6尺（約4.8メートル）もあったという。

claims.statement: In yōkai literature since the Shōwa era the name is also read Itsumaden; explanations also say that when the bodies of those who died in war or famine are left, this bird perches near them and cries 「いつまで、いつまで」 (until when?), or that it is the vengeful spirit of those who died thus, turned into a bird.
claims.statement_id: Dalam literatur yōkai sejak era Shōwa, namanya juga dibaca Itsumaden; dijelaskan pula bahwa jika jenazah korban perang atau kelaparan dibiarkan, burung ini hinggap di dekatnya dan berseru 「いつまで、いつまで」 (sampai kapan?), atau bahwa ia adalah arwah penasaran orang-orang yang mati demikian yang berubah menjadi burung.
claims.quote: 昭和以降の妖怪関連の文献では、いつまでんとも読まれている。戦乱や飢餓などで死んだ人の死体をそのまま放っておくと、この怪鳥が死体の近くに止まり、「死体をいつまで放っておくのか」との意味で「いつまで、いつまで」と鳴くもの、またはそうして死んだ者たちの怨霊が鳥と化したものであるという解説がつけられて紹介されてもいる。

claims.statement: In the 『太平記』 the bird is only described as a 「怪鳥」 with no clear name; the name 「以津真天」 in 『今昔画図続百鬼』 is regarded as given by Toriyama Sekien from its cry when he drew this episode.
claims.statement_id: Dalam 『太平記』 burung ini hanya disebut 「怪鳥」 tanpa nama jelas; nama 「以津真天」 dalam 『今昔画図続百鬼』 dianggap diberikan Toriyama Sekien berdasarkan suara cuitnya ketika menggambar kisah ini.
claims.quote: 『太平記』において、この鳥は「怪鳥」と記述されているのみで明確な名前などは記載されていない。『今昔画図続百鬼』において付された「以津真天」という名称は、鳥山石燕がこの逸話を『今昔画図続百鬼』に描く際、その鳴き声をもとに名づけたものとされる。

claims.statement: Taiheiki: that year an epidemic spread through the land and many died; moreover, from that autumn an eerie bird appeared above the Shishinden crying 「いつまで、いつまで」.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki: pada tahun itu wabah melanda negeri dan banyak orang meninggal; selain itu, sejak musim gugur seekor burung aneh muncul di atas Shishinden dan berseru 「いつまで、いつまで」.
claims.quote: 今年天下に疫癘有て、病死する者甚多し。是のみならず、其秋の比より紫宸殿の上に怪鳥出来て、「いつまで／＼。」とぞ鳴ける。

claims.statement: Taiheiki: its head was like a human's and its body snake-shaped; its beak curved forward with saw-like teeth, both feet had long spurs sharp as swords, and its outstretched wings measured one jō six shaku.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki: kepalanya seperti manusia dan tubuhnya berbentuk ular; paruhnya bengkok ke depan dengan gigi seperti gergaji, kedua kakinya bertaji panjang setajam pedang, dan bila sayapnya dibentangkan panjangnya satu jō enam shaku.
claims.quote: 頭は如人して、身は蛇の形也。嘴の前曲て歯如鋸生違。両の足に長距有て、利如剣。羽崎を延て見之、長一丈六尺也。

claims.statement: Taiheiki: when it cried, it seemed to spit flames from its mouth, lightning flashed from within its voice, and the light penetrated through to the inside of the blinds.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki: saat berseru, seakan-akan api keluar dari mulutnya dan kilat memancar dari dalam suaranya, cahayanya menembus hingga ke dalam tirai istana.
claims.quote: 鳴時口より火炎を吐歟と覚て、声の内より電して、其光御簾の内へ散徹す。

claims.statement: Taiheiki: it was said that Oki Jirōzaemon Hiroari, in the service of the Nijō Kanpaku and Minister of the Left, was fit for the task.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki: dikatakan bahwa Oki Jirōzaemon Hiroari, pelayan Menteri Kiri Kanpaku dari Nijō, adalah orang yang mampu menangani tugas itu.
claims.quote: 二条関白左大臣殿の被召仕候、隠岐次郎左衛門広有と申者こそ、其器に堪たる者にて候へ。

claims.statement: Taiheiki: that same night Hiroari was raised to the fifth rank, and the next day was granted two large estates in Inaba Province.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki: pada malam itu juga Hiroari dinaikkan ke pangkat kelima, dan keesokan harinya diberi dua perkebunan besar di Provinsi Inaba.
claims.quote: 主上弥叡感有て、其夜軈て広有を被成五位、次の日因幡国に大庄二箇所賜てけり。

claims.statement: Yokai.com: Itsumade are kaichō, strange birds, with a human face and pointed beak, a snake's body with wings, and terrible claws; their wingspan is 4.8 meters.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: Itsumade adalah kaichō, burung aneh, berwajah manusia dengan paruh runcing, bertubuh ular bersayap, dan bercakar mengerikan; bentang sayapnya 4,8 meter.
claims.quote: Itsumade are kaichō, or strange birds. They have the face of a human with a pointed beak, and the body of a snake with wings, and terrible claws. Their wingspan is 4.8 meters.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: itsumade appear in the night sky during times of trouble, such as plagues and disasters, or flying over battlegrounds where many have died.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: Itsumade muncul di langit malam pada masa sulit, seperti wabah dan bencana, atau terbang di atas medan perang tempat banyak orang tewas.
claims.quote: Itsumade appear in the night sky during times of trouble—such as plagues and disasters, or flying over battlegrounds where many have died.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: the strange birds fly about in circles all night long, crying out in a terrible voice.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: burung aneh ini terbang berputar-putar sepanjang malam sambil berseru dengan suara mengerikan.
claims.quote: The strange birds fly about in circles all night long, crying out in a terrible voice.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: it is thought that the spirits of the dead and suffering form into onryō that take the shape of these birds, demanding recognition of their suffering and torment.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: diduga arwah orang mati dan yang menderita membentuk onryō yang berwujud burung-burung ini, menuntut pengakuan atas penderitaan mereka.
claims.quote: It is thought that the spirits of the dead and suffering form into onryō which take the shape of these birds. They demand recognition of their suffering and torment.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: afterwards Hiroari was given the name Mayumi, meaning "true bow".
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: setelah itu Hiroari diberi nama Mayumi, yang berarti "busur sejati".
claims.quote: Afterwards, Hiroari was given the name Mayumi, meaning true bow.

claims.statement: Daijisen Plus: a Japanese yōkai, an eerie bird in the 「太平記」 said to cry 「いつまで、いつまで」; it had no name in the Taiheiki, but Toriyama Sekien named it after its cry in his picture collection; also called 「イツマデン」.
claims.statement_id: Daijisen Plus: yōkai Jepang, burung aneh dalam 「太平記」 yang konon berseru 「いつまで、いつまで」; tidak bernama dalam Taiheiki, tetapi Toriyama Sekien menamainya dari suara cuitnya dalam kumpulan gambarnya; juga disebut 「イツマデン」.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。「太平記」に記述のある怪鳥で、「いつまで、いつまで」と鳴くとされる。「太平記」においては名前はなかったが、江戸時代の画家、鳥山石燕が、自身の画集「今昔画図続百鬼」において、その鳴き声にちなみ命名した。「イツマデン」ともする。

claims.statement: English Wikipedia: Itsumade, alternatively Itsumaden, has been featured in various fantasy productions such as GeGeGe no Kitarō, Hell Teacher: Jigoku Sensei Nube, Garo, Nioh, Touhou Project, Fate/Grand Order, Z/X, Onmyōji and Phantom Beast Story.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Inggris: Itsumade, atau Itsumaden, muncul dalam berbagai karya fantasi seperti GeGeGe no Kitarō, Hell Teacher: Jigoku Sensei Nube, Garo, Nioh, Touhou Project, Fate/Grand Order, Z/X, Onmyōji, dan Phantom Beast Story.
claims.quote: Itsumade, alternatively as Itsumaden, has been featured in various fantasy productions such as GeGeGe no Kitarō, Hell Teacher: Jigoku Sensei Nube, Garo, Nioh, Touhou Project, Fate/Grand Order, Z/X, Onmyōji, and Phantom Beast Story.

claims.statement: Iwanagahime is a kami in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Iwanagahime adalah kami dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Iwanagahime is a kami in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: She is associated with immortality.
claims.statement_id: Ia dikaitkan dengan keabadian.
claims.quote: She is the goddess of immortality.

claims.statement: She is named as Ōyamatsumi’s daughter and Sakuyahime’s sister.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut sebagai putri Ōyamatsumi dan saudari Sakuyahime.
claims.quote: She is also the daughter of Ōyamatsumi, and sister to Sakuyahime.

claims.statement: One tale says Ninigi rejected her and sent her home.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kisah menyebut Ninigi menolaknya dan memulangkannya.
claims.quote: However Ninigi rejected Iwanagahime due to her ugliness and returned her to her father.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, the August Grandchild thought the elder sister ugly and would not take her.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, cucu agung (Ninigi) menganggap kakak perempuan itu buruk rupa dan tidak mau mengambilnya.
claims.quote: Now the August Grandchild thought the elder sister ugly, and would not take her.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, Iwanagahime, ashamed, cursed him, saying that had he taken her, his children would have been long-lived and enduring like massy rocks.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, Iwanagahime dalam rasa malunya mengutuk: andai ia diterima, anak-anak sang cucu agung akan berumur panjang dan kekal seperti batu karang.
claims.quote: If the August Grandchild had taken me and not rejected me, the children born to him would have been long-lived, and would have endured for ever like the massy rocks.

claims.statement: In one version recorded in the Nihongi she says that mankind will change swiftly like the flowers of the trees and pass away, which is given as the reason human life is short.
claims.statement_id: Dalam salah satu versi Nihongi, ia berkata bahwa umat manusia akan cepat berubah dan lenyap seperti bunga pepohonan; inilah sebab hidup manusia singkat.
claims.quote: The race of visible mankind shall change swiftly like the flowers of the trees, and shall decay and pass away.’ This is the reason why the life of man is so short.

claims.statement: The dictionary describes her as a deity of the Kiki (Kojiki and Nihon Shoki), daughter of Ōyamatsumi, offered with her younger sister to Ninigi but returned because of her ugliness.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menyebut ia dewi dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki, putri Ōyamatsumi, yang dipersembahkan bersama adiknya kepada Ninigi tetapi dikembalikan karena dianggap buruk rupa.
claims.quote: 記紀などに見える神。大山祇神(おおやまつみのかみ)の娘。妹の木花開耶姫(このはなのさくやびめ)とともに瓊瓊杵尊(ににぎのみこと)に献上されたが、醜いために返され

claims.statement: As a result the magical power of longevity entrusted to her is said to have been lost to Ninigi and the emperors after him; in later times she is worshipped among the people as a god of longevity.
claims.statement_id: Akibatnya, kuasa magis umur panjang yang dititipkan padanya dianggap hilang dari Ninigi dan para kaisar sesudahnya; pada masa kemudian ia dipuja rakyat sebagai dewi umur panjang.
claims.quote: その結果、磐長姫に託されていた長寿の呪力を瓊瓊杵尊以下の天皇は失ったとされる。後世、長寿の神として民間で信仰される。

claims.statement: The biographical dictionary explains that her name means a woman who, like rock, is eternally unchanging.
claims.statement_id: Kamus nama menjelaskan bahwa namanya berarti perempuan yang abadi tak berubah seperti batu.
claims.quote: 岩のように永久にかわらない女性を意味する。父の大山祇(おおやまつみの)神により妹の木花開耶(このはなさくや)姫とともに瓊瓊杵尊(ににぎのみこと)の妻としてさしだされたが

claims.statement: Her name is written 石長比売 in the Kojiki and 磐長姫 in the Nihon Shoki and Sendai Kuji Hongi; she is also called 苔牟須売神.
claims.statement_id: Namanya ditulis 石長比売 dalam Kojiki dan 磐長姫 dalam Nihon Shoki dan Sendai Kuji Hongi; ia juga disebut 苔牟須売神.
claims.quote: 『古事記』では石長比売、『日本書紀』・『先代旧事本紀』では磐長姫と表記する。他に苔牟須売神とも称される。

claims.statement: In the Kojiki account, Ōyamatsumi was angry and explained that Iwanagahime was offered so the heavenly grandchild would be eternal like rock, and that sending her back would shorten his life.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Kojiki, Ōyamatsumi marah dan menjelaskan bahwa Iwanagahime dipersembahkan agar sang cucu langit abadi seperti batu, dan karena ia dikembalikan, umur sang cucu langit akan menjadi pendek.
claims.quote: 大山津見神はそれを怒り、「石長比売を差し上げたのは天孫が岩のように永遠のものとなるように、木花之佐久夜毘売を差し上げたのは天孫が花のように繁栄するようにと誓約を立てたからである」ことを教え、石長比売を送り返したことで天孫の寿命が短くなるだろうと告げた。

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki also records that Iwanagahime cursed the pregnant Konohanasakuyahime, and gives this as the origin of the shortness of human life.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki juga mencatat bahwa Iwanagahime mengutuk Konohanasakuyahime yang hamil, dan menyebut itu asal-usul umur pendek manusia.
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』には、妊娠した木花開耶姫を石長比売が呪ったとも記され、それが人の短命の起源であるとしている。

claims.statement: She is regarded as representing the eternity of rock, and one theory holds that her name means a woman who, like rock, endures unchanging.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap melambangkan keabadian batu, dan ada teori bahwa namanya berarti perempuan yang kekal tak berubah seperti batu.
claims.quote: 石長比売は岩の永遠性を表すものとされ、名義は「岩のように長久に変わることのない女性」と考える説がある。

claims.statement: At the Yui no Yashiro auxiliary shrine of Kifune Shrine (Sakyō-ku, Kyoto) she is enshrined as a god of matchmaking.
claims.statement_id: Di sub-kuil Yui no Yashiro milik Kifune Shrine (Sakyō-ku, Kyoto) ia dipuja sebagai dewi jodoh.
claims.quote: 貴船神社（京都市左京区）の結社（ゆいのやしろ）では、縁結びの神として祀られている。

claims.statement: She is said to be enshrined at Kifune Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Ia dikatakan dipuja di Kifune Shrine.
claims.quote: She is said to be enshrined at Kifune Shrine.

claims.statement: Jubokko is a tree-like yōkai described in modern Japanese books.
claims.statement_id: Jubokko adalah yōkai mirip pohon yang digambarkan dalam buku Jepang modern.
claims.quote: is a yōkai tree in Japanese folklore that appears in many books related to Japanese yōkai

claims.statement: Stories place it on former battlefields.
claims.statement_id: Cerita tentangnya menempatkannya di bekas medan perang.
claims.quote: According to folklore, it appears in former battlefields where many people have died, and its appearance does not differ that much from ordinary trees.

claims.statement: In those stories its branches seize people and draw their blood.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita itu, dahannya menangkap manusia dan mengisap darahnya.
claims.quote: When a human being happens to pass by, it supposedly captures the victim and, changing its branches into the shape of a tube, sucks the blood out of the victim.

claims.statement: A group of experts (the To Gakkai) stated that there is no source of appearance for this yōkai tree and theorized that it is a fictional creature conceived by Shigeru Mizuki.
claims.statement_id: Sekelompok pakar (To Gakkai) menyatakan tidak ada sumber kemunculan yōkai pohon ini dan menduga ia makhluk rekaan yang digagas Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.quote: A group of experts from a group called To Scholar Conference (と学会, to gakkai), run by yōkai scholars Natsuhiko Kyogoku and Tada Natsumi, writer Murakami Kenji, and SF writer Yamamoto Hiroshi, stated that there is no source of appearance for this yōkai tree and that it can be theorized that this yōkai is a fictional creature conceived by Shigeru Mizuki.

claims.statement: According to Japanese Wikipedia, the first appearance of "jubokko" was in an article by Saitō Morihiro in the November 1966 issue of Bessatsu Shōjo Friend, and the yōkai is probably Saitō's own invention.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Jepang, kemunculan pertama "jubokko" adalah dalam artikel Saitō Morihiro di majalah Bessatsu Shōjo Friend edisi November 1966, dan makhluk ini kemungkinan ciptaan Saitō.
claims.quote: 斎藤守弘が『別冊少女フレンド』1966年11月号に掲載した記事「あなたのそばにいる日本の妖怪特集」（無記名）が「じゅぼっこ」の初出で、おそらく斎藤による創作の妖怪である。

claims.statement: Because that article kept being used in Mizuki's works, beginning with Nihon Yōkai Taizen (1968), the yōkai was thought to be Mizuki's creation before Saitō's article was rediscovered.
claims.statement_id: Artikel itu terus dipakai dalam karya Mizuki, mulai dari Nihon Yōkai Taizen (1968), sehingga sebelum artikel Saitō ditemukan kembali makhluk ini dikira ciptaan Mizuki.
claims.quote: この記事が『週刊少年マガジン増刊 日本妖怪大全』（1968年）をはじめとする水木の著作で使われつづけたため、斎藤の記事が再発見される以前は水木の創作物であると思われていた。

claims.statement: Jubokko (樹木子) is a tree yōkai described in books on Japanese yōkai, including those of Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.statement_id: Jubokko (樹木子) adalah yōkai berwujud pohon yang dicatat dalam buku-buku tentang yōkai Jepang, termasuk karya Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.quote: 樹木子（じゅぼっこ）は、水木しげるの著書を始めとする日本の妖怪関連の書籍に記述のある木の妖怪。

claims.statement: The dictionary describes it as a tree that turned into a yōkai after absorbing the blood of many dead on battlefields, said to seize people who approach and drink their blood; it is considered originally a creation of the manga artist Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menjelaskan jubokko sebagai pohon yang menjelma setelah menyerap banyak darah orang mati di medan perang dan dikatakan menangkap orang yang mendekat untuk mengisap darahnya; asalnya dianggap ciptaan komikus Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.quote: 戦地などで死者の血を大量に吸った樹木が化けたもので、近づいた人を捕え生き血を吸うとされる。もとは漫画家、水木しげるによる創作と考えられている。

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, folklore scholars such as Kunio Yanagita and Iwao Hino state in their works that there is no yōkai that became the origin of the Jubokko.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, sarjana folklor seperti Yanagita Kunio dan Hino Iwao menyatakan dalam karya mereka bahwa tidak ada yōkai yang menjadi asal-usul jubokko.
claims.quote: Folklore scholars such as Kunio Yanagita and Iwao Hino, who wrote works such as "Youkai Stories" and "Vocabulary of Changes in Japanese Youkai", respectively, state in written works about folklore yōkai that there is no yōkai that became the origin of the Jubokko.

claims.statement: Mizuki stated that he created around 30 yōkai in his comic GeGeGe no Kitaro but did not specify which ones were his original creations.
claims.statement_id: Mizuki menyatakan ia menciptakan sekitar 30 yōkai dalam komik GeGeGe no Kitaro, tetapi tidak menyebut yōkai mana saja yang ciptaannya.
claims.quote: Mizuki stated that he created around 30 different yōkai in his comic book GeGeGe no Kitaro, but he did not specify which among the yōkai described in his work were his original creations.

claims.statement: Blood is said to trickle out when a Jubokko is cut, and a branch is said to be able to heal and decontaminate an injured person.
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan darah menetes bila jubokko ditebang, dan dahannya dapat menyembuhkan serta menyucikan orang yang terluka.
claims.quote: When a Jubokko is cut, blood trickles out. It is said that a Jubokko branch could heal and decontaminate an injured person.

claims.statement: Keneō is an underworld oni beside the Sanzu River.
claims.statement_id: Keneō adalah oni dunia bawah di tepi Sungai Sanzu.
claims.quote: Keneō (懸衣翁) is a Japanese Oni who sits at the edge of the Sanzu River in the Buddhist underworld.

claims.statement: His name refers to an old man who hangs clothing.
claims.statement_id: Namanya merujuk pada kakek penggantung pakaian.
claims.quote: His name translates to clothes hanging old man.

claims.statement: He hangs clothing taken from dead souls by Datsue-ba on a riverside tree.
claims.statement_id: Ia menggantung pakaian yang diambil Datsue-ba dari arwah pada pohon di tepi sungai.
claims.quote: Once the adult soul arrives at the river Datsue-ba forces the sinners to take off their clothes, and Keneō hangs these clothes on a riverside branch that bends to reflect the gravity of the sins.

claims.statement: One account says he hangs a soul’s skin when no clothing is available.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menyebut ia menggantung kulit arwah yang tidak berpakaian.
claims.quote: If a soul arrives without clothes, Keneō flays the person's skin and hangs it from the tree instead.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Datsueba hands the clothing to her partner Keneō, who hangs it from a riverside tree; how far the branch bends measures the weight of each soul's sin and serves as evidence in the trials to come.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Datsueba menyerahkan pakaian kepada pasangannya, Keneō, yang menggantungnya di pohon tepi sungai; lengkungan dahan menjadi ukuran berat dosa setiap arwah dan dipakai sebagai bukti dalam pengadilan berikutnya.
claims.quote: Datsueba hands the clothing to her partner, Keneō, who hangs it from a tree by the riverside. The amount that the branch bends under the weight of the clothes serves as a measure of the weight of the sin each soul carries, and is used as evidence in the trials to come.

claims.statement: Yokai.com says Datsueba and Keneō also carry out some torture themselves, for example breaking the fingers of thieves.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut Datsueba dan Keneō juga menyiksa sendiri, misalnya mematahkan jari para pencuri.
claims.quote: Datsueba and Keneō perform a little bit of torture themselves, breaking the fingers of those guilty of theft, and so on.

claims.statement: They also roam the riverbank tormenting the souls of children too young to cross the river, who must wait for salvation to come to them.
claims.statement_id: Keduanya juga berkeliling di tepi sungai dan menyiksa arwah anak-anak yang terlalu muda untuk menyeberang dan harus menunggu keselamatan datang.
claims.quote: They also roam the banks of the river, tormenting the souls of children who are too young to cross the river and must wait for salvation to come to them instead.

claims.statement: The encyclopedia says that by the Sanzu River stands a great tree called Eryōju, under which an oni-formed old woman and old man, Datsue-ba and Keneō, take the dead's clothes and hang them on the tree; the branch hangs differently according to the weight of sins in life.
claims.statement_id: Ensiklopedia menyebut di tepi Sungai Sanzu ada pohon besar bernama Eryōju; di bawahnya ada nenek dan kakek berwujud oni, Datsue-ba dan Keneō. Sang nenek merampas pakaian arwah, sang kakek menerimanya dan menggantungnya di pohon, dan lengkung dahan berbeda menurut berat dosa semasa hidup.
claims.quote: 三途の川のほとりには衣領樹（えりようじゆ）という大樹があり，その下に奪衣婆（だつえば），懸衣翁（けんえおう）という鬼形の姥と翁がいて，姥は亡者の衣服を奪い取り，それを翁が受け取って衣領樹に掛ける。亡者の生前の罪の軽重によって枝の垂れ方が異なるという。

claims.statement: The encyclopedia states that the Sanzu River, taught together with the Mountain of Death, is not Buddhist doctrine but folk belief.
claims.statement_id: Ensiklopedia menyatakan bahwa ajaran tentang Sungai Sanzu, yang diajarkan bersama Gunung Shide, bukan ajaran Buddha melainkan kepercayaan populer.
claims.quote: 三途の川のことは，死出の山とともに説かれるが，仏説ではなく，俗説である。

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia says Keneō, together with Datsueba, serves under the Ten Kings (Jūō) and hangs the clothes Datsueba strips from the dead on a branch of the Eryōju tree to weigh their sins.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang menyebut Keneō, bersama Datsueba, berada di bawah Sepuluh Raja (Jūō) dan menggantung pakaian yang dilucuti Datsueba di dahan pohon Eryōju untuk menimbang dosa arwah.
claims.quote: 奪衣婆と共に十王の配下で、奪衣婆が亡者から剥ぎ取った衣類を衣領樹の枝にかけ、その枝の垂れ具合で亡者の生前の罪の重さを計るとされる。

claims.statement: Keneō (read けんえおう ken'eō or けんねおう kenneō) is an old-man yōkai said to be on the Eryōju tree by the Sanzu River of the afterlife, or beside Datsueba on the riverbank.
claims.statement_id: Keneō (dibaca ken'eō atau kenneō; けんえおう atau けんねおう) adalah yōkai lelaki tua yang dikatakan berada di atas pohon Eryōju di tepi Sungai Sanzu atau di samping Datsueba di tepi sungai.
claims.quote: 懸衣翁（けんえおう）または（けんねおう）とは、死後の世界の三途の川のほとりにある衣領樹（えりょうじゅ）という木の上、または川辺にいる奪衣婆の隣にいるといわれる老人の妖怪である。

claims.statement: In Japanese tradition when someone dies, 6 mon, an old form of currency, are placed with the body as payment to enter the underworld.
claims.statement_id: Dalam tradisi Jepang, saat seseorang meninggal, enam mon (mata uang lama) diletakkan bersama jenazah sebagai bayaran untuk memasuki dunia bawah.
claims.quote: In Japanese tradition when someone dies 6 mon, an old form of currency, are placed with the body to be used as payment to enter the underworld.

claims.statement: Kunado-no-Kami names protective local deities in Japan.
claims.statement_id: Kunado-no-Kami adalah sebutan dewa penjaga setempat di Jepang.
claims.quote: Kunado-no-Kami (Japanese: 岐の神), alternately Kunato-no-Kami, Funado-no-Kami, Funato-no-Kami, or Chimata-no-Kami, are Japanese local gods connected chiefly with protection against disaster and malicious spirits.

claims.statement: The name is linked to a phrase for a place that must not be entered.
claims.statement_id: Namanya dikaitkan dengan tempat yang tidak boleh dimasuki.
claims.quote: The term "Kunado-no-Kami" and its variants are derived ultimately from Japanese: 来な処 ku-na-do, meaning a place that is not to be entered, a taboo or sacred space.

claims.statement: These kami are believed to guard village boundaries from harmful spirits.
claims.statement_id: Para kami ini dipercaya menjaga batas desa dari roh berbahaya.
claims.quote: These kami are regarded as protecting the boundaries of a village and forestalling entry by malicious or harmful spirits and influences, thereby preventing disasters.

claims.statement: Some traditions extend their protection to roads and paths.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian tradisi memperluas penjagaannya hingga jalan dan lintasan.
claims.quote: In some cases the protection of these kami extends to roads and paths, in which capacity the variant name Chimata-no-Kami is particularly likely to be applied.

claims.statement: A common origin myth connects them with the fundoshi cast aside by Izanagi on his return from the underworld, as recorded in the Kojiki.
claims.statement_id: Mitos asal-usul yang umum mengaitkan mereka dengan cawat (fundoshi) yang dibuang Izanagi sekembalinya dari dunia bawah, seperti tercatat dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: A common origin myth connects them with the fundoshi cast aside by Izanagi upon his return from the underworld as recorded in the Kojiki.

claims.statement: In the Kojiki, when Izanagi returned from Yomi and performed purification, the Chimata-no-Kami was born from the loincloth he cast off; the Nihon Shoki and Kogo Shūi treat this deity as the same as Sarutahiko.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Kojiki, ketika Izanagi yang pulang dari Yomi melakukan penyucian, dewa jalan simpang (Chimata-no-Kami) lahir dari cawat yang ia lepaskan; Nihon Shoki dan Kogo Shūi menyamakan dewa ini dengan Sarutahiko.
claims.quote: 神話では、『古事記』の神産みの段において、黄泉から帰還したイザナギが禊をする際、脱ぎ捨てた褌から道俣神（ちまたのかみ）が化生したとしている。この神は、『日本書紀』や『古語拾遺』ではサルタヒコと同神としている。

claims.statement: In the Nihon Shoki, at Yomotsu Hirasaka, Izanagi fleeing Izanami threw a staff saying "do not come any further", and Kunato-no-Sae-no-Kami was born from it.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihon Shoki, di Yomotsu Hirasaka, Izanagi yang lari dari Izanami melempar tongkat sambil berkata "jangan datang lebih jauh dari ini", dan dari tongkat itu lahir Kunato-no-Sae-no-Kami.
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』では、黄泉津平坂（よもつひらさか）で、イザナミから逃げるイザナギが「これ以上は来るな」と言って投げた杖から来名戸祖神（くなとのさえのかみ）が化生したとしている。

claims.statement: In the Kojiki, the deity born from the first thrown staff is called Tsukitatsu-Funado-no-Kami.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Kojiki, dewa yang lahir dari tongkat yang pertama dilempar disebut Tsukitatsu-Funado-no-Kami.
claims.quote: これは『古事記』では、最初に投げた杖から化生した神を衝立船戸神（つきたつふなどのかみ）としている。

claims.statement: "Kunado" means "a place one must not come to"; originally a deity at road forks, mountain passes or village boundaries who kept out outside enemies and evil spirits, regarded as one of the prototypes of the Dōsojin.
claims.statement_id: "Kunado" berarti "tempat yang tidak boleh didatangi"; semula dewa di persimpangan jalan, celah gunung atau batas desa yang menghalangi musuh dan roh jahat dari luar, dan dianggap salah satu bentuk awal Dōsojin.
claims.quote: 「くなど」は「来な処」すなわち「きてはならない所」の意味。もとは、道の分岐点、峠、あるいは村境などで、外からの外敵や悪霊の侵入をふせぐ神であり、道祖神の原型の１つとされる。

claims.statement: It is called by many other names, including 久那土神, 久那止神, 久那戸神, 車戸神, 来名戸祖神, 岐神, 衝立船戸神 and 車戸大明神.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut dengan banyak nama lain, antara lain 久那土神, 久那止神, 久那戸神, 車戸神, 来名戸祖神, 岐神, 衝立船戸神, dan 車戸大明神.
claims.quote: 別称として、久那土神、久那止神、久那戸神、久那斗神、車戸神、来名戸祖神、岐神、衝立船戸神、車戸大明神、久那度神、クナド大神、クナトの神、クナト大神、熊野大神、久刀、車戸、輦止、熊野などと呼ばれる例がある。

claims.statement: Since ancient times it has been worshipped as a protector of cattle and horses and a god of fertility, and also as a god of purification, warding off evil and safe travel.
claims.statement_id: Sejak dahulu ia dipuja sebagai dewa pelindung sapi dan kuda serta kesuburan, dan juga sebagai dewa penyucian, penolak bala, dan keselamatan perjalanan.
claims.quote: 古より牛馬守護の神、豊穣の神としてはもとより、禊、魔除け、厄除け、道中安全の神として信仰されている。

claims.statement: The dictionary describes a deity enshrined at road forks, believed to prevent the entry of evil spirits and to protect travelers.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menjelaskan ia dewa yang dipuja di persimpangan jalan, dipercaya mencegah masuknya roh jahat dan melindungi para pelancong.
claims.quote: 道の分岐点などに祭られる神。邪霊の侵入を防ぎ、旅人を守護すると信じられた。

claims.statement: The Heibonsha encyclopedia lists Funado-gami among the names of the folk deity Dōsojin (also Sae-no-Kami and Dōrokujin), placed at village boundaries to block or repel evil spirits, demons and plague gods from outside.
claims.statement_id: Ensiklopedia Heibonsha menyebut Funado-gami sebagai salah satu nama dewa rakyat Dōsojin (juga Sae-no-Kami dan Dōrokujin), yang ditempatkan di batas desa untuk menghalangi roh jahat, setan, dan dewa wabah dari luar.
claims.quote: サエノカミ(塞の神)，ドウロクジン(道陸神)，フナドガミ(岐神)などとも呼ばれ，村の境域に置かれて外部から侵入する邪霊，悪鬼，疫神などをさえぎったり，はねかえそうとする民俗神である。

claims.statement: Mazoku is a broad Japanese term for supernatural beings often portrayed as malign.
claims.statement_id: Mazoku adalah istilah luas dalam bahasa Jepang bagi makhluk gaib yang sering dianggap jahat.
claims.quote: In Japanese mythology and fantasy, mazoku (魔族) are supernatural beings, normally evil ones such as devils or demons.

claims.statement: A maō is described as a ruler of such beings.
claims.statement_id: Maō digambarkan sebagai penguasa kelompok tersebut.
claims.quote: A maō (魔王) or maou is a ruler of mazoku, or in fiction more generically a dark lord or powerful monster.

claims.statement: The term "mazoku" was used to describe the asura and yaksha of Hindu mythology and the daeva of Zoroastrianism.
claims.statement_id: Istilah "mazoku" pernah dipakai untuk menyebut asura dan yaksha dalam mitologi Hindu serta daeva dalam Zoroastrianisme.
claims.quote: The term "mazoku" was used to describe the asura and yaksha in Hindu mythology, as well as Zoroastrianism's daeva.

claims.statement: It is a general term for devils, demons and evil beings.
claims.statement_id: Istilah ini merupakan sebutan umum bagi iblis, setan, dan makhluk jahat.
claims.quote: It is a general term for devils, demons and evil beings.

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, "ma" (魔, devil) suggests a threat to human existence or defiance of the gods, while "-zoku" (族, kin, clan, family) indicates a family.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, "ma" (魔, iblis) menyiratkan ancaman bagi keberadaan manusia atau pembangkangan terhadap dewa, sedangkan "-zoku" (族) menunjukkan kekerabatan atau keluarga.
claims.quote: The name ma (魔 – devil) suggests that they are meant to threaten human existence or defy the gods, while -zoku (族 – kin, clan, family) indicates that they are a family.

claims.statement: In Japanese polytheism, mazoku is an antonym of 神族 (shinzoku), "the kin of gods".
claims.statement_id: Dalam politeisme Jepang, mazoku adalah lawan kata 神族 (shinzoku), "kerabat para dewa".
claims.quote: In Japanese polytheism, it is an antonym of 神族 (shinzoku), "the kin of gods".

claims.statement: According to Japanese Wikipedia, the word "mazoku" is not listed in Japanese dictionaries, but books on myths and legends sometimes use it for beings hostile to gods or harmful to humans, chiefly the asura of Indian mythology and the daeva of Zoroastrianism.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Jepang, kata "mazoku" tidak tercantum dalam kamus bahasa Jepang, tetapi buku tentang mitos dan legenda kadang memakainya untuk makhluk yang memusuhi dewa atau merugikan manusia, terutama asura dalam mitologi India dan daeva dalam Zoroastrianisme.
claims.quote: 「魔族」という語は国語辞典には載っていないが、神話・伝説について解説した書籍などにおいて、神と敵対する、または人間に害をなす存在を「魔族」と呼ぶ場合があり、おもにインド神話のアスラ、ゾロアスター教のダエーワなどがこう呼ばれる。

claims.statement: The book Shitte Okitai Densetsu no Mazoku, Yōzoku, Shinzoku (Seibidō, 2009), supervised by Takebe Nobuaki, calls it "in a sense close to a coined word" rather than an official term, and explains that it spread through use in games and manga.
claims.statement_id: Buku Shiratteokitai Densetsu no Mazoku, Yōzoku, Shinzoku (Seibidō, 2009) yang disupervisi Takebe Nobuaki menyebutnya "dalam arti tertentu mendekati istilah rekaan" ketimbang istilah resmi, dan menjelaskan bahwa kata ini menyebar karena dipakai dalam gim dan manga.
claims.quote: 健部伸明監修『知っておきたい伝説の魔族・妖族・神族』（西東社、2009年（平成21年））では、正式な用語というよりは「ある意味では造語に近い」としており、実情としてはゲームや漫画などで使用されて広まったものと解説している。

claims.statement: In works of fantasy fiction the definition of mazoku varies: sometimes it is a general term for races hostile to humans and benevolent gods (devils, yōkai, monsters), sometimes it refers to one specific race.
claims.statement_id: Dalam karya fiksi fantasi, definisi mazoku berbeda-beda: kadang dipakai sebagai sebutan umum bagi ras yang memusuhi manusia dan dewa baik (iblis, yōkai, monster), kadang untuk satu ras tertentu.
claims.quote: 魔族の定義は作品によって様々であり、人間や善神（神族）に敵対する種族（悪魔、妖怪、怪物など）の総称として用いられる場合もあれば、特定の一種族を指して言う場合もある。

claims.statement: The dictionary defines maō in the Buddhist sense as the king of the 天魔 (heavenly demons) who lives in the sixth heaven (第六他化自在天) at the summit of the realm of desire, always harming the true Dharma and obstructing beings from entering the Buddhist path.
claims.statement_id: Kamus mendefinisikan maō dalam arti Buddhis sebagai raja 天魔 (iblis langit), tinggal di surga keenam (第六他化自在天) di puncak alam keinginan, yang selalu merusak ajaran yang benar dan menghalangi makhluk memasuki jalan Buddha.
claims.quote: 天魔の王。欲界の頂にある第六他化自在天に住し、常に正法を害し衆生が仏道にはいるのを妨げる者。

claims.statement: In an extended sense, maō means a demon that brings misfortune to people or lures them onto an evil path; it is also used to revile a person; a devil.
claims.statement_id: Dalam arti turunan, maō berarti makhluk jahat yang mendatangkan malapetaka atau menjerumuskan orang ke jalan jahat; juga dipakai untuk mengumpat orang; setan.
claims.quote: 転じて、人に災いを与えたり悪の道に誘い込んだりする魔物。また、人をののしっていう。悪魔。

claims.statement: Mikoshi-nyūdō is a long-necked yōkai resembling a bald monk.
claims.statement_id: Mikoshi-nyūdō adalah yōkai botak mirip biksu dengan leher yang memanjang.
claims.quote: Mikoshi-nyūdō (見越し入道 or 見越入道) is a type of bald-headed yōkai "goblin" with an ever-extending neck.

claims.statement: Edo-period ghost tales describe it startling people.
claims.statement_id: Kisah hantu zaman Edo menggambarkannya menakuti orang.
claims.quote: In Japanese folklore and Edo period (1603–1868) kaidan "ghost story" texts, mikoshi-nyūdō will frighten people who look over the top of things such as byōbu folding screens.

claims.statement: Some accounts place its sudden appearance on roads at night.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa cerita menempatkan kemunculannya mendadak di jalan malam.
claims.quote: When walking to the end of a road at night or a hill road, something the shape of a monk would suddenly appear, and if one looks up, it becomes taller the further one looks up.

claims.statement: In some stories looking up at it can endanger a traveler.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebagian kisah, menengadah kepadanya dapat membahayakan pejalan.
claims.quote: It is said that getting flown over by a mikoshi-nyūdō results in death or getting strangled by the throat, and if one falls back due to looking up at the nyūdō, one's windpipe would get gnawed at and killed.

claims.statement: The name combines mikoshi 見越し ("see over"; looking over the top of a fence, anticipation) and nyūdō 入道 ("enter the Way"; a Buddhist priest or a tonsured monster).
claims.statement_id: Nama ini menggabungkan mikoshi 見越し ("melihat ke seberang"; mengintip dari atas pagar, antisipasi) dan nyūdō 入道 ("memasuki Jalan"; pendeta Buddha atau makhluk gundul).
claims.quote: The name combines mikoshi 見越し (lit. "see over") "looking over the top (of a fence); anticipation; expectation" and nyūdō 入道 (lit. "enter the Way") "a (Buddhist) priest; a bonze; a tonsured monster".

claims.statement: It is said it can be made to disappear by saying "mikoshita" ("I've seen past you").
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan makhluk ini dapat dibuat lenyap dengan mengucapkan "mikoshita" ("aku sudah melihat melewatimu").
claims.quote: but they can be made to disappear by saying "mikoshita (見こした, I've seen past you)."

claims.statement: The true identity of the mikoshi-nyūdō is often unclear, but in some regions it is an animal that can transform.
claims.statement_id: Wujud asli mikoshi-nyūdō sering tidak jelas, tetapi di beberapa daerah ia dianggap hewan yang dapat berubah wujud.
claims.quote: There are many where the true identity of mikoshi-nyūdō is unclear, but there are regions where they are animals that possess the ability to transform.

claims.statement: In the Tonoigusa it is a shapeshifted tanuki; in some regions a fox (kitsune), and in Shinano Province (now Nagano Prefecture) a mujina.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Tonoigusa ia adalah tanuki yang berubah wujud; di beberapa daerah rubah (kitsune), dan di Provinsi Shinano (kini Prefektur Nagano) mujina.
claims.quote: In the "Tonoigusa," they are shapeshifted tanuki, and there are also some regions where they are shapeshifted foxes (kitsune). In the Shinano Province (now Nagano Prefecture), they are said to be shapeshifted mujina.

claims.statement: In the Edo-period essay Enka Kidan by Hakuchō Nishimura, the mikoshi-nyūdō is a yakubyōgami (plague deity) that afflicts people with fever.
claims.statement_id: Dalam esai zaman Edo Enka Kidan karya Hakuchō Nishimura, mikoshi-nyūdō adalah yakubyōgami (dewa wabah) yang menjangkitkan demam pada orang.
claims.quote: In the essay Enka Kidan (煙霞綺談) by Hakuchō Nishimura from the Edo period, the mikoshi-nyūdō is a yakubyōgami that inflicts people with fever

claims.statement: The length of its neck was exaggerated over the eras, and by the late Edo period it became standard for the neck to be long and thin and the face to have three eyes.
claims.statement_id: Panjang lehernya dilebih-lebihkan dari zaman ke zaman; pada akhir zaman Edo menjadi baku bahwa lehernya panjang dan kurus serta wajahnya bermata tiga.
claims.quote: The length of its neck has been exaggerated over the passage of eras, and in the late Edo period, it has become standard for its neck to be long and thin, and for its face to have three eyes.

claims.statement: The dictionary describes a long-necked, tall yōkai in the form of a nyūdō, carrying an iron rod and the like, that grows taller and its neck longer the more a person looks up.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menggambarkannya sebagai yōkai berwujud nyūdō berleher panjang dan bertubuh tinggi yang membawa tongkat besi dan sebagainya; semakin orang menengadah, semakin tinggi tubuhnya dan semakin panjang lehernya.
claims.quote: 首が長く、背の高い入道姿で、金棒などを持っている妖怪。人が見上げれば見上げるほど背が高くなり、また首が長くなるという。

claims.statement: The dictionary calls it a yōkai that appears on roads and is said to grow as the person raises their eyes; handed down in the Chūgoku region, with similar yōkai such as the miage-nyūdō, shidaidaka, taka-nyūdō and nyūdō-bōzu.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menyebutnya yōkai yang muncul di jalan dan dikatakan membesar seiring orang mengangkat pandangan; diwariskan di wilayah Chūgoku, dengan yōkai serupa seperti miage-nyūdō, shidaidaka, taka-nyūdō, dan nyūdō-bōzu.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。路上に現れ、出会ったものが目線を上げるほど巨大化するとされる。中国地方に伝わる。類似した特徴のものに「見上げ入道」「次第高」「高入道」「入道坊主」などがある。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the only escape is to anticipate the mikoshi nyūdō (hence its name): meet it eye to eye and show no fear.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, satu-satunya jalan lolos adalah mengantisipasi mikoshi nyūdō (dari situlah namanya): hadapi ia mata ke mata dan jangan menunjukkan rasa takut.
claims.quote: The only possible escape is to anticipate the mikoshi nyūdō (thus its name). Meet it face-to-face, eye-to-eye, and show no fear.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, mikoshi nyūdō is a popular form for some shape-shifting animals; in particular itachi and tanuki transform into these giants to hunt humans.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, mikoshi nyūdō adalah wujud yang populer bagi beberapa hewan penjelma; terutama itachi (musang) dan tanuki berubah menjadi raksasa ini untuk memburu manusia.
claims.quote: Mikoshi nyūdō is a popular form of some shape-shifting animals. In particular, itachi and tanuki transform into these giants in order to hunt humans.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia says the mikoshi-nyūdō appears in Edo-period kaidan books and essays such as Tonoigusa, Enka Kidan and Kokon Hyakumonogatari Hyōban, and in folklore materials from across Japan.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang menyebut mikoshi-nyūdō terlihat dalam buku kaidan dan esai zaman Edo seperti Tonoigusa, Enka Kidan, dan Kokon Hyakumonogatari Hyōban, serta dalam bahan folklor di berbagai daerah Jepang.
claims.quote: 見越し入道、見越入道（みこしにゅうどう）とは、日本の妖怪のひとつ。『宿直草』『煙霞奇談』『古今百物語評判』などの江戸時代の怪談本や随筆、及び日本各地の民俗資料に見られる。

claims.statement: Some think it is related to the rokurokubi, and since legendary rokurokubi are often female, it is sometimes pointed out as an example of a male rokurokubi.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian orang menganggapnya berkaitan dengan rokurokubi, dan karena rokurokubi dalam legenda sering perempuan, ia kadang disebut contoh rokurokubi lelaki.
claims.quote: There are those who think that they are related to the rokurokubi, and since the rokurokubi of legends are frequently female, they are sometimes pointed out as examples of male rokurokubi.

claims.statement: Saleos is also called Sallos in demonological writing.
claims.statement_id: Saleos juga disebut Sallos dalam tulisan demonologi.
claims.quote: サロス（Sallos）、ザレオス（Zaleos）またはザエボス（Zaebos）とも呼ばれる。

claims.statement: The Goetia calls him the nineteenth spirit and a duke.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menyebutnya roh ke-19 dengan gelar adipati.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の30の軍団を率いる序列19番の偉大にして強力な公爵。

claims.statement: He appears as a crowned soldier riding a crocodile.
claims.statement_id: Ia tampil sebagai prajurit bermahkota yang menunggangi buaya.
claims.quote: 公爵の宝冠をかぶり、ワニに乗った雄々しい兵士の姿で現れるが、その立ち振る舞いは穏和である。

claims.statement: The Goetia associates him with creating affection between men and women.
claims.statement_id: Goetia mengaitkannya dengan timbulnya cinta antara pria dan wanita.
claims.quote: 公爵の宝冠をかぶり、ワニに乗った雄々しい兵士の姿で現れるが、その立ち振る舞いは穏和である。 ... 男女間に愛情を芽生えさせることができる。

claims.statement: In the Goetia text the nineteenth spirit is Sallos (or Saleos), a great and mighty duke who appears as a gallant soldier riding a crocodile, wearing a ducal crown, and comes peaceably.
claims.statement_id: Dalam teks Goetia, roh ke-19 adalah Sallos (atau Saleos), seorang adipati agung dan perkasa yang tampil sebagai prajurit gagah berkuda buaya, bermahkota adipati, dan datang dengan damai.
claims.quote: The Nineteenth Spirit is Sallos (or Saleos). He is a Great and Mighty Duke, and appeareth in the form of a gallant Soldier riding on a Crocodile, with a Ducal Crown on his head, but peaceably.

claims.statement: He causes the love of women for men and of men for women, and governs 30 legions of spirits.
claims.statement_id: Ia menimbulkan cinta wanita kepada pria dan pria kepada wanita, dan memimpin 30 legiun roh.
claims.quote: He causeth the Love of Women to Men, and of Men to Women; and governeth 30 Legions of Spirits.

claims.statement: Wikipedia calls Saleos (also Sallos, Zaleos) a mighty Great Duke of Hell ruling 30 legions of demons, and a Great Earl according to Johann Weyer.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia menyebut Saleos (juga Sallos, Zaleos) sebagai Adipati Agung Neraka yang perkasa dan memimpin 30 legiun iblis; menurut Johann Weyer ia seorang Earl Agung.
claims.quote: Saleos (also Sallos, Zaleos) is a mighty Great Duke (a Great Earl according to Johann Weyer) of Hell, ruling 30 legions of demons

claims.statement: Wikipedia describes Saleos as being of a pacifist nature, causing men to love women and women to love men.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia menggambarkan Saleos berwatak pasifis, dan ia membuat pria mencintai wanita dan wanita mencintai pria.
claims.quote: He is of a pacifist nature, and causes men to love women and women to love men.

claims.statement: Yomotsu-shikome is an underworld woman in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Yomotsu-shikome adalah perempuan dunia bawah dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: in Japanese mythology, was a hag sent by the dead Izanami to pursue her husband Izanagi

claims.statement: She appears in the Kojiki account of Izanagi’s escape.
claims.statement_id: Ia muncul dalam kisah pelarian Izanagi dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: The hag appears by the Yomotsu-shikome (or Ugly-Female-of-the-Underworld") name in the eldest Japanese chronicle Kojiki.

claims.statement: In that story she pursues Izanagi out of the underworld.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu ia mengejar Izanagi keluar dari dunia bawah.
claims.quote: Kojiki version Izanagi was fleeing the Underworld with Yomotsu-shikome in hot pursuit.

claims.statement: Izanagi first cast down his black headdress, which turned into a kind of grapes and slowed the hag's advance as she devoured them.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi pertama-tama menjatuhkan penutup kepala hitamnya, yang berubah menjadi sejenis anggur dan memperlambat laju sang nenek sihir yang melahapnya.
claims.quote: Izanagi first cast down his black headdress, which turned into a kind of grapes and slowed the hag's advance as she devoured them.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, shikome is a broad term for kijo, or female oni, who look like ugly human women and often have beast-like features such as claws, paws, pointed ears or patches of furry hair.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, shikome adalah istilah luas untuk kijo, yakni oni perempuan yang berwujud perempuan manusia yang buruk rupa, dan sering berciri binatang seperti cakar, telapak, telinga runcing, atau bercak bulu.
claims.quote: Shikome is a broad term describing kijo, or female oni, who look like ugly human women. In addition to being ugly, they often have beast-like features such as claws, paws, pointed ears, or patches of furry hair.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, shikome are attendants of the land of the dead and quite dangerous; they are very fast, able to leap one thousand ri (about four thousand kilometres) in a single bound.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, shikome adalah pelayan negeri orang mati, cukup berbahaya, dan sangat cepat: mampu melompat seribu ri (sekitar empat ribu kilometer) dalam satu lompatan.
claims.quote: Shikome are attendants of the land of the dead, and are quite dangerous. They are fast, able to leap one thousand ri (approximately four thousand kilometers) in a single bound.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, shikome are also ravenous and can devour food at an incredible speed.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, shikome juga sangat rakus dan dapat melahap makanan dengan kecepatan luar biasa.
claims.quote: They are also ravenous, and can devour food at an incredible speed.

claims.statement: In the story as told by Yokai.com, Izanami ordered her servants, the yomotsu shikome, to catch Izanagi; as they closed in, Izanagi threw down his woven headdress, which turned into a vine of grapes.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah menurut Yokai.com, Izanami memerintahkan para pelayannya, yomotsu shikome, menangkap Izanagi; ketika mereka mendekat, Izanagi melempar penutup kepala anyaman yang berubah menjadi rambatan anggur.
claims.quote: Izanami ordered her servants, the yomotsu shikome, to catch Izanagi. The shikome were incredibly fast. As they closed in, Izanagi threw his woven headdress to the floor. It transformed into a vine of grapes.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Izanagi broke the teeth off his comb and scattered them; they turned into bamboo shoots, which the shikome also devoured, buying him a little more time.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Izanagi mematahkan gigi sisirnya dan menebarkannya; gigi itu menjadi rebung, yang juga dilahap para shikome sehingga ia mendapat sedikit waktu lagi.
claims.quote: Izanagi broke the teeth off of his comb and scattered them. They turned into bamboo shoots. The shikome devoured these too, buying him just a little more time.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Izanagi finally escaped to the surface and rolled a large boulder over the entrance to Yomi, trapping the shikome and his furious wife in the underworld forever.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Izanagi akhirnya lolos ke permukaan dan menggulingkan batu besar menutup pintu masuk Yomi, memerangkap para shikome dan istrinya yang murka di dunia bawah selamanya.
claims.quote: At last, he was able to escape to the surface. He rolled a large boulder over the entrance to Yomi, trapping the shikome and his furious wife in the underworld forever.

claims.statement: Yokai.com gives 醜女 (しこめ) with the translation "ugly woman", the alternate name yomotsu shikome, and Yomi, the Shintō underworld, as habitat.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis 醜女 (しこめ) dengan terjemahan "perempuan buruk rupa", nama lain yomotsu shikome, dan habitat Yomi, dunia bawah Shinto.
claims.quote: Shikome 醜女 しこめ Translation: ugly woman Alternate names: yomotsu shikome ("ugly woman from hell") Habitat: Yomi (the Shintō underworld)

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, early shikome illustrations served as the basis for many yōkai satirizing unattractive women, such as ao nyōbo, taka onna and kerakera onna.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ilustrasi shikome awal menjadi dasar bagi banyak yōkai yang menyindir perempuan tidak menarik, seperti ao nyōbo, taka onna, dan kerakera onna.
claims.quote: Early shikome illustrations have served as the basis for a great number of yōkai which satirize unattractive women, such as ao nyōbo, taka onna, and kerakera onna.

claims.statement: Wikipedia records the alternative name Yomotsu-hisame and says the name may have been a collective term for eight hags, not just one.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat nama lain Yomotsu-hisame, dan menyebut nama ini mungkin istilah kolektif untuk delapan nenek sihir, bukan satu.
claims.quote: Also recorded by the name Yomotsu-hisame (泉津日狭女 ), the name may have been a term referring collectively to eight hags, not just one.

claims.statement: According to the Nihon Shoki, it was either eight demon-hags (female oni) or a woman or women named Yomotsu-hisame who hunted after Izanagi.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nihon Shoki, yang memburu Izanagi adalah delapan nenek iblis (oni perempuan) atau perempuan bernama Yomotsu-hisame.
claims.quote: But either eight demon-hags (female oni) or a woman/women named Yomotsu-hisame hunted after Izanagi according to the Nihon Shoki

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, Izanagi brandished his sword Totsuka-no-Tsurugi but the pursuers kept on, until he climbed the "flat slope" at the entrance to the Underworld and flung three peaches, whereupon the pursuers retreated.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, Izanagi mengayunkan pedang Totsuka-no-Tsurugi tetapi pengejar tetap mengejar, hingga ia mendaki "lereng datar" di pintu masuk Dunia Bawah dan melempar tiga buah persik, sehingga para pengejar mundur.
claims.quote: Izanagi brandished his Totsuka-no-Tsurugi (十拳剣 ) but still they pursued, until he climbed atop the "flat slope" or "Even Pass" at the entrance to the Underworld, and flung three peaches, whereby the pursuers retreated.

claims.statement: The Digital Daijisen defines 黄泉醜女 (yomotsu-shikome) as a female oni in the land of Yomi.
claims.statement_id: Digital Daijisen mendefinisikan 黄泉醜女 (yomotsu-shikome) sebagai oni perempuan yang berada di negeri Yomi.
claims.quote: よも-つ-しこめ【黄=泉▽醜女】 黄泉 よみ の国にいる鬼女。 「すなはち-を遣はして追はしめき」〈記・上〉

claims.statement: Sitri is a demon named in Japanese demonological writing.
claims.statement_id: Sitri adalah iblis yang disebut dalam tulisan demonologi Jepang.
claims.quote: シトリー(Sitri)は、悪魔学における悪魔の一人。 ... 別名にビトル(Bitru)、シュトリ(Sytry)がある。

claims.statement: The Goetia ranks him as its twelfth spirit and a prince.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menempatkannya sebagai roh ke-12 dengan gelar pangeran.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると72人の魔神の一人で、60の軍団を支配し、序列12番の地獄の偉大なる君主である。

claims.statement: He is pictured with a leopard head and griffin wings.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan berkepala macan tutul dan bersayap griffin.
claims.quote: He is depicted with the face of a leopard and the wings of a griffin, but under the conjurer's request he changes into a very beautiful man.

claims.statement: At the conjurer's request he changes into a very beautiful man.
claims.statement_id: Atas permintaan sang pemanggil, ia berubah menjadi pria yang sangat rupawan.
claims.quote: under the conjurer's request he changes into a very beautiful man.

claims.statement: In the Goetia text the twelfth spirit is Sitri, a great prince who first appears with a leopard's head and a gryphon's wings, then at the command of the Master of the Exorcism takes human shape, a very beautiful one.
claims.statement_id: Dalam teks Goetia, roh ke-12 adalah Sitri, seorang pangeran agung yang mula-mula tampil berkepala macan tutul dan bersayap griffin, lalu atas perintah sang pemanggil mengambil wujud manusia yang sangat rupawan.
claims.quote: The Twelfth Spirit is Sitri. He is a Great Prince and appeareth at first with a Leopard's head and the Wings of a Gryphon, but after the command of the Master of the Exorcism he putteth on Human shape, and that very beautiful.

claims.statement: He inflames men with love for women and women with love for men, and also makes them show themselves naked if desired; he governs 60 legions of spirits.
claims.statement_id: Ia membangkitkan cinta pria kepada wanita dan wanita kepada pria, dan juga membuat mereka menampakkan diri tanpa busana bila dikehendaki; ia memimpin 60 legiun roh.
claims.quote: He enflameth men with Women's love, and Women with Men's love; and causeth them also to show themselves naked if it be desired. He governeth 60 Legions of Spirits.

claims.statement: Wikipedia lists other spellings of Sitri (Bitru, Sytry, Sytri) and calls him a Great Prince of Hell reigning over 60 legions of demons.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat ejaan lain Sitri: Bitru, Sytry, dan Sytri; ia disebut Pangeran Agung Neraka yang memerintah 60 legiun iblis.
claims.quote: Sitri (also Bitru, Sytry, Sytri) is a Great Prince of Hell, and reigns over 60 legions of demons.

claims.statement: Sumiyoshi sanjin names a group of three Japanese kami.
claims.statement_id: Sumiyoshi sanjin adalah sebutan bagi tiga kami Jepang.
claims.quote: Sumiyoshi sanjin (住吉三神) is the generic name for the three kami (deities) in Japan: Sokotsutsu no O (底筒男命), Nakatsutsu no O (中筒男命), and Uwatsutsu no O (表筒男).

claims.statement: They are associated with the sea and navigation.
claims.statement_id: Mereka dikaitkan dengan laut dan pelayaran.
claims.quote: The Sumiyoshi sanjin are regarded as the gods of the sea and sailing.

claims.statement: Sumiyoshi-taisha has shrines for them and for Empress Jingū.
claims.statement_id: Sumiyoshi-taisha memiliki bangunan pemujaan bagi mereka dan Permaisuri Jingū.
claims.quote: Sumiyoshi-taisha has four buildings dedicated to four kami: the three Sumiyoshi brothers and Empress Jingū, who is also enshrined.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki give a myth about their birth.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki memuat kisah tentang kelahiran mereka.
claims.quote: According to Japanese mythology recorded in works like the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, the Sumiyoshi sanjin were born together with the three Watatsumi deities (綿津見三神) when Izanagi performed a misogi after returning from Yomi.

claims.statement: According to Sumiyoshi Taisha, the shrine's deities are the three kami Sokotsutsu no O, Nakatsutsu no O and Uwatsutsu no O, who emerged from the sea when Izanagi performed misogi-harai, together with Empress Jingū, who is enshrined there.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Sumiyoshi Taisha, dewa yang dipuja di sana adalah tiga kami Sokotsutsu no O, Nakatsutsu no O, dan Uwatsutsu no O yang muncul dari laut ketika Izanagi melakukan misogi harai, serta Permaisuri Jingū yang dipuja di kuil itu.
claims.quote: 住吉大社の祭神は、伊弉諾尊が禊祓を行われた際に海中より出現された底筒男命・中筒男命・表筒男命の三神、そして当社鎮斎の神功皇后を祭神とします。

claims.statement: Sumiyoshi Taisha states that the deities are revered as guardians of voyages, as exemplified by the missions to Sui and Tang China; in the dynastic era they were also worshipped as gods of waka poetry and literature and as gods who appear in person, and are honoured as ancestral deities of purification, industry, trade and diplomacy.
claims.statement_id: Sumiyoshi Taisha menyatakan para dewa ini dipuja sebagai pelindung pelayaran, sebagaimana tampak pada utusan ke Sui dan Tang; pada masa kekaisaran juga dipuja sebagai dewa puisi waka dan sastra, serta dewa yang menampakkan diri secara nyata, dan dihormati sebagai dewa leluhur penyucian, industri, perdagangan, dan diplomasi.
claims.quote: 遣隋使・遣唐使に代表される航海の守護神として崇敬をあつめ、また、王朝時代には和歌・文学の神として、あるいは現実に姿を現される神としての信仰もあり、禊祓・産業・貿易・外交の祖神と仰がれています。

claims.statement: According to the tradition from the Nihon Shoki and Kojiki as explained by the shrine, when Izanagi went into the sea to purify himself by misogi, Sokotsutsu no O, Nakatsutsu no O and Uwatsutsu no O, the great kami of Sumiyoshi, were born.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi yang dicatat dalam Nihon Shoki dan Kojiki sebagaimana dijelaskan kuil, ketika Izanagi masuk ke laut untuk misogi membersihkan kenajisan, lahirlah Sokotsutsu no O, Nakatsutsu no O, dan Uwatsutsu no O, yaitu Sumiyoshi Ōkami.
claims.quote: 「日本書紀」や「古事記」の神代の巻での言い伝え ... そのケガレを清めるために海に入って禊祓いしたとき、住吉大神である底筒男命 (そこつつのおのみこと) 、中筒男命 (なかつつのおのみこと) 、表筒男命 (うわつつのおのみこと) が生まれました。

claims.statement: According to the shrine, Empress Jingū subdued powerful Silla with the protection of Sumiyoshi Ōkami and returned safely; on the triumphal return, by the deity's oracle, the deity was enshrined at the present site of Sumiyoshi.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kuil, Permaisuri Jingū menaklukkan Silla yang kuat dengan perlindungan Sumiyoshi Ōkami dan pulang dengan selamat; dalam perjalanan pulang itu, atas wahyu sang dewa, beliau memuliakan dewa tersebut di tempat Sumiyoshi yang sekarang.
claims.quote: 神功皇后は、住吉大神の加護を得て強大な新羅を平定せられ無事帰還を果たされます。この凱旋の途中、住吉大神の神託によって現在の住吉の地に鎮斎されました。

claims.statement: Sumiyoshi Taisha describes itself as the head shrine of some 2,300 Sumiyoshi shrines across the country.
claims.statement_id: Sumiyoshi Taisha menyebut dirinya kuil induk dari sekitar 2.300 lebih kuil Sumiyoshi di seluruh Jepang.
claims.quote: という社格がつけられ、人々に親しまれてきました。昭和21年までは官幣大社であり、全国約2300社余の住吉神社の総本社でもあります。

claims.statement: According to Sumiyoshi Taisha, because Sumiyoshi Ōkami emerged from the sea during Izanagi's misogi-harai, the deity presides over harai (purification), the most important rite in Shinto.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Sumiyoshi Taisha, karena Sumiyoshi Ōkami muncul dari laut saat misogi-harai Izanagi, beliau adalah dewa yang menguasai "harai" (penyucian), hal terpenting dalam Shinto.
claims.quote: 住吉大神は伊邪那岐命の禊祓 (みそぎはらえ) の際に海中より出現されたので、神道でもっとも大事な「祓(はらえ)」を司る神です。

claims.statement: Because the deity emerged from the sea, Sumiyoshi Ōkami is worshipped as a sea god and has long been revered as a powerfully efficacious deity among seafarers and fishermen.
claims.statement_id: Karena muncul dari laut, Sumiyoshi Ōkami dipercaya sebagai dewa laut dan sejak lama dihormati sebagai dewa yang manjur oleh para pelaut dan nelayan.
claims.quote: 住吉大神は海中より出現されたため、海の神としての信仰があり、古くから航海関係者や漁民の間で、霊験あらたかな神として崇敬されてきました。

claims.statement: In the Nara period, whenever a mission to Tang China was dispatched, prayers for safety at sea were always offered.
claims.statement_id: Pada zaman Nara, setiap kali utusan ke Tang diberangkatkan, selalu dipanjatkan doa untuk keselamatan di laut.
claims.quote: 奈良時代、遣唐使の派遣の際には、必ず海上の無事を祈りました。

claims.statement: According to a legend that Sumiyoshi Ōkami taught how to make a rice seedbed without laying down grass, the deity has long been deeply revered as a god of farming.
claims.statement_id: Menurut legenda, Sumiyoshi Ōkami mengajarkan cara membuat persemaian padi tanpa menghamparkan rumput, sehingga sejak lama sangat dihormati sebagai dewa pertanian.
claims.quote: 住吉大神が草を敷かずに苗代をつくる方法を教えたという伝説により、古くから「農耕の神」として篤い崇敬を受けてきました。

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes a theory that the Sumiyoshi sanjin are the deification of the three main stars of Orion, a constellation used for navigation in antiquity.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat teori bahwa Sumiyoshi sanjin adalah pendewaan tiga bintang utama rasi Orion, yang pada zaman kuno dipakai untuk navigasi.
claims.quote: there is a theory that suggests the Sumiyoshi sanjin are the deification of the three main stars in Orion. In antiquity, the constellation Orion was used for navigation; perhaps for this reason, it was deified.

claims.statement: They are sometimes referred to as the Sumiyoshi daijin (住吉大神).
claims.statement_id: Mereka kadang disebut Sumiyoshi daijin (住吉大神).
claims.quote: They are sometimes referred to as the Sumiyoshi daijin (住吉大神 ).

claims.statement: Sumiyoshi Taisha records the enshrinement (chinza) in the 11th year of Empress Jingū's regency (211 CE).
claims.statement_id: Sumiyoshi Taisha mencatat pemuliaan (chinza) dewa-dewa itu pada tahun ke-11 masa pemerintahan Permaisuri Jingū sebagai wali takhta (sesshō), tahun 211 M.
claims.quote: 鎮座 神功皇后摂政11年(西暦211年) 社格 ・延喜式名神大社

claims.statement: Takaonna is a yōkai in Toriyama Sekien’s illustrated book.
claims.statement_id: Takaonna adalah yōkai dalam buku bergambar karya Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Takaonna (高女, "tall woman") was a Japanese yōkai that appeared in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien.

claims.statement: Its image shows a woman with an elongated lower body.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya menunjukkan perempuan dengan tubuh bagian bawah yang memanjang.
claims.quote: The Gazu (illustrated reference) above depicts a woman with an elongated lower body next to what appears to be a brothel.

claims.statement: Sekien supplied no explanatory text for the picture.
claims.statement_id: Sekien tidak memberi penjelasan tertulis pada gambar itu.
claims.quote: However, the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō has no explanatory text, so it is unclear what kind of yōkai this depiction was intended to be.

claims.statement: One interpretation considers it a satirical invention from the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Satu tafsir menganggapnya ciptaan satiris dari zaman Edo.
claims.quote: Some believe that this yōkai was an original invention designed to parody the Yoshiwara Yūkaku of the Edo period.

claims.statement: Wikipedia records the folklorist Morihiko Fujisawa's explanation that in a story from Wakayama Prefecture called Takanyōbō ("Tall Woman"), a Takaonna would frighten people on the second floors of girō (brothels).
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat penjelasan folkloris Morihiko Fujisawa bahwa dalam sebuah cerita dari Prefektur Wakayama bernama Takanyōbō ("Perempuan Tinggi"), Takaonna menakuti orang di lantai dua rumah bordil (girō).
claims.quote: by the folklorist Morihiko Fujisawa explains that in a story from the Wakayama Prefecture called Takanyōbō (高女房, "Tall Woman"), a Takaonna would frighten people on the second floors of girō (brothels).
