claims.statement: In the kaidan "Takaonna" by the novelist Norio Yamada, she is a homely woman who could never be with a man in life; transformed into a yōkai by her own desire, she wanders the earth, elongating her body to peek into the second floor of brothels.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kaidan "Takaonna" karya novelis Norio Yamada, ia digambarkan sebagai perempuan sederhana yang semasa hidup tak pernah bisa bersama seorang pria; berubah menjadi yōkai karena hasratnya, ia berkeliaran dan memanjangkan tubuh untuk mengintip lantai dua rumah bordil.
claims.quote: by the novelist Norio Yamada, the kaidan (mysterious tale) titled "Takaonna" depicts the Takaonna as a homely woman who could never be with a man when she was alive. Transformed into a yōkai from her own desire, she wanders the earth, elongating her body to peek into the second floor of brothels

claims.statement: The yōkai researcher Kenji Murakami notes that Fujisawa's explanation is only one interpretation of Sekien's painting and that Yamada's kaidan is a completely different tale sharing the name Takaonna.
claims.statement_id: Peneliti yōkai Kenji Murakami mencatat bahwa penjelasan Fujisawa hanyalah satu tafsir atas lukisan Sekien, dan kaidan Yamada adalah kisah yang sama sekali berbeda yang kebetulan bernama sama.
claims.quote: yōkai researcher Kenji Murakami notes that Fujisawa's explanation is nothing more than one interpretation of Sekien's painting and that Yamada's kaidan is a completely different tale that shares the name of Takaonna.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, taka onna appear most of the time as ordinary, homely women, but have the power to elongate their bodies to several meters in height.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, taka onna sebagian besar waktu tampak seperti perempuan biasa yang sederhana, tetapi mereka mampu memanjangkan tubuh hingga setinggi beberapa meter.
claims.quote: Taka onna appear as ordinary, homely human women most of the time. But they have the power to elongate their bodies and grow to several meters in height.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, taka onna are often seen peering into second-story windows of brothels and homes where romantic liaisons take place; their activities are generally limited to peeping.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, taka onna sering terlihat mengintip jendela lantai dua rumah bordil dan rumah tempat pertemuan asmara berlangsung; kegiatan mereka umumnya terbatas pada mengintip.
claims.quote: Taka onna are frequently spotted peering into the second-story windows of brothels and homes where romantic liaisons are taking place. Their activities are generally limited to peeping into windows.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, taka onna rarely attack humans physically but enjoy scaring and harassing the men and women who frequent the pleasure districts.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, taka onna jarang menyerang manusia secara fisik, tetapi senang menakut-nakuti dan mengganggu pria dan wanita yang sering mendatangi kawasan hiburan.
claims.quote: Though they rarely attack humans physically, taka onna do enjoy scaring and harassing both men and women who frequent the pleasure districts

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, taka onna were originally ordinary women too unattractive to marry or to find work in the red light districts they haunt.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, taka onna semula adalah perempuan biasa yang terlalu tidak menarik untuk menikah atau untuk mendapat pekerjaan di kawasan lampu merah yang mereka hantui.
claims.quote: Taka onna were originally ordinary women who were too unattractive to marry (or to find work in the red light districts which they haunt).

claims.statement: In one account on Yokai.com, a woodcutter pretending to sleep saw his wife jump into a well, then elongate her body and climb back out.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu kisah menurut Yokai.com, seorang penebang kayu yang berpura-pura tidur melihat istrinya melompat ke dalam sumur, lalu memanjangkan tubuhnya dan memanjat keluar.
claims.quote: One night while pretending to sleep in bed, he witnessed his wife jump into a well. She then elongated her body and climbed back out.

claims.statement: Yokai.com gives 高女 (たかおんな) with the translation "tall woman", the alternate name takajo, and red light districts as habitat.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis 高女 (たかおんな) dengan terjemahan "perempuan tinggi", nama lain takajo, dan habitat kawasan lampu merah.
claims.quote: Taka onna 高女 たかおんな Translation: tall woman Alternate names: takajo Habitat: red light districts

claims.statement: Yokai.com states that sightings of these yōkai peaked during the Edo period and continued up to the post-war period.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyatakan penampakan yōkai ini memuncak pada zaman Edo dan berlanjut hingga masa pascaperang.
claims.quote: Sightings of these yōkai peaked during the Edo period and continued up to the post-war period

claims.statement: Wikipedia records a Takaonna statue based on Mizuki Shigeru's design, displayed alongside 9 other yōkai statues since 2009.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat patung Takaonna berdasarkan desain Mizuki Shigeru yang dipajang bersama 9 patung yōkai lain sejak 2009.
claims.quote: This Takaonna statue was based on Mizuki Shigeru's design and has been displayed alongside 9 other yōkai statues since 2009.

claims.statement: Tōfu-kozō is a childlike Japanese yōkai carrying tofu.
claims.statement_id: Tōfu-kozō adalah yōkai Jepang mirip anak kecil yang membawa tahu.
claims.quote: In Japanese folklore, tōfu-kozō (Japanese: 豆腐小僧, literally "tofu boy") is a yōkai that looks like a child holding a tray of tōfu.

claims.statement: It appears repeatedly in popular books of the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Ia kerap muncul dalam buku populer zaman Edo.
claims.quote: It frequently appears in the kusazōshi, kibyōshi and kaidan books from the Edo period, and from the Bakumatsu to the Meiji period, people have become familiar with them as a character illustrated on toys such as kites, sugoroku, and karuta.

claims.statement: Pictures commonly give it a bamboo hat and a tray.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya biasa menampilkan topi bambu dan nampan.
claims.quote: They are generally depicted wearing bamboo and kasa on their heads, and possessing a round tray with a momiji-dōfu on it (a tōfu with a momiji (autumn leaf) shape pressed into it).

claims.statement: Early stories did not assign it any special powers.
claims.statement_id: Cerita awal tidak memberinya kekuatan khusus.
claims.quote: In the original kusazōshi, they did not possess any special powers, and they often appear as servants that bring tōfu and sake here and there in the town, and it is also changed in senryū such poems like "tōfu-kozō are servant monsters (豆腐小僧ハ化ものゝ小間使ひ)." With regards to humans, they sometimes follow humans on rainy nights, but they don't do anything particularly bad, and they usually don'

claims.statement: The tōfu-kozō is observed to have appeared suddenly in the literature of the An'ei era (1772–1781) and became very popular as a character in kusazōshi, kibyōshi, kaidan books and toys of the time.
claims.statement_id: Tōfu-kozō teramati sebagai yōkai yang tiba-tiba muncul dalam sastra era An'ei (1772–1781) dan sangat populer sebagai tokoh dalam kusazōshi, kibyōshi, buku kaidan, dan mainan pada masa itu.
claims.quote: The tōfu-kozō has been observed to be a yōkai that suddenly appeared in the literature of the An'ei era (1772–1781), and earned great popularity as a character in the kusazōshi and kibyōshi, kaidan books, and toys of that time

claims.statement: The "Bakemono Shiuchi Hyōbanki" is observed to be their first appearance, and there is no confirmation of the tōfu-kozō in any earlier literature.
claims.statement_id: "Bakemono Shiuchi Hyōbanki" teramati sebagai kemunculan pertamanya, dan tidak ada konfirmasi bahwa tōfu-kozō muncul dalam sastra yang lebih awal.
claims.quote: The aforementioned "Bakemono Shiuchi Hyōbanki" was observed to be their first appearance, and there have been no confirmations that the tōfu-kozō appeared in any earlier literature.

claims.statement: Since they are not confirmed in folkloristic material such as folklore, kaidan collections like hyakumonogatari, or legends, they are seen as a yōkai created in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Karena belum terkonfirmasi muncul dalam bahan folkloristik seperti cerita rakyat, kumpulan kaidan seperti hyakumonogatari, atau legenda, tōfu-kozō dipandang sebagai yōkai ciptaan zaman Edo.
claims.quote: Since they have not been confirmed to appear in folkloristics material such as folklore, kaidan collections such as hyakumonogatari, or legends, they are seen as a yōkai created from the Edo period.

claims.statement: Shōwa- and Heisei-era literature often says they appear on rainy nights offering tōfu to passers-by, with mold growing halfway through eating it; but according to yōkai researchers Natsuhiko Kyogoku and Bintarō Yamaguchi, this idea was created after the Shōwa era in children's books.
claims.statement_id: Dalam bacaan era Shōwa dan Heisei serta sesudahnya sering ditulis bahwa ia muncul pada malam hujan dan menawarkan tahu kepada orang lewat, tetapi jamur tumbuh di tengah makan; namun menurut peneliti yōkai Natsuhiko Kyogoku dan Bintarō Yamaguchi, teori ini dibuat setelah era Shōwa dalam buku anak.
claims.quote: In literature from the Shōwa and Heisei eras and beyond, it is frequently written that they would appear on rainy nights, and recommend the relish of tōfu to people passing by, but halfway into eating it a mold would grow. However, according to the yōkai researchers Natsuhiko Kyogoku and Bintarō Yamaguchi, this theory was created after the Shōwa era in books for children.

claims.statement: In the kibyōshi "Bakemono Shiuchi Hyōbanki" by Koikawa Harumachi of the An'ei era, weasels turn into tōfu-kozō, and in later books their father is specified as mikoshi-nyūdō and their mother as rokurokubi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kibyōshi "Bakemono Shiuchi Hyōbanki" karya Koikawa Harumachi dari era An'ei, musang menjelma menjadi tōfu-kozō, dan dalam buku-buku berikutnya ayahnya ditetapkan sebagai mikoshi-nyūdō dan ibunya sebagai rokurokubi.
claims.quote: In the kibyōshi the "Bakemono Shiuchi Hyōbanki (妖怪仕内評判記)" by Koikawa Harumachi from the An'ei era, weasels turn into tōfu-kozō, and in later books, their father has been specified to be mikoshi-nyūdō and their mother has been specified to be rokurokubi.

claims.statement: On the Mizuki Shigeru Road in Sakaiminato, Tottori Prefecture, hometown of the yōkai painter and manga artist Shigeru Mizuki, next to the restaurant "Tōfuya" stands a statue of a tōfu-kozō based on one of Mizuki's illustrations.
claims.statement_id: Di Mizuki Shigeru Road, Sakaiminato, Prefektur Tottori, kampung halaman pelukis yōkai dan komikus Shigeru Mizuki, di samping restoran "Tōfuya" ada patung tōfu-kozō berdasarkan salah satu ilustrasi Mizuki.
claims.quote: On the Mizuki Shigeru Road in Sakaiminato, Tottori Prefecture, the hometown of the yōkai painter and manga artist Shigeru Mizuki, next to the restaurant "Tōfuya (東府屋)," there is a statue of a tōfu-kozō based on one of Mizuki's illustrations.

claims.statement: In the late Edo period they were often depicted with one eye.
claims.statement_id: Pada akhir zaman Edo, tōfu-kozō sering digambarkan bermata satu.
claims.quote: In the late Edo period, they were often depicted with one eye.

claims.statement: Because the hitotsume-kozō and the kappa have been depicted holding tōfu, there is a theory that these yōkai are related to the tōfu-kozō and another that the tōfu-kozō was based on them.
claims.statement_id: Karena hitotsume-kozō dan kappa pernah digambarkan membawa tahu, ada teori bahwa yōkai-yōkai itu berkaitan dengan tōfu-kozō, serta teori bahwa tōfu-kozō berdasar pada mereka.
claims.quote: since the hitotsume-kozō and the kappa have been depicted possessing tōfu, there is the theory that these yōkai are related to the tōfu-kozō as well as the theory that the tōfu-kozō was based on these yōkai.

claims.statement: It has been pointed out that tōfu-kozō may be no more than another name for hitotsume-kozō, but since many tōfu-kozō do not have one eye, there is also a claim denying they are the same.
claims.statement_id: Ada yang menunjukkan bahwa tōfu-kozō hanyalah nama lain hitotsume-kozō, tetapi karena banyak tōfu-kozō yang tidak bermata satu, ada pula klaim yang menyangkal bahwa keduanya sama.
claims.quote: it has been pointed out that tōfu-kozō would thus be no more than an alternate name for hitotsume-kozō, but since there are many tōfu-kozō that don't have one eye, there is also the claim denying that they are the same as hitotsume-kozō

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: 豆腐小僧 (とうふこぞう) is a Japanese yōkai in the form of a child holding tōfu, depicted mainly in kusazōshi and nishiki-e from the late Edo period onward.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: 豆腐小僧 (とうふこぞう) adalah yōkai Jepang berwujud anak yang membawa tahu, yang terutama digambarkan dalam kusazōshi dan nishiki-e sejak akhir zaman Edo.
claims.quote: 豆腐小僧（とうふこぞう）は豆腐を持っている子供の姿をした日本の妖怪。主に江戸時代後期以降の草双紙や錦絵などに描かれている存在である。

claims.statement: The tōfu-kozō is confirmed in kusazōshi from the An'ei era; the kibyōshi "Yōkai Shiuchi Hyōbanki" (1779) is confirmed as an early work, so it can be called a yōkai born in urban culture.
claims.statement_id: Tōfu-kozō dapat dipastikan dalam kusazōshi sejak era An'ei; kibyōshi "Yōkai Shiuchi Hyōbanki" (1779) dipastikan sebagai karya awalnya, sehingga ia dapat disebut yōkai yang lahir dalam budaya perkotaan.
claims.quote: 豆腐小僧は安永年間から草双紙で確認することが出来、黄表紙『妖怪仕内評判記』（1779年）が初期のものであると確認されており、都市文化の中で生まれた妖怪であると言える。

claims.statement: From the Shōwa era it was drawn in yōkai encyclopedias; in the Heisei era Edo picture-book works featuring it were widely introduced through Adam Kabat's editions, and it came to be used widely in creative works, listed with Natsuhiko Kyogoku's 2003 book.
claims.statement_id: Sejak era Shōwa ia digambarkan dalam ensiklopedia yōkai; pada era Heisei karya-karya bergambar Edo yang memuatnya diperkenalkan luas melalui suntingan Adam Kabat, dan ia banyak dipakai dalam karya kreatif, misalnya karya Natsuhiko Kyogoku tahun 2003.
claims.quote: 昭和以後、妖怪図鑑などでも描かれていた妖怪であったが、平成期にはアダム・カバットの編著、『江戸化物草紙』（1999年）や『大江戸化物細見』（2000年）などで豆腐小僧の登場する絵双紙作品が広く紹介・翻刻され、妖怪を用いた創作にも幅広く用いられていった。 京極夏彦 『豆腐小僧双六道中ふりだし 本朝妖怪盛衰録』 （2003年）

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, tōfu kozō are small yokai closely resembling human children except for their large heads and clawed fingers and toes.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, tōfu kozō adalah yōkai kecil yang sangat mirip anak manusia, kecuali kepalanya besar serta jari tangan dan kakinya bercakar.
claims.quote: Tōfu kozō are small yokai who closely resemble human children except for their large heads and clawed fingers and toes.

claims.statement: Tōfu kozō are timid and weak yokai and are not known to be aggressive toward humans.
claims.statement_id: Tōfu kozō adalah yōkai penakut dan lemah yang tidak dikenal agresif terhadap manusia.
claims.quote: Tōfu kozō are timid and weak yokai, and are not known to be aggressive towards humans.

claims.statement: Some say tōfu kozō are just one of many forms taken by an itachi, a shape-shifting weasel yokai; others say they are the offspring of a mikoshi-nyūdō and a rokuro-kubi.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian orang berkata tōfu kozō hanyalah salah satu wujud itachi, yōkai musang pengubah wujud; yang lain berkata mereka keturunan mikoshi-nyūdō dan rokuro-kubi.
claims.quote: Some say that they are just one of many forms taken by an itachi, a shape-shifting weasel yokai. Others say that they are the offspring of a mikoshi-nyūdō and a rokuro-kubi.

claims.statement: Another possibility is that they are the invention of a creative artist looking to sell illustrated storybooks.
claims.statement_id: Kemungkinan lain adalah bahwa mereka ciptaan seorang seniman kreatif yang ingin menjual buku cerita bergambar.
claims.quote: Another possibility is that they are an invention of a creative artist looking to sell illustrated storybooks.

claims.statement: Tōfu kozō are first and foremost servant yokai; even among other yokai they are often bullied and teased for their lack of strength.
claims.statement_id: Tōfu kozō pada dasarnya adalah yōkai pelayan; di antara yōkai lain pun mereka sering dirundung dan diejek karena lemah.
claims.quote: Tōfu kozō are first and foremost servant yokai. Even among other yokai, they are often bullied and teased for their lack of strength.

claims.statement: Tsurube-otoshi is a yōkai reported in several Japanese prefectures.
claims.statement_id: Tsurube-otoshi adalah yōkai yang diceritakan di beberapa prefektur Jepang.
claims.quote: Tsurube-otoshi (釣瓶落とし) or tsurube-oroshi (釣瓶下ろし) is a yōkai told about in Kyoto Prefecture, Shiga Prefecture, Gifu Prefecture, Aichi Prefecture, and Wakayama Prefecture, among other places.

claims.statement: Stories say it drops from trees to attack people.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menyebut ia jatuh dari pohon untuk menyerang orang.
claims.quote: They are said to drop from above the trees and attack, and even devour humans.

claims.statement: One local version describes a severed head falling from above.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu versi daerah menggambarkannya sebagai kepala terpenggal yang jatuh dari atas.
claims.quote: Also, in the Tera section of Sogabe village, tsurube-oroshi are said to appear as a severed head that would drop down from an old pine tree and then eat and feed on someone and after that not appear for about two to three days, and then they would appear once again.

claims.statement: Another version says it devours humans.
claims.statement_id: Versi lain menyebut ia memangsa manusia.
claims.quote: In the Tsuchida section of the village of Ōi, it is also said that tsurube-oroshi would devour humans.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, tsurube otoshi are gigantic disembodied heads of a human, a tengu or an oni, sometimes appearing wreathed in flames like large fireballs with facial features.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, tsurube otoshi adalah kepala raksasa tanpa tubuh milik manusia, tengu, atau oni, dan kadang tampak diselubungi api seperti bola api besar berwajah.
claims.quote: Tsurube otoshi are a gigantic disembodied heads of either a human, a tengu, or an oni. Sometimes they appear wreathed in flames like large fireballs with facial features.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, tsurube otoshi lurk in the treetops late at night, waiting for unsuspecting creatures to pass underneath, and drop to the ground like a stone when they need to feed.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, tsurube otoshi mengintai di pucuk pohon larut malam, menunggu makhluk yang tak curiga lewat di bawahnya, lalu jatuh cepat ke tanah seperti batu saat perlu makan.
claims.quote: Tsurube otoshi lurk in the treetops late at night and wait for unsuspecting creatures to pass underneath. When they need to feed, they drop quickly to the ground like a stone.

claims.statement: Yokai.com states that this is the reason for its name, which means "falling well bucket".
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyatakan bahwa itulah asal namanya, yang berarti "ember sumur yang jatuh".
claims.quote: This is the reason for its name, which means "falling well bucket."

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, they also drop large rocks or even well buckets on their victims from up high, laughing at the damage they inflict.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, mereka juga menjatuhkan batu besar atau bahkan ember sumur dari ketinggian ke korbannya sambil menertawakan kerusakan yang ditimbulkan.
claims.quote: They also drop large rocks or even well buckets (they have a sense of humor) on their victims from up high, laughing at the damage they inflict.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, tsurube otoshi in the Kansai region are most often solitary gargantuan heads, while in the Tohoku region they usually come in larger groups of slightly smaller heads.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, tsurube otoshi di wilayah Kansai paling sering berupa kepala raksasa tunggal, sedangkan di wilayah Tohoku biasanya berupa kelompok kepala yang sedikit lebih kecil.
claims.quote: Tsurube otoshi encountered in the Kansai region are most often solitary, gargantuan heads. In the Tohoku region, tsurube otoshi are usually encountered in larger groups of slightly smaller heads.

claims.statement: In an oral legend from the Hōki section of Sogabe village (now Kameoka), Kyoto Prefecture, recorded by Wikipedia, a tsurube-oroshi suddenly drops from a kaya tree with a sniggering laugh, saying "has your night work ended, how 'bout let's drop a bucket, gii-gii", and then rises above the tree again.
claims.statement_id: Dalam tuturan lisan dari bagian Hōki, desa Sogabe (kini Kameoka), Prefektur Kyoto, yang dicatat Wikipedia, sebuah tsurube-oroshi tiba-tiba jatuh dari pohon kaya sambil terkekeh dan berkata "sudah selesai kerja malammu? mau kujatuhkan ember? gii-gii", lalu naik lagi ke atas pohon.
claims.quote: in the Hōki section of the village of Sogabe in Kyoto Prefecture (now Kameoka), a tsurube-oroshi would suddenly drop down from a kaya tree and make a sniggering laugh saying "has your night work ended, how 'bout let's drop a bucket, gii-gii" ("yagyō sunda ka, tsurube oroso ka, gii-gii") and then rise up above the tree again.

claims.statement: In an account recorded by Wikipedia, someone who reaches for something shining at the base of an old tree, thinking it a koban coin, is dragged into a bucket, lifted above the tree, menaced and then devoured by the tsurube-otoshi living there.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah zaman Genroku yang dicatat Wikipedia, orang yang mengulurkan tangan ke sesuatu yang berkilau di pangkal pohon tua karena mengira itu koin koban akan diseret ke dalam ember, diangkat ke atas pohon, lalu diteror dan dimakan oleh tsurube-otoshi yang tinggal di sana.
claims.quote: In a Genroku period yōkai tale told about in the Kuroe part of Kainan, Wakayama Prefecture, it is said that a certain old tree would have something shining at its base ... they would get dragged into a bucket and lifted up to above the tree where they would be menaced and then devoured by the tsurube-otoshi living there

claims.statement: In the Edo-period kaidan collection Kokon Hyakumonogatari Hyōban, recorded by Wikipedia, they are depicted under the name "tsurube-oroshi" as a yōkai that is the spirit of a large tree turned into flames that rain down.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kumpulan kaidan zaman Edo, Kokon Hyakumonogatari Hyōban, yang dicatat Wikipedia, ia digambarkan dengan nama "tsurube-oroshi" sebagai yōkai berupa roh pohon besar yang berubah menjadi api yang menghujan.
claims.quote: In the Edo Period collection of kaidan (mysterious tales), the Kokon Hyakumonogatari Hyōban, they are depicted under the name of "tsurube-oroshi" (釣瓶おろし ) as a yōkai that is a spirit of a large tree that has turned into flames that rain down.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes a theory that originally both the tsurube-otoshi and the tsurubebi were similarly atmospheric ghost lights dangling from trees like buckets.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat teori bahwa pada mulanya tsurube-otoshi dan tsurubebi sama-sama berupa cahaya hantu atmosferik yang menggantung di pohon seperti ember.
claims.quote: there is also the theory that originally both the tsurube-otoshi and the tsurubebi were similarly atmospheric ghost lights that dangle from trees like buckets.

claims.statement: The White Hare of Inaba belongs to Japanese myth.
claims.statement_id: Kelinci Putih Inaba merupakan bagian dari mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: The White Hare of Inaba (因幡の白兎, Inaba no Shirousagi) can refer to two distinct Japanese myths, both from the ancient province of Inaba, now the eastern part of Tottori Prefecture.

claims.statement: Its legend is part of the Izumo tradition.
claims.statement_id: Legendanya termasuk dalam tradisi Izumo.
claims.quote: The White Hare of Inaba legend belongs to the Izumo denrai, or tradition of myths originating from the Izumo region.

claims.statement: The hare’s tale forms part of the story of the deity Ōnamuchi.
claims.statement_id: Kisah kelinci itu terkait dengan cerita dewa Ōnamuchi.
claims.quote: The White Hare of Inaba forms an essential part of the legend of the Shinto god Ōnamuchi-no-kami, which was the name for Ōkuninushi within this legend.

claims.statement: A version of the tale is recorded in the Kojiki.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu versinya tercatat dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: One version of the tale of the White Hare of Inaba is found in the Kojiki, the oldest extant chronicle in Japan, which dates from early in the 8th century (711-712).

claims.statement: The Digital Daijisen describes the White Hare of Inaba as the hare of Izumo myth who tricked the wanizame (sharks) to cross their backs from Oki Island to Inaba province, but was stripped bare by the last wanizame.
claims.statement_id: Digital Daijisen menyebut kelinci Inaba sebagai kelinci dalam mitos Izumo yang menipu para wanizame (hiu) untuk menyeberang dari Pulau Oki ke negeri Inaba, tetapi dilucuti kulitnya oleh wanizame terakhir.
claims.quote: いなば-の-しろうさぎ【因幡の白兎】 出雲神話に出てくる兎。 淤岐島 おきのしま から因幡国へ行くため、 鰐鮫 わにざめ を欺いてその背を渡ったが、最後の鰐鮫に丸裸にされ、

claims.statement: According to the Digital Daijisen, the hare believed the Yasogami's advice as it was, bathed in seawater and wept in pain, and was saved by Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Digital Daijisen, kelinci itu percaya begitu saja pada ajaran para Yasogami lalu mandi air laut dan menangis kesakitan, hingga diselamatkan Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: さらに 八十神 やそかみ の教えをそのまま信じて潮を浴び、痛くて泣いていたところを、 大国主命 おおくにぬしのみこと に救われる。

claims.statement: Nipponica says the hare-and-shark tale in the Kojiki is an animal story of a cunning animal deceiving a dull one, related to tales existing on Java and in Indonesia.
claims.statement_id: Nipponica menyebut kisah kelinci dan hiu dalam Kojiki sebagai kisah binatang cerdik yang menipu binatang dungu, yang berkaitan dengan kisah-kisah di Pulau Jawa dan Indonesia.
claims.quote: この『古事記』にみえる兎と鮫の話は、狡猾(こうかつ)な動物が魯鈍(ろどん)な動物をだます動物譚(たん)として、ジャワ島やインドネシアに存在している説話などとも関係がある。

claims.statement: Nipponica stresses that in the Kojiki the story is recast as one in which the cunning hare fails, and the rescued hare plays the role of a hare deity predicting the success of the lowest-ranking Ōnamuchi.
claims.statement_id: Nipponica menekankan bahwa dalam Kojiki kisah ini diubah menjadi kisah kegagalan kelinci licik, dan kelinci yang ditolong berperan sebagai dewa kelinci yang meramalkan keberhasilan Ōnamuchi yang paling rendah kedudukannya.
claims.quote: しかし『古事記』では狡猾な兎が失敗する話につくりかえられており、助けられた兎が、いちばん卑しい大汝神の成功を予言する兎神としての役割を演じている点に注意する必要がある。

claims.statement: According to Heibonsha, the hare predicted that Ōnamuchi, not the Yasogami, would marry Yakami-hime of Inaba, and the prediction came true; this hare is said to have gained worship as a hare deity (usagi-kami).
claims.statement_id: Menurut Heibonsha, kelinci itu meramalkan bahwa Ōnamuchi, bukan para Yasogami, akan menikahi Yakami-hime dari Inaba, dan ramalan itu terbukti; kelinci ini konon dipuja sebagai dewa kelinci (usagi-kami).
claims.quote: そこで兎は八十神ではなくオオナムチが因幡の八上比売(やかみひめ)と結婚すると予言し,的中する。この兎は〈兎神(うさぎかみ)〉として信仰を得たという。

claims.statement: In the Kojiki version as given by Wikipedia, a hare tricks wanizame (sharks) into serving as a land bridge from the Island of Oki to Cape Keta; he challenges the sharks to compare whose clan is larger and has them lie in a row across the sea.
claims.statement_id: Dalam versi Kojiki menurut Wikipedia, seekor kelinci menipu wanizame (hiu) agar dijadikan jembatan dari Pulau Oki ke Tanjung Keta; ia menantang para hiu membandingkan klan mana yang lebih besar dan menyuruh mereka berbaris melintasi laut.
claims.quote: In the Kojiki version of the myth, a hare tricks some wanizame into being used as a land bridge in order to travel from the Island of Oki to Cape Keta. ... The hare challenges the sharks to see whose clan is larger-that of the sharks, or that of the hares. The hare had the sharks lie in a row across the sea.

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, near the end the hare exclaims that he has deceived the sharks to use them as a bridge, and the last shark attacks him, ripping his fur from him.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, menjelang ujung barisan kelinci berseru bahwa ia telah menipu para hiu untuk dijadikan jembatan, dan hiu terakhir menyerangnya serta merobek bulunya.
claims.quote: Nearing the end, the hare exclaims that he has deceived the sharks in order to use them as a bridge. The last shark attacks the hare, ripping his fur from him.

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, Ōnamuchi told the hare to bathe in fresh water at a river mouth and roll in cattail pollen; the hare's body was restored and after recovery it revealed its true form as a god.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, Ōnamuchi menyuruh kelinci mandi air tawar di muara sungai lalu berguling di serbuk sari rumput kattail; tubuh kelinci pulih dan setelah sembuh ia menyingkapkan wujud aslinya sebagai dewa.
claims.quote: Ōnamuchi, unlike his quarreling elder brothers, told the hare to bathe in fresh water from the mouth of a river, and then roll in the pollen of cattails. The body of the hare was restored to its original state, and after its recovery, revealed its true form as a god.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that Japanese scholars have traditionally interpreted the struggle between the kind Ōnamuchi and his wrathful eighty brothers as a symbolic representation of civilization and barbarism in the emergent Japanese state.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa para sarjana Jepang secara tradisional menafsirkan pertentangan antara Ōnamuchi yang baik hati dan delapan puluh saudaranya yang murka sebagai lambang peradaban dan barbarisme dalam negara Jepang yang baru muncul.
claims.quote: Japanese scholars have traditionally interpreted the struggle between the kind Ōnamuchi and his wrathful eighty brothers as a symbolic representation of civilization and barbarism in the emergent Japanese state.

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, when the Japanese goddess Amaterasu and her entourage traveled around the boundary of Yakami in Inaba looking for a place for a temporary palace, a white hare appeared, bit Amaterasu's clothes and took her to a suitable place for a temporary palace.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, ketika dewi Jepang Amaterasu dan rombongannya berkeliling di perbatasan Yakami di Inaba mencari tempat istana sementara, seekor kelinci putih muncul, menggigit pakaian Amaterasu, dan membawanya ke tempat yang cocok untuk istana sementara.
claims.quote: Long ago, when Japanese goddess Amaterasu and her entourage traveled around at the boundary of Yakami in Inaba, they were looking for a place for their temporary palace, suddenly a white hare appeared. the white hare bit Amaterasu's clothes and took her to an appropriate place for a temporary palace

claims.statement: In that account according to Wikipedia, Amaterasu reached a mountaintop plain now called Ise ga naru, and the white hare disappeared there.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah itu menurut Wikipedia, Amaterasu tiba di dataran puncak gunung yang kini disebut Ise ga naru, dan kelinci putih menghilang di sana.
claims.quote: Amaterasu reached a mountain top plain, which is now called Ise ga naru. Then, the white hare disappeared at Ise ga naru.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes the place of this legend is in Yazu town and Tottori city, Tottori Prefecture, where Hakuto Jinja shrine reveres the white hare.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat tempat legenda ini berada di kota Yazu dan kota Tottori, Prefektur Tottori, tempat kuil Hakuto Jinja memuliakan kelinci putih.
claims.quote: The place of this legend is in Yazu town and Tottori city, in Tottori Prefecture (ancient Inaba and Houki), where the shrine Hakuto Jinja reveres the white hare.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes the hare in the legend is Lepus brachyurus, the Japanese hare, possibly the Oki Islands subspecies Lepus brachyurus okiensis.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa kelinci dalam legenda ini adalah Lepus brachyurus (kelinci Jepang), mungkin subspesies Pulau Oki, Lepus brachyurus okiensis.
claims.quote: The hare referred to in the legend is the Lepus brachyurus, or Japanese hare, possibly the subspecies found on the Oki Islands known as the Lepus brachyurus okiensis.

claims.statement: Yako is a fox spirit in stories from Kyūshū.
claims.statement_id: Yako adalah roh rubah dalam cerita dari Kyūshū.
claims.quote: Yako or nogitsune (野狐) is a type of kitsune (fox spirit), as told in Kyūshū.

claims.statement: Possession by this spirit is called yako-tsuki.
claims.statement_id: Kerasukan roh ini disebut yako-tsuki.
claims.quote: To be possessed by it is called "yako-tsuki" (野狐憑き).

claims.statement: Its written name can also mean an ordinary wild fox.
claims.statement_id: Bentuk tulis namanya juga dapat berarti rubah liar biasa.
claims.quote: is also used for foxes in the wild in general.

claims.statement: Accounts give it black or white coloring and a small body.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kisah, tubuhnya kecil dan berwarna hitam atau putih.
claims.quote: The appearance of a yako is almost completely consistent among all legends; they are black or white, are slightly larger than a mouse, and smaller than a cat.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, nogitsune, also frequently called yako, are a type of kitsune; the term refers to low-ranking wild kitsune that have no divine soul and are not messengers of the gods.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nogitsune, yang sering juga disebut yako, adalah jenis kitsune; istilah ini merujuk pada kitsune liar berpangkat rendah yang tidak memiliki jiwa ilahi dan bukan utusan dewa.
claims.quote: Nogitsune, also frequently called yako, are a type of kitsune-magical foxes found in East Asian folklore. Specifically the term refers to low ranking, wild kitsune that do not have a divine soul or serve as messengers of the gods.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, nogitsune are particularly known for transforming into humans, and in folktales where humans are tormented, tricked or possessed by kitsune, the culprit is almost always a nogitsune.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nogitsune terutama dikenal karena menjelma manusia, dan dalam dongeng tentang manusia yang disiksa, ditipu, atau dirasuki kitsune, pelakunya hampir selalu nogitsune.
claims.quote: They are particularly known for transforming into humans. In folktales where humans are tormented, tricked, or possessed by kitsune, the culprit is almost always a nogitsune.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, nogitsune dislike bright light and hide from the sun by day, fear bladed objects such as swords and knives, and are frightened of dogs.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nogitsune tidak suka cahaya terang dan bersembunyi dari matahari di siang hari, takut pada benda tajam seperti pedang dan pisau, dan takut pada anjing.
claims.quote: They dislike bright light, and hide from the sun during the daytime. They are also afraid of bladed objects, and will avoid swords and knives. They are frightened of dogs as well.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, to change shape a nogitsune needs a magical focus, usually a bone from a cow or horse; kitsunetsuki, possession by a fox spirit, is also commonly performed by nogitsune.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, untuk berubah wujud nogitsune memerlukan benda sihir, biasanya tulang sapi atau kuda; kitsunetsuki (perasukan oleh roh rubah) juga sering dilakukan nogitsune.
claims.quote: In order to change its shape, a nogitsune requires a magical focus of some kind; usually a bone from a cow or a horse. Kitsunetsuki-possession by a fox spirit-is also commonly performed by nogitsune.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, nogitsune sneak into human-inhabited areas at night to steal favourite foods: wax candles, lamp oil, lacquer, alcohol and fried tofu.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nogitsune menyelinap ke permukiman manusia pada malam hari untuk mencuri makanan kesukaan mereka: lilin, minyak lampu, pernis, alkohol, dan tahu goreng.
claims.quote: they like to sneak into human-inhabited areas at night to steal some of their favorite foods: wax candles, lamp oil, lacquer, alcohol, and fried tofu.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, yako is simply another reading of the kanji of its name, while the name yakan (野干) is more archaic and originates from a different animal.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, yako hanyalah cara baca lain kanji nama nogitsune, sedangkan nama yakan (野干) lebih arkais dan berasal dari hewan yang berbeda.
claims.quote: The most common one-yako-is simply another reading of the kanji in its name. The name yakan (野干) is more archaic, and has its origins in a different animal.

claims.statement: Yokai.com gives 野狐 (のぎつね) with the translation "wild fox" and the alternate names yako and yakan.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis 野狐 (のぎつね) dengan terjemahan "rubah liar" dan nama lain yako dan yakan.
claims.quote: Nogitsune 野狐 のぎつね Translation: wild fox Alternate names: yako, yakan

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that the original yako is said to be invisible to the eye, and that in Hirado, Nagasaki Prefecture, they normally bring along a great crowd that walks with them.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa yako asli dikatakan tak terlihat mata, dan di Hirado, Prefektur Nagasaki, mereka biasanya membawa serombongan besar yang berjalan bersama mereka.
claims.quote: The original yako is said to be invisible to the eye. In Hirado, Nagasaki Prefecture, they normally bring along a great crowd that walks with them

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that in Southern Kyūshū family lines would get possessed by a yako, their progeny would be possessed, and if they could no longer support it, it would possess their cattle and horses.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa di Kyūshū selatan garis keluarga dapat dirasuki yako, keturunannya ikut dirasuki, dan bila tak sanggup lagi memeliharanya, yako merasuki ternak dan kuda mereka.
claims.quote: In Southern Kyūshū, family lines would get possessed by a yako, and family lines that raised yako (possessed by a yako) would have their progeny possessed, and if they were no longer able to support it, it would possess its cattle and horses.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that on Iki Island they are also called yako and resemble weasels; when one conceals itself under a person's armpits, that person is said to become possessed by a yako.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa di Pulau Iki mereka juga disebut yako dan menyerupai musang; bila salah satunya bersembunyi di ketiak seseorang, orang itu dikatakan dirasuki yako.
claims.quote: On Iki Island, they are also called yako, and since they resemble weasels, it is said that when one of them conceals themselves under a person's armpits, that person would become possessed by a yako.

claims.statement: Zagan is named in demonological writing.
claims.statement_id: Zagan disebut dalam tulisan demonologi.
claims.quote: ザガン（Zagan）またはザガム（Zagam）は、悪魔学における悪魔の一人。

claims.statement: The Goetia ranks him as its sixty-first spirit, a king and president.
claims.statement_id: Goetia menempatkannya sebagai roh ke-61, raja sekaligus pemimpin.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の33の軍団を率いる序列61番の大王にして総裁。

claims.statement: Wikipedia says Zelba, one of Zagan's alternative names, is depicted as a griffin-winged bull that turns into a man after a while.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia menyebut Zelba, salah satu nama lain Zagan, digambarkan sebagai banteng bersayap griffin yang setelah beberapa lama berubah menjadi manusia.
claims.quote: Zelba is depicted as a griffin-winged bull that turns into a man after a while.

claims.statement: The text credits him with changing wine to water and water to wine.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu menyebut ia dapat mengubah anggur menjadi air dan air menjadi anggur.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、ワインを水に、血をワインに、また水をワインに変質させることができる。

claims.statement: In the Goetia text the sixty-first spirit is Zagan, a great king and president who appears at first as a bull with gryphon's wings but after a while takes human shape.
claims.statement_id: Dalam teks Goetia, roh ke-61 adalah Zagan, raja agung sekaligus presiden, yang mula-mula tampil sebagai banteng bersayap griffin lalu setelah beberapa lama mengambil wujud manusia.
claims.quote: The Sixty-first Spirit is Zagan. He is a Great King and President, appearing at first in the Form of a Bull with Gryphon's Wings; but after a while he putteth on Human Shape.

claims.statement: According to the Goetia text he makes men witty and can turn wine into water, blood into wine, and water into wine.
claims.statement_id: Menurut teks Goetia, ia membuat orang cerdik, dan dapat mengubah anggur menjadi air, darah menjadi anggur, serta air menjadi anggur.
claims.quote: He maketh Men Witty. He can turn Wine into Water, and Blood into Wine, also Water into Wine.

claims.statement: According to the Goetia text he can turn all metals into coin of the dominion that metal is of, can even make fools wise, and governs 33 legions of spirits.
claims.statement_id: Menurut teks Goetia, ia dapat mengubah semua logam menjadi koin wilayah asal logam itu, bahkan membuat orang bodoh menjadi bijak, dan memimpin 33 legiun roh.
claims.quote: He can turn all Metals into Coin of the Dominion that Metal is of. He can even make Fools wise. He governeth 33 Legions of Spirits

claims.statement: Wikipedia lists other spellings of Zagan (Zagam, Zelbam, Zelba, Zelban, Zelbal, Zelbini) and calls him a Great King and President of Hell commanding 33 legions of demons.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat ejaan lain Zagan (Zagam, Zelbam, Zelba, Zelban, Zelbal, Zelbini) dan menyebutnya Raja Agung dan Presiden Neraka yang memimpin 33 legiun iblis.
claims.quote: Zagan (also Zagam, Zelbam, Zelba, Zelban, Zelbal, Zelbini) is a Great King and President of Hell, commanding 33 legions of demons.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that according to the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum he can also turn blood into oil, oil into blood, and a fool into a wise man.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa menurut Pseudomonarchia Daemonum ia juga dapat mengubah darah menjadi minyak, minyak menjadi darah, dan orang bodoh menjadi bijak.
claims.quote: (According to the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum, he can also turn blood into oil, oil into blood, and a fool into a wise man)

claims.statement: Zepar is the sixteenth spirit in the Goetia.
claims.statement_id: Zepar adalah roh ke-16 dalam Goetia.
claims.quote: ゼパル(Zepar)は、悪魔学における悪魔の一人。 ... 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の26の軍団を率いる序列16番の大公爵。

claims.statement: The text ranks him as a duke.
claims.statement_id: Teks itu memberinya gelar adipati.
claims.quote: 『ゴエティア』によると、地獄の26の軍団を率いる序列16番の大公爵。

claims.statement: He appears like a soldier wearing red clothing and armor.
claims.statement_id: Ia tampak seperti prajurit dengan busana dan zirah merah.
claims.quote: He is depicted with red clothes and armor, like a soldier.

claims.statement: The Goetia associates him with bringing men and women together in love.
claims.statement_id: Goetia mengaitkannya dengan mempertemukan pria dan wanita dalam cinta.
claims.quote: His office is to cause women to love men, and bring them together in love.

claims.statement: In the Goetia text the sixteenth spirit is Zepar, a great duke who appears in red apparel and armour like a soldier; his office is to cause women to love men and bring them together in love.
claims.statement_id: Dalam teks Goetia, roh ke-16 adalah Zepar, adipati agung yang tampil berpakaian dan berbaju zirah merah seperti prajurit; tugasnya membuat wanita mencintai pria dan menyatukan mereka dalam cinta.
claims.quote: The Sixteenth Spirit is Zepar. He is a Great Duke, and appeareth in Red Apparel and Armour, like a Soldier. His office is to cause Women to love Men, and to bring them together in love.

claims.statement: According to the Goetia text he also makes them barren, governs 26 legions of inferior spirits, and obeys his seal when he sees it.
claims.statement_id: Menurut teks Goetia, ia juga membuat mereka mandul, memimpin 26 legiun roh bawahan, dan menaati meterainya bila melihatnya.
claims.quote: He also maketh them barren. He governeth 26 Legions of Inferior Spirits, and his Seal is this, which he obeyeth when he seeth it.

claims.statement: Wikipedia calls Zepar a Great Duke of Hell commanding 26 legions of inferior spirits, whose office is to make women love men and bring them together in love, and who makes women barren.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia menyebut Zepar sebagai Adipati Agung Neraka yang memimpin 26 legiun roh bawahan, bertugas membuat wanita mencintai pria dan menyatukan mereka dalam cinta, serta membuat wanita mandul.
claims.quote: Zepar is a Great Duke of Hell, commanding 26 legions of inferior spirits. His office is to cause women to love men, and bring them together in love. He makes women barren.

claims.statement: Akugyo is a sea monster in Japanese legend.
claims.statement_id: Akugyo adalah monster laut dalam legenda Jepang.
claims.quote: Akugyo (悪魚 or 悪樓, "evil fish") or daigyo (giant fish) or raichōgyo (thunderbird fish) is a type of sea monster or aquatic yōkai in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: Accounts place these giant fish near the former Kibi Province.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menempatkan ikan raksasa ini di laut dekat bekas Provinsi Kibi (Prefektur Okayama).
claims.quote: Akugyo are monstrous fish usually encountered in the seas near Kibi Province (Okayama Prefecture).

claims.statement: Stories say they overturn ships and prey on sailors.
claims.statement_id: Konon mereka membalikkan kapal dan memangsa pelaut.
claims.quote: They're large in size and are known to capsize entire ships, before feasting upon the drowning sailors.

claims.statement: Different depictions give them fiery breath or shining scales.
claims.statement_id: Beragam gambaran memberinya napas api atau sisik berkilau.
claims.quote: Some Akugyo breathe fire, while others resemble gigantic versions of Ningyo with gold and silver scales.

claims.statement: The akugyo variety that appears as colossal mermaids usually has a pair of white oni-like horns on its head.
claims.statement_id: Ragam akugyo yang tampil sebagai putri duyung raksasa biasanya memiliki sepasang tanduk putih mirip oni di kepalanya.
claims.quote: The variety which appear as colossal mermaids usually have a pair of two white oni-like horns sprouting from their head.

claims.statement: Fishermen fear them because boats can easily get lodged between an akugyo's fins, letting the yōkai eat the crew.
claims.statement_id: Para nelayan takut karena perahu mereka mudah tersangkut di antara sirip akugyo, sehingga yōkai itu dapat memakan awaknya.
claims.quote: Fishermen fear them because their boats can easily become lodged between the fins of an Akugyo, allowing the yōkai to eat the crew.

claims.statement: An akugyo is said to have been sighted off the coast of Echigo Province in June 1805.
claims.statement_id: Seekor akugyo dikisahkan pernah terlihat di lepas pantai Provinsi Echigo pada Juni 1805.
claims.quote: An akugyo was once sighted off the coast of Echigo Province (present-day Toyama Prefecture) in June 1805.

claims.statement: Its body was about 11 meters long and its horns over 60 centimeters; it was eventually killed by Lord Matsudaira of Kaga, who sent an armada of 1500 men and 450 cannons.
claims.statement_id: Tubuhnya sekitar 11 meter dan tanduknya lebih dari 60 sentimeter. Makhluk itu akhirnya dibunuh oleh Tuan Matsudaira dari Kaga yang mengirim armada berisi 1500 orang dan 450 meriam.
claims.quote: Its body was approximately 11 meters long, and its horns measured over 60 centimeters long. This yōkai was eventually killed by Lord Matsudaira of Kaga, who sent out an armada of 1500 men and 450 cannons to slay it.

claims.statement: The famous Kaga taiko drummer Izutsuya Kanroku was crossing the Sea of Japan when his boat suddenly stopped, having sailed over an akugyo's back and gotten stuck.
claims.statement_id: Penabuh taiko terkenal dari Kaga, Izutsuya Kanroku, sedang menyeberangi Laut Jepang ketika perahunya tiba-tiba berhenti karena melintasi punggung seekor akugyo dan tersangkut.
claims.quote: A famous taiko drummer from Kaga, Izutsuya Kanroku, was traveling across the Sea of Japan when his boat suddenly stopped moving. It had sailed over the back of an akugyo and gotten stuck.

claims.statement: He drummed so loudly that the sound carried across the sky and sea; soon his boat was shaken loose from the akugyo and he escaped unharmed.
claims.statement_id: Ia menabuh drum sekeras mungkin hingga suaranya merambat ke langit dan seluruh laut; tak lama kemudian perahunya terlepas dari akugyo dan ia selamat tanpa cedera.
claims.quote: He drummed so loud that the sound traveled across the sky and throughout the sea. Soon, his boat was shaken loose from the akugyo, and he escaped unharmed.

claims.statement: Wanpaku Ōji no Orochi Taiji is a 1963 animated movie by Toei Animation with a scene in which Susanoo battles an akugyo.
claims.statement_id: Wanpaku Ōji no Orochi Taiji adalah film animasi Toei Animation tahun 1963 yang memuat adegan Susanoo melawan seekor akugyo.
claims.quote: Wanpaku Ōji no Orochi Taiji - An animated movie by Toei Animation from 1963.  There is a scene where Susanoo battles against an Akugyo.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, akugyo are an enormous kind of mermaid in the waters around Japan, with heads and arms like human women and fish-like bodies.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, akugyo adalah jenis putri duyung raksasa di perairan sekitar Jepang; kepala dan lengannya menyerupai perempuan manusia, sedangkan sisa tubuhnya seperti ikan.
claims.quote: Akugyo are an enormous species of mermaid found in the waters surrounding Japan. Their head and arms resemble those of human women, but the rest of their body is fish-like.

claims.statement: Akugyo spend most of their time beneath the seas, so little is known of their natural behavior.
claims.statement_id: Akugyo menghabiskan sebagian besar waktunya di bawah laut, sehingga perilaku alaminya sedikit diketahui.
claims.quote: Akugyo spend most of their time beneath the seas, so little is known of their natural behavior.

claims.statement: Ame no Tajikarao is a strength deity in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Ame no Tajikarao adalah dewa kekuatan dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Ame no Tajikarao (アメノタヂカラオ) is a Japanese deity (kami) of physical strength who appears in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki write his name differently.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki menulis namanya secara berbeda.
claims.quote: Ame no Tajikarao is written as 天手力男神 in Kojiki, and 天手力雄神 in Nihon Shoki.

claims.statement: His name refers to heavenly hand strength.
claims.statement_id: Nama Tajikarao berarti "Dewa Lelaki Kekuatan-Tangan Surgawi".
claims.quote: Tajikarao's name means "Heavenly Hand-Strength-Male Deity".

claims.statement: In the cave myth he helps draw Amaterasu back into the world.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah gua, ia membantu mengeluarkan Amaterasu kembali ke dunia.
claims.quote: During the incident of Ame no Iwato , Ame no Tajikarao waited at the cave's door to pull out (in the Nihon Shoki and the Kogo Shūi, 'to pull open') Amaterasu from the cave, and thus return light to the world.

claims.statement: Another name for him is Oosugutama-no-mikoto or Takuzutama-no-mikoto (多久豆魂命).
claims.statement_id: Nama lain baginya adalah Oosugutama-no-mikoto atau Takuzutama-no-mikoto (多久豆魂命).
claims.quote: Another name is Oosugutama-no-mikoto or Takuzutama-no-mikoto (多久豆魂命)

claims.statement: During the Tenson Kōrin, Amaterasu had Omoikane, Tajikarao and Ame no Iwatowake accompany the Imperial Regalia of Japan as it went to Ise Province to be enshrined at Ise Grand Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Pada Tenson Kōrin, Amaterasu menyuruh Omoikane, Tajikarao, dan Ame no Iwatowake menyertai Regalia Kekaisaran Jepang ketika dibawa ke Provinsi Ise untuk disemayamkan di Kuil Agung Ise.
claims.quote: During the Tenson Kōrin, Amaterasu had Omoikane, Tajikarao, and Ame no Iwatowake accompany the Imperial Regalia of Japan when it went to the Ise province to be enshrined at Ise Grand Shrine.

claims.statement: According to the Inbe clan genealogy cited in the Yamato Shiryō, Ame no Tajikarao was the son of Omoikane and a distant ancestor of the Achi clan.
claims.statement_id: Menurut silsilah klan Inbe yang dikutip dalam Yamato Shiryō, Ame no Tajikarao adalah putra Omoikane sekaligus leluhur jauh klan Achi.
claims.quote: According to the genealogy of the Inbe clan cited in the Yamato Shiryō, Ame no Tajikarao was the son of Omoikane as well as a distant ancestor of the Achi clan.

claims.statement: According to the Mochizuki clan genealogy he was also a grandson of the primordial goddess Kamimusubi and an ancestor of a clan of the ancient kingdom of Ki no Kuni Miyatsuko.
claims.statement_id: Menurut silsilah klan Mochizuki, ia juga cucu dewi purba Kamimusubi dan leluhur sebuah klan dari kerajaan kuno Ki no Kuni Miyatsuko.
claims.quote: According to the genealogy of the Mochizuki clan, he was also the grandson of the primordial goddess Kamimusubi and the ancestor of a clan of the ancient kingdom of Ki no Kuni Miyatsuko.

claims.statement: He is the father of Ame no Hiwashi, an ancestor of the Inbe clan of Awa Province.
claims.statement_id: Ia adalah ayah Ame no Hiwashi, leluhur klan Inbe di Provinsi Awa.
claims.quote: He is the father of Ame no Hiwashi who was an ancestor of the Inbe clan of Awa Province.

claims.statement: At Togakushi Shrine there is a legend that the cave-door of Ame no Iwato that Ame no Tajikarao threw away fell to earth and became Mount Togakushi.
claims.statement_id: Di Kuil Togakushi ada legenda bahwa pintu gua Ame no Iwato yang dilemparkan Ame no Tajikarao jatuh ke bumi dan menjadi Gunung Togakushi.
claims.quote: At the Togakushi Shrine, there is a legend that says that the cave-door of Ame no Iwato that Ame no Tajikarao threw away actually fell to Earth and became Mount Togakushi.

claims.statement: The name Ame no Tajikarao carries the connotation of a male god with extreme and surmounting physical brute strength.
claims.statement_id: Nama Ame no Tajikarao mengandung kesan dewa laki-laki dengan kekuatan fisik yang ekstrem dan luar biasa.
claims.quote: The name Ame no Tajikarao carries the connotation of a male god with extreme and surmounting physical brute strength.

claims.statement: The Japanese sports-equipment company Tachikara is named after the god because he is "known historically as the 'god of power' in Japanese folklore."
claims.statement_id: Perusahaan Jepang Tachikara, yang berspesialisasi dalam perlengkapan olahraga, dinamai menurut dewa ini karena ia "dikenal secara historis sebagai 'dewa kekuatan' dalam cerita rakyat Jepang".
claims.quote: The Japanese company, Tachikara, which specializes in sports equipment, is named after the god, because he is "known historically as the 'god of power' in Japanese folklore."

claims.statement: Ame no Tajikarao is believed to be a god of sports and physical power.
claims.statement_id: Ame no Tajikarao diyakini sebagai dewa olahraga dan kekuatan fisik.
claims.quote: Ame no Tajikaro is believed to be a god of sports and physical power

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: 天之手力男神 (Ame no Tajikarao no Kami) is a deity who appears in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: 天之手力男神 (Ame no Tajikarao no Kami) adalah dewa yang muncul dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: 天之手力男神（あめのたぢからおのかみ）は、日本神話に登場する神。

claims.statement: During the hiding in the rock cave he waited beside the door, and when Amaterasu peeked out he dragged her out (in a version of the Nihon Shoki and in the Kogo Shūi, "pulled it open"), so that light returned to the world.
claims.statement_id: Saat Amaterasu bersembunyi di gua batu, ia menunggu di samping pintu, dan ketika Amaterasu mengintip keluar, ia menariknya keluar (dalam satu versi Nihon Shoki dan Kogo Shūi: "membuka tarik pintu"), sehingga dunia kembali terang.
claims.quote: 岩戸隠れの際は岩戸の脇に控えており、アマテラスが岩戸から顔をのぞかせた時、アマテラスを引きずり出して（『日本書紀』の一書や『古語拾遺』では「引き開けて」）、それにより世界に明るさが戻った。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi: Ta-jikara-wo no Kami at once took Ama-terasu no Oho-kami by the hand and led her out.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi: Ta-jikara-wo no Kami segera menggenggam tangan Ama-terasu no Oho-kami dan menuntunnya keluar.
claims.quote: Then Ta-jikara-wo no Kami forthwith took Ama-terasu no Oho-kami by the hand, and led her out.

claims.statement: In another Nihongi version, Ama no Tajikara-wo no Kami, waiting beside the Rock-door, at once pulled it open, and the radiance of the Sun-Goddess filled the universe.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu versi Nihongi, Ama no Tajikara-wo no Kami yang menunggu di samping Pintu Batu segera membukanya, dan cahaya Dewi Matahari memenuhi alam semesta.
claims.quote: Thereupon the God Ama no Tajikara-wo no Kami, who was waiting beside the Rock-door, forthwith pulled it open, and the radiance of the Sun-Goddess filled the universe.

claims.statement: Amenohiboko is a legendary prince from Silla who comes to Japan.
claims.statement_id: Amenohiboko adalah pangeran legendaris dari Silla yang datang ke Jepang.
claims.quote: Amenohiboko (天日槍; アメノヒボコ) was a legendary prince of Silla who settled in Japan during the era of Emperor Suinin, around the 3rd or 4th century.

claims.statement: Accounts associate him with Tajima Province.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah mengaitkannya dengan Provinsi Tajima.
claims.quote: Amenohiboko is said to have lived in Tajima Province; the Tajima clan (多遅摩氏) and the Miyake clan have claimed to be his descendants.

claims.statement: He is revered as an ancestral deity of Tajima.
claims.statement_id: Ia dihormati sebagai dewa leluhur Tajima.
claims.quote: He is the ancestral god of Tajima Province and is supposedly enshrined in the Shinto Shrine (Izushi jinja) at Toyooka in Hyōgo Prefecture.

claims.statement: A shrine tradition links him with treasures brought from Silla.
claims.statement_id: Tujuh atau delapan pusaka yang dibawa Amenohiboko dari Silla diperkirakan tersimpan di Kuil Izushi, Prefektur Hyōgo.
claims.quote: Seven or eight treasures brought by Amenohiboko from Silla are thought to be housed in Izushi Shrine in Hyōgo Prefecture.

claims.statement: His descendant Tajimahitaka (多遅摩比多訶)'s daughter, Kazuraki no Takanukahime (葛城高顙媛), became the mother of Empress Jingū.
claims.statement_id: Putri Tajimahitaka (多遅摩比多訶), keturunannya, yaitu Kazuraki no Takanukahime (葛城高顙媛), menjadi ibu Permaisuri Jingū.
claims.quote: His descendant, Tajimahitaka (多遅摩比多訶)'s daughter, Kazuraki no Takanukahime (葛城高顙媛) became the mother of Empress Jingū

claims.statement: After accepting the offer Amenohiboko took the red ball home, where it turned into a fully grown, beautiful woman; the prince married her and they lived fairly happily until he lashed out at his new wife over a trivial cause.
claims.statement_id: Setelah menerima tawaran itu, Amenohiboko membawa bola merah pulang, dan bola itu menjadi perempuan dewasa yang sangat cantik; sang pangeran menikahinya dan mereka hidup cukup bahagia sampai Amenohiboko memarahi istrinya karena hal sepele.
claims.quote: After accepting the offer, Amenohiboko brought the red ball home, where it turned into a fully grown woman of great beauty. The prince decided to marry the woman, and the two lived relatively happily—until Amenohiboko lashed out at his new wife over a trivial cause.

claims.statement: The woman became upset and said she would return to her "homeland"; she boarded a small boat and sailed to Namba (Japan).
claims.statement_id: Sang perempuan kecewa dan menyatakan akan kembali ke "tanah airnya"; ia naik perahu kecil dan berlayar ke Namba (Jepang).
claims.quote: The woman became upset and stated that she was going to return to her "homeland"; then she got on a small boat and sailed to Namba (Japan).

claims.statement: Realizing his mistake and seeking forgiveness, Amenohiboko sailed to Namba himself, but the guardian kami prevented him from entering; he had to stop in Tajima, where he remained.
claims.statement_id: Menyadari kesalahannya dan ingin dimaafkan, Amenohiboko berlayar sendiri ke Namba, tetapi kami penjaga mencegahnya masuk; ia harus berhenti di Tajima dan menetap di sana.
claims.quote: Realizing his mistake and seeking forgiveness, Amenohiboko set sail for Namba himself, but the guardian kami prevented him from entering the land; he had to stop in Tajima, where he remained.

claims.statement: He then found another wife named "Maemitsu (前津見)"; the original wife who had arrived in Namba became a deity to its people and was called "Akaruhime (阿加流比売)".
claims.statement_id: Ia kemudian mendapat istri lain bernama "Maemitsu (前津見)"; istri pertamanya yang tiba di Namba menjadi dewi bagi penduduknya dan disebut "Akaruhime (阿加流比売)".
claims.quote: He then found another wife named "Maemitsu (前津見)". The original wife who had arrived in Namba became a deity to its people, and she was called "Akaruhime (阿加流比売)".

claims.statement: According to the Nihon Shoki, "In Kagami Village, Omi Province, there was a craftsman of Sue pottery (Sueki) who served the prince of Silla, Amenohiboko, who came to Japan."
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nihon Shoki, "Di Desa Kagami, Provinsi Omi, ada pengrajin tembikar Sue (Sueki) yang melayani pangeran Silla, Amenohiboko, yang datang ke Jepang."
claims.quote: According to the Nihon Shoki, "In Kagami Village, Omi Province, there was a craftsman of Sue pottery (Sueki) who served the prince of Silla, Amenohiboko, who came to Japan."

claims.statement: Scholars have compared the story of Akaruhime's birth from the red ball with similar legends of the region, most closely those of Dongmyeong of Goguryeo, Suro of Geumgwan Gaya and Hyeokgeose of Silla, born from eggs.
claims.statement_id: Para sarjana membandingkan kisah kelahiran Akaruhime dari bola merah dengan legenda serupa di kawasan itu, terutama tentang Dongmyeong dari Goguryeo, Suro dari Geumgwan Gaya, dan Hyeokgeose dari Silla yang lahir dari telur.
claims.quote: Scholars have compared the story of Akaruhime's birth with the red ball to similar legends that were told in the region—the most similar stories being about Dongmyeong of Goguryeo, Suro of Geumgwan Gaya and Hyeokgeose of Silla all being born from an egg.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: Amenohiboko is a person of Silla on the Korean Peninsula or a migrant god, as recorded in the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki and other sources; his name is written 天日槍 in the Nihon Shoki and 天之日矛 in the Kojiki.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Amenohiboko adalah orang Silla dari Semenanjung Korea atau dewa pendatang, seperti yang tercatat dalam Kojiki, Nihon Shoki, dan sumber lain; namanya ditulis 天日槍 dalam Nihon Shoki dan 天之日矛 dalam Kojiki.
claims.quote: アメノヒボコは、記紀等に伝わる朝鮮半島の新羅からの新羅人または渡来神。 『日本書紀』では「天日槍」、『古事記』では「天之日矛」、

claims.statement: In Japanese mythology and the Kojiki he is described as a prince of Silla, while in the Harima no Kuni Fudoki he is described as a migrant god.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Jepang dan Kojiki ia digambarkan sebagai pangeran Silla, sedangkan dalam Harima no Kuni Fudoki ia digambarkan sebagai dewa pendatang.
claims.quote: 『日本神話』・『古事記』等では新羅王子、『播磨国風土記』では渡来神と位置づけて記述される。

claims.statement: His name is written 天日槍 in the Nihon Shoki, 天之日矛 in the Kojiki, and in other texts 日桙 (ひぼこ), 天日槍命, 天日桙命 and 海檜槍 (あまのひぼこ).
claims.statement_id: Namanya ditulis 天日槍 dalam Nihon Shoki, 天之日矛 dalam Kojiki, dan dalam sumber lain 日桙 (ひぼこ), 天日槍命, 天日桙命, serta 海檜槍 (あまのひぼこ).
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』では「天日槍」、『古事記』では「天之日矛」、他文献では「日桙（ひぼこ）」のほか「天日槍命」・「天日桙命」・「海檜槍（あまのひぼこ）」とも表記される。

claims.statement: In the Harima no Kuni Fudoki, the guest god (foreign god) Amenohiboko-no-mikoto crossed the sea from the land of Kara to the bank of the Uzu River and asked the local chief Ashihara-no-Shikoo-no-mikoto for lodging land, but Shikoo allowed him to stay only in the sea.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Harima no Kuni Fudoki, dewa tamu (dewa asing) Amenohiboko-no-mikoto menyeberangi laut dari negeri Han dan tiba di tepi Sungai Uzu, lalu meminta tanah penginapan kepada kepala setempat Ashihara-no-Shikoo-no-mikoto, yang hanya mengizinkannya menginap di tengah laut.
claims.quote: 客神（外来神）の天日槍命が、韓の国から海を渡って宇頭川（揖保川・林田川の合流点付近か）の川辺に着き、当地の長たる葦原志挙乎命（あしはらのしこおのみこと）に宿所としての土地を求めると、志挙は海中に宿ることのみを許した。

claims.statement: In response Amenohiboko stirred the sea with his sword and lodged on the island that formed; Shikoo, awed by his spiritual power, went north to claim the land before him and took a meal at Iibo-oka.
claims.statement_id: Menanggapi hal itu, Amenohiboko mengaduk laut dengan pedang dan menginap di pulau yang terbentuk; Shikoo gentar akan kesaktiannya dan bergerak ke utara untuk menguasai negeri lebih dulu, lalu makan di Iibo-oka.
claims.quote: これを受けて天日槍命は剣で海をかき回し、出来た島に宿った。志挙はその霊力に畏れをなし、天日槍命よりも先に国を抑えるべく北上し、粒丘に至って食事を取った。

claims.statement: Today the spirits of the eight treasures brought by Amenohiboko are enshrined as "Izushi-no-yamae-no-ōkami", together with the spirit of Amenohiboko himself.
claims.statement_id: Kini roh delapan pusaka yang dibawa Amenohiboko dimuliakan sebagai "Izushi-no-yamae-no-ōkami", bersama roh Amenohiboko sendiri.
claims.quote: 現在では、アメノヒボコが将来した八種神宝の神霊が「伊豆志八前大神」として祀られるとともに、アメノヒボコの神霊が併せ祀られている。

claims.statement: There is a view that this is generally not the tale of a single historical person but a story symbolizing a group of immigrants from the Korean Peninsula through an ancestral god named Amenohiboko.
claims.statement_id: Ada pandangan bahwa kisah ini umumnya bukan cerita satu tokoh sejarah, melainkan kisah yang melambangkan kelompok pendatang dari Semenanjung Korea dengan leluhur-dewa bernama Amenohiboko.
claims.quote: 一般には1人の歴史上の人物の説話ではなく、朝鮮半島の土着民渡来人集団をアメノヒボコという始祖神に象徴した説話ではないかという考えもある。「アメノヒボコ（天日槍/天之日矛）」の名称自体も日本名（もしくは新羅名）であり、

claims.statement: This Himegoso deity tradition is also recorded in the Suinin chapter of the Nihon Shoki as the tale of Tsunuga-arashito; being a variation on the Amenohiboko legend, they are regarded as traditions about the same god.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi dewi Himegoso ini juga tercatat dalam bab Kaisar Suinin pada Nihon Shoki sebagai kisah Tsunuga-arashito; karena mirip dengan legenda Amenohiboko, kedua kisah dipandang sebagai tradisi tentang dewa yang sama.
claims.quote: このようなヒメコソの神の伝承は『日本書紀』垂仁天皇紀にも記され、そちらでは都怒我阿羅斯等（つぬがあらしと）の伝承として記述されるが、その伝承はアメノヒボコ伝説と同工異曲のため同一の神に関する伝承と見られている。

claims.statement: The Kojiki explains the origin of the Himegoso (Himekoso) shrine as a tale of Amenohiboko and the goddess Akaruhime, whereas the Nihon Shoki, in a note under Suinin's second year, explains it as a tale of Tsunuga-arashito and his wife.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menjelaskan asal kuil Himegoso (Himekoso) sebagai kisah Amenohiboko dan dewi Akaruhime, sedangkan Nihon Shoki, dalam catatan pada tahun ke-2 pemerintahan Kaisar Suinin, menjelaskannya sebagai kisah Tsunuga-arashito dan istrinya.
claims.quote: 後述の『古事記』では、比売碁曾社（比売許曾神社）の由来が天日槍と阿加流比売神の伝承として記述されるが、『日本書紀』では垂仁天皇2年条の注において都怒我阿羅斯等とその妻の伝承として記述されている。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi, the Silla prince Ama no hi-hoko arrived bringing one Ha-buto gem, one Ashi-daka gem, one red-stone Ukaka gem, one Idzushi short sword, one Idzushi spear, one sun-mirror and one Kuma-himorogi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi, pangeran Silla Ama no hi-hoko tiba membawa satu permata Ha-buto, satu permata Ashi-daka, satu permata Ukaka batu merah, satu pedang pendek Idzushi, satu tombak Idzushi, satu cermin matahari, dan satu Kuma-himorogi.
claims.quote: The Silla prince, Ama no hi-hoko, arrived. The objects which he brought were—one Ha-buto gem, one Ashi-daka gem, one red-stone Ukaka gem, one Idzushi short sword, one Idzushi spear, one sun-mirror, one Kuma-himorogi

claims.statement: In the Nihongi these objects were stored in the Land of Tajima and made divine things for ever.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, benda-benda itu disimpan di Negeri Tajima dan dijadikan benda ilahi untuk selamanya.
claims.quote: These were stored in the Land of Tajima, and made divine things for ever.

claims.statement: In one Nihongi version Ama no hi-hoko says that, hearing of a sage monarch in the Land of Japan, he gave his country to his younger brother Chiko and came to offer his allegiance.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu versi Nihongi, Ama no hi-hoko berkata bahwa setelah mendengar ada raja bijak di Negeri Jepang, ia menyerahkan negerinya kepada adiknya, Chiko, dan datang menyatakan kesetiaan.
claims.quote: Hearing that in the Land of Japan there was a sage monarch, I gave my country to my younger brother, Chiko, and have come to offer my allegiance

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, Ama no hi-hoko took to wife Matawo, daughter of Futomimi, a man of Idzushi in Tajima, who bore him Tajima Morosuke, father of Tajima no Hinaraki, father of Kiyohiko, father of Tajima-mori.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, Ama no hi-hoko menikahi Matawo, putri Futomimi, orang Idzushi di Tajima, yang melahirkan Tajima Morosuke, ayah Tajima no Hinaraki, ayah Kiyohiko, ayah Tajima-mori.
claims.quote: Accordingly Ama no hi-hoko took to wife Matawo, the daughter of Futomimi, a man of Idzushi in Tajima, who bore to him Tajima Morosuke, who was the father of Tajima no Hinaraki, who was the father of Kiyohiko, who was the father of Tajima-mori.

claims.statement: Aston's note: the name means "the sun-spear of Heaven" and is purely Japanese; it cannot be a Korean name.
claims.statement_id: Catatan Aston: nama ini berarti "tombak matahari dari Surga" dan murni Jepang; tidak mungkin nama Korea.
claims.quote: This means “The sun-spear of Heaven,” and is purely Japanese. It cannot be a Corean name.

claims.statement: Azumi-no-isora is a shore deity in Shinto tradition.
claims.statement_id: Azumi-no-isora adalah dewa pesisir dalam tradisi Shinto.
claims.quote: Azumi-no-isora (阿曇磯良) is a Shinto kami of the seashore.

claims.statement: He is regarded as an ancestor of the Azumi people.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap leluhur suku Azumi.
claims.quote: He is considered to be the ancestor of the Azumi people.

claims.statement: Several shrines worship him.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa kuil memujanya.
claims.quote: He is worshiped at a number of shrines, including Mekari Shrine (和布刈神社) of Kitakyushu, Shikaumi Shrine on Shika Island, and Shiga Shrine (志賀神社) of Tsushima.

claims.statement: One later legend gives him a role in a journey to the Dragon King.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda belakangan, ia berperan dalam perjalanan menuju Raja Naga.
claims.quote: Azumi-no-isora is considered a (lesser) sea deity hired as navigator to bring the emissary Takenouchi no Sukune to the Dragon King (i.e., Dragon God, Ryūjin) in the late legend regarding the loan of the tide jewels to Empress Jingū, attested in various foundation myth documents of the Hachiman cult.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: Azumi no Isora (also written 安曇磯良) is a Shinto deity, regarded as a sea god and the ancestral deity of the Azumi clan; he is also called Atobe no Isora and Isotakera.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Azumi no Isora (juga ditulis 安曇磯良) adalah dewa Shinto, dianggap dewa laut dan leluhur klan Azumi; ia juga disebut Atobe no Isora dan Isotakera.
claims.quote: 阿曇磯良（あづみのいそら、安曇磯良とも書く）は、神道の神である。海の神とされ、また、安曇氏（阿曇氏）の祖神とされる。阿度部磯良（あとべのいそら）や磯武良（いそたけら）とも。

claims.statement: The Hachiman Gudokun states that Isora is the same deity as Ame no Koyane, who is enshrined at Kasuga Taisha.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman Gudokun menyatakan bahwa Isora adalah dewa yang sama dengan Ame no Koyane yang dipuja di Kasuga Taisha.
claims.quote: また、『八幡愚童訓』では、磯良は春日大社に祀られる天児屋根命と同神であるとしている。

claims.statement: The tradition of the Isora dance is also handed down at 風浪宮 in Ōkawa, Fukuoka Prefecture, at 高祖神社 in Itoshima (高祖神楽), and in the Iwato Kagura of Nakagawa.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi Tarian Isora juga diwariskan di 風浪宮 (Kota Ōkawa, Prefektur Fukuoka), Kuil 高祖神社 (Itoshima; 高祖神楽), dan Iwato Kagura di Nakagawa.
claims.quote: この地方では福岡県大川市の風浪宮や、糸島市の高祖神社（高祖神楽）、那珂川市の岩戸神楽にも磯良の舞の伝承が伝わる。

claims.statement: Isora is also enshrined at Kasuga Taisha in Nara, where the Isora dance is offered as the Seinō dance at the Kasuga Wakamiya On-matsuri festival.
claims.statement_id: Isora juga dipuja di Kasuga Taisha di Nara, tempat Tarian Isora dipersembahkan sebagai tarian Seinō pada festival Kasuga Wakamiya On-matsuri.
claims.quote: 磯良の明神は上述したように奈良春日大社でも祀られており、春日若宮おん祭の細男（せいのう/せいのお/さいのお）と称して磯良の舞が奉納される。

claims.statement: The Kasuga Taisha dance depicts the story in which Empress Jingū, told by an old man on the Tsukushi shore that dancing the Seinō would make Isora appear and grant the jewels, had it danced and Isora appeared hiding his ugly shell-covered face with white cloth; the dancers wear white-cloth masks.
claims.statement_id: Tarian di Kasuga Taisha menggambarkan kisah ketika Permaisuri Jingū, setelah mendengar dari seorang tua di pantai Tsukushi bahwa menari Seinō akan memunculkan Isora yang memberi permata, menyuruh orang menari lalu Isora yang menyembunyikan wajah buruk berkerang dengan kain putih muncul; para penari memakai penutup wajah kain putih.
claims.quote: 春日大社のそれは、筑紫の浜で老人から「細男の舞をすれば、磯良が出てきて干珠・満珠を授ける」と聞いた神功皇后が舞わせたところ、貝殻のついた醜い顔を白布で隠した磯良が現れたという物語を表現したもので、白布の覆面姿の男たちが舞う。

claims.statement: According to the official Shikaumi Shrine site, when sending forces to the Three Han Empress Jingū summoned Azumi no Isora of Shika Island, received the ebb and flood tide jewels from the dragon god, and returned after pacifying the Three Han.
claims.statement_id: Menurut situs resmi Kuil Shikaumi, saat mengirim pasukan ke Tiga Han, Permaisuri Jingū memanggil Azumi no Isora dari Pulau Shika, menerima permata surut dan pasang dari dewa naga, lalu kembali setelah menaklukkan Tiga Han.
claims.quote: 神功皇后は三韓出兵に際して、志賀島の阿曇磯良を召されました。そして龍神より干珠満珠を授かり、無事に三韓を平定して帰還されました。

claims.statement: According to shrine tradition, between the second and fourth centuries the shrine 表津宮 was moved to its present site at the foot of 勝山, and the Azumi people, who take the three 綿津見三神 deities as ancestral deities, have served the shrine for generations.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi kuil, antara abad ke-2 dan ke-4 kuil 表津宮 dipindahkan ke lokasi sekarang di kaki 勝山, dan suku Azumi, yang menjadikan tiga dewa 綿津見三神 sebagai leluhur, melayani kuil itu turun-temurun.
claims.quote: 二世紀から四世紀の間に表津宮を勝山の麓である現在の場所に遷座し、併せて仲津綿津見神、表津綿津見神が奉祀されたと伝えられています。綿津見三神を祖神とする阿曇族が代々奉斎してきました。

claims.statement: On Shika Island, the place where kagura was played for seven days and nights to summon Azumi no Isora from the sea country is called 舞能ヶ浜; the place where the empress dismounted is 下馬ヶ浜, and the place where the horse whinnied with joy is 勝馬.
claims.statement_id: Di Pulau Shika, tempat kagura dimainkan tujuh hari tujuh malam untuk memanggil Azumi no Isora dari negeri laut disebut 舞能ヶ浜; tempat sang permaisuri turun dari kuda disebut 下馬ヶ浜, dan tempat kuda meringkik gembira disebut 勝馬.
claims.quote: 阿曇磯良を海国から召し出そうと7日7晩神楽を奏したところが舞能ヶ浜、志賀島にお着きになり願いがかなったと仰せられたところが叶ヶ浜、皇后が馬から下りられたところが下馬ヶ浜、志賀大明神に奉賽した際に馬が喜びいなないたので勝馬となったといわれています。

claims.statement: According to the Taiheiki, Empress Jingū summoned the gods of heaven and earth to Kashima in Hitachi; all came except Atobe no Isora, who had manifested himself on the sea floor.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Taiheiki, Permaisuri Jingū memanggil para dewa langit dan bumi ke Kashima di Hitachi; semuanya datang, kecuali Atobe no Isora yang menampakkan diri di dasar laut.
claims.quote: 皇后諸の天神地祇を請じ給ふに、日本一万の大小の神祇冥道、皆勅請に随て常陸の鹿島に来給ふ。雖然、海底に迹を垂給阿度部の磯良一人不応召。

claims.statement: The Taiheiki records that, after the gods sang, Isora could not hold back and came to the gods' playing ground; shellfish, clams and seaweed-dwelling insects clung to his body so that he did not look like a human at all.
claims.statement_id: Taiheiki mencatat bahwa setelah para dewa menyanyi, Isora tak tahan lagi dan datang ke tempat pesta dewa; tubuhnya ditempeli kerang, kerang laut, dan serangga rumput laut sehingga sama sekali tidak tampak seperti manusia.
claims.quote: 磯良感に堪兼て、神遊の庭にぞ参たる。其貌を御覧ずるに、細螺・石花貝・藻に棲虫、手足五体に取付て、更に人の形にては無りけり。

claims.statement: Isora was then made the messenger to borrow the ebb and flood jewels (kanju and manju) treasured in the dragon palace, and the dragon god promptly presented the two jewels.
claims.statement_id: Isora kemudian dijadikan utusan untuk meminjam permata surut dan pasang (kanju dan manju) yang menjadi harta istana naga; dewa naga segera menyerahkan kedua permata itu.
claims.quote: 軈て是を御使にて、竜宮城に宝とする干珠・満珠を被借召。竜神即応神勅二の玉を奉る。

claims.statement: According to Heibonsha's encyclopedia, he is an ancient spirit who appears in traditions from the medieval period onward, and is also called Atobe no Isora.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Heibonsha (Sekai Daihyakka Jiten), ia adalah roh kuno yang muncul dalam tradisi sejak abad pertengahan, dan juga disebut Atobe no Isora.
claims.quote: 中世以降の伝承に現れる古代の精霊。阿度部（あとべの）磯良ともいう。

claims.statement: The Heibonsha encyclopedia's author interprets the Azumi as an ancient clan that supervised the ama (sea people), and Isora as probably a half-divine, half-human shaman handed down among them.
claims.statement_id: Penulis ensiklopedia Heibonsha menafsirkan bahwa klan Azumi adalah bangsawan kuno pemimpin para ama (pelaut dan penyelam), dan Isora mungkin seorang syaman setengah dewa setengah manusia yang diwariskan di antara mereka.
claims.quote: 安曇氏は海人（あま）を宰領した古代豪族で，おそらく安曇磯良は海人の間に伝承された半神半人のシャーマンであったかと思われる。

claims.statement: The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten calls him a god of the sea floor said to live in Chikuzen and the enshrined deity of Shikaumi Shrine on Shika Island, Fukuoka; he is attested in 「九州道の記」 and the 「八幡愚童訓」.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten menyebutnya dewa dasar laut yang konon tinggal di Chikuzen dan dewa utama Kuil Shikaumi di Pulau Shika, Fukuoka; ia tercantum dalam 「九州道の記」 dan 「八幡愚童訓」.
claims.quote: 筑前に住むといわれた海底の神。福岡市東区志賀島の志賀海神社の祭神。「九州道の記」「八幡愚童訓」に所見。

claims.statement: Binbōgami is a poverty-associated kami in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Binbōgami adalah kami yang berkaitan dengan kemiskinan dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: A binbōgami (貧乏神; lit. "kami of poverty") is a kami (god or spirit) in Japanese folklore said to inhabit a person or their house, bringing poverty and misery.

claims.statement: It appears in tales, essays and stage storytelling.
claims.statement_id: Ia muncul dalam cerita, esai, dan pertunjukan kisah.
claims.quote: References to binbōgami appear in classic Japanese tales, essays, and rakugo performances.

claims.statement: A binbōgami typically appears as a skinny, dirty old man with a pale complexion, often carrying a paper fan (shibu-uchiwa) and wearing a sad expression.
claims.statement_id: Binbōgami biasanya digambarkan sebagai lelaki tua yang kurus, kotor, dan berwajah pucat, sering membawa kipas kertas (shibu-uchiwa) dan berwajah sedih.
claims.quote: A binbōgami typically appears as a skinny, dirty old man with a pale complexion, often carrying a paper fan (shibu-uchiwa) and wearing a sad expression.
