claims.statement: When inhabiting a house, binbōgami reportedly prefer to live in closets.
claims.statement_id: Bila menghuni sebuah rumah, binbōgami dikatakan lebih suka tinggal di lemari (closet).
claims.quote: When inhabiting a house, they reportedly prefer to live in closets.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: the binbōgami is a god who makes the person it possesses and their family poor; its name appears in folktales, essays and rakugo across Japan.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Binbōgami adalah dewa yang membuat orang yang dihinggapinya beserta keluarganya menjadi miskin; namanya terdapat dalam dongeng, esai, dan rakugo di berbagai daerah Jepang.
claims.quote: 貧乏神（びんぼうがみ）は、取りついた人間やその家族を貧乏にする神。日本各地の昔話、随筆、落語などに名が見られる。

claims.statement: Being a god it cannot be exterminated, but ways of driving it off exist; in Niigata, lighting a fire in the irori hearth on New Year's Eve is said to make the binbōgami flee from the heat while a god of fortune comes in its place, pleased by the warmth.
claims.statement_id: Karena ia adalah dewa, binbōgami tidak dapat dibunuh, tetapi ada cara mengusirnya; di Niigata, menyalakan api di perapian irori pada malam tahun baru dipercaya membuatnya kepanasan dan pergi, sementara dewa keberuntungan datang karena senang pada kehangatannya.
claims.quote: 仮にも神なので退治することは出来ないが、追い払う方法はないわけではない。新潟では、大晦日の夜に囲炉裏で火を焚くと、貧乏神が熱がって逃げていくが、代わりに暖かさを喜んで福の神がやって来るとされる。

claims.statement: The term binbōgami itself goes back to the Muromachi period; a record of Kyoto devastated by the Ōnin War contains a rumor of June 1481 (Bunmei 13) that the wives of the fortune gods of Sakai entered the capital while their husbands, the binbōgami of Kyoto, went down to Sakai.
claims.statement_id: Istilah 貧乏神 sendiri dapat ditelusuri hingga zaman Muromachi; sebuah catatan tentang Kyoto yang rusak akibat Perang Ōnin memuat desas-desus pada Juni 1481 (Bunmei 13) bahwa para istri dewa keberuntungan Sakai memasuki ibu kota sementara para suami mereka, binbōgami Kyoto, turun ke Sakai.
claims.quote: 貧乏神という表現自体は、古くは室町時代にまでさかのぼり、応仁の乱で荒廃した京の記録として、「文明13年（1481年）6月、堺の福神の女房達が入洛し、京都の貧乏神の男達が堺へ下った」という風説があり

claims.statement: According to the poet 中村光行, the binbōgami loves miso, and holds a fan to waft and enjoy its aroma.
claims.statement_id: Menurut penyair 中村光行, binbōgami menyukai miso dan memegang kipas untuk mengipasi serta menikmati aroma miso itu.
claims.quote: 詩人・中村光行によれば、貧乏神は味噌が好物で、団扇を手にしているのはこの味噌の芳香を扇いで楽しむためとされている。

claims.statement: The binbōgami of 『日本永代蔵』 is regarded as a god who turns poverty into fortune and is now enshrined as the Ōta Shrine beside Ushi-Tenjin Kitano Shrine in Kasuga, Bunkyō, Tokyo; one makes a wish, welcomes it into the home, and after 21 days respectfully sends it off to sever ties with it.
claims.statement_id: Binbōgami dalam 『日本永代蔵』 dianggap dewa yang mengubah kemiskinan menjadi keberuntungan, dan kini dipuja sebagai Kuil Ōta di samping Ushi-Tenjin Kitano Shrine di Kasuga, Bunkyō, Tokyo; orang mengundangnya ke rumah dan setelah 21 hari melepasnya dengan hormat agar terputus hubungannya dengan kemiskinan.
claims.quote: 前述の『日本永代蔵』の貧乏神は貧乏を福に転じる神とされ、現在では東京都文京区春日の牛天神北野神社の脇に「太田神社」として祠が祀られている、祠に願掛けをして貧乏神を一旦家に招きいれ、満願の21日目に丁寧に祀って送り出すと、貧乏神と縁が切れるといわれている。

claims.statement: Related to the belief that the binbōgami likes baked miso, there was a binbōgami-sending-off ritual in Senba, Osaka until around Meiji 10; at the end of each month miso was baked in merchants' houses and a head clerk carried the plate-shaped miso around the houses, filling the area with a savory smell.
claims.statement_id: Berkaitan dengan anggapan bahwa binbōgami menyukai miso panggang, di Senba, Osaka, hingga sekitar tahun Meiji 10 terdapat upacara melepas binbōgami; tiap akhir bulan di rumah para pedagang miso dipanggang, lalu seorang kepala pelayan membawa miso berbentuk piring itu berkeliling rumah sehingga aroma harum memenuhi tempat itu.
claims.quote: 貧乏神が焼き味噌を好むという説に関連し、大阪の船場には明治10年頃まで貧乏神送りの行事があった。毎月末、船場の商人の家で味噌を焼き、それを皿状にしたものを番頭が持って家々を回り、香ばしい匂いがあちこちに満ちる。

claims.statement: At Myōsen-ji temple in Taitō, Tokyo, there is also a stone statue of a binbōgami modeled on the binbōgami of Hudson's game series 『桃太郎』.
claims.statement_id: Di kuil Myōsen-ji, Taitō, Tokyo, terdapat pula patung batu binbōgami yang motifnya diambil dari binbōgami dalam seri game 『桃太郎』 buatan Hudson.
claims.quote: 東京都台東区の妙泉寺にも貧乏神の石像（モチーフはハドソンのゲーム『桃太郎シリーズ』に登場する貧乏神）が祀られている。

claims.statement: The proverb 「柿団扇は貧乏神がつく」 comes from the belief that a binbōgami attaches itself to astringent-persimmon fans.
claims.statement_id: Peribahasa 「柿団扇は貧乏神がつく」 berasal dari kepercayaan bahwa binbōgami melekat pada kipas berlapis tanin kesemek.
claims.quote: ことわざの「柿団扇は貧乏神がつく」は、渋団扇に貧乏神が憑くという俗信からきている。

claims.statement: In renga the term appears in Arakida Moritake's 『守武千句』 (Tenbun 9 / 1540).
claims.statement_id: Dalam renga, istilah ini terdapat pada 『守武千句』 karya Arakida Moritake (Tenbun 9 / 1540).
claims.quote: 連歌の記述例としては、荒木田守武の『守武千句』墨何第10（天文9年 / 1540年）に見られる。

claims.statement: Nipponica: a god who settles in a house and impoverishes it; an urban belief that began to appear in early-modern essays, pictured as a shabby figure like a beggar monk with a bluish-dark face, sunken eyes and a thin body.
claims.statement_id: Nipponica: dewa yang menetap di rumah dan memiskinkan rumah itu; kepercayaan perkotaan yang mulai muncul dalam esai zaman awal modern, digambarkan berpenampilan lusuh seperti biksu pengemis dengan wajah kebiruan, mata cekung, dan tubuh kurus.
claims.quote: 家に居着いてその家を貧乏にさせるという神。近世の随筆類から現れ始めた都市的な俗信である。乞食(こじき)坊主のようなしょぼくれた姿をしており、顔は青黒く、目は落ち込んで、体はやせているという。

claims.statement: Heibonsha: the binbōgami appears in documents, short tales and rakugo from the early-modern period when a money economy developed; if the house it haunts venerates it respectfully, it turns into a fortune god bringing wealth, and some became popular gods like the binbōgami beside Ushi-Tenjin in Koishikawa, Tokyo.
claims.statement_id: Heibonsha: binbōgami muncul dalam tulisan, cerita pendek, dan rakugo sejak zaman modern awal ketika ekonomi uang berkembang; bila rumah yang dihinggapinya memujanya dengan hormat, ia berubah menjadi dewa keberuntungan pembawa kekayaan, dan ada yang menjadi dewa yang digemari seperti binbōgami di dekat Ushi-Tenjin, Koishikawa, Tokyo.
claims.quote: 貧乏神は貨幣経済の発達をみた近世以後の文献や小咄・落語などに登場するが，注意されるのは貧乏神に憑かれた家でこの神を丁重にまつると逆に富や福をもたらす福神に転化することであり，こうして東京小石川の牛天神のそばの貧乏神のように流行神（はやりがみ）となった貧乏神もある。

claims.statement: Heibonsha: China too once had a rite called 送窮 or 送窮鬼, sending the poverty god out of the house on New Year's Eve or the last day of the first month and welcoming gods of fortune and prosperity.
claims.statement_id: Heibonsha: di Tiongkok dahulu juga ada upacara 送窮 atau 送窮鬼, mengirim keluar dewa kemiskinan dari rumah pada malam tahun baru atau akhir bulan pertama dan menyambut dewa keberuntungan serta kemakmuran.
claims.quote: 中国にもかつては〈送窮〉とか〈送窮鬼〉といい，大晦日や正月晦日などに家の中の貧乏神を送り出し，福禄の神を迎えて一年の幸福と安寧を祈る行事があった。

claims.statement: Nipponica: there are beliefs that the binbōgami attaches itself to astringent-persimmon fans, likes the smell of baked miso, and appears when the hearth fire is allowed to die out; there is also a way of sending it off by floating baked miso down a river.
claims.statement_id: Nipponica: ada kepercayaan bahwa binbōgami melekat pada kipas tanin, menyukai bau miso panggang, dan muncul bila bara perapian dibiarkan padam; ada pula cara melepasnya dengan menghanyutkan miso panggang ke sungai.
claims.quote: 渋うちわに貧乏神がつくとか、貧乏神は焼きみそのにおいを好むとか、いろりの火種を絶やすと貧乏神が出るなどの俗信があり、焼きみそを川に流して貧乏神を送り出す作法もある。

claims.statement: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten: it is said to appear like a beggar monk, aged and pale, holding a torn astringent-persimmon fan with a sad air.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten: ia konon muncul seperti biksu pengemis, tua renta, berwajah pucat, memegang kipas tanin yang sobek dengan tampang sedih.
claims.quote: 乞食坊主のような姿で、老いさらばえて色青ざめ、破れた渋団扇(しぶうちわ)を持って悲しそうな姿で現われるという。

claims.statement: Biwa-bokuboku (琵琶牧々, "Biwa goblin") is a being from Japanese folklore, described in this source as fictitious.
claims.statement_id: Biwa-bokuboku (琵琶牧々, "goblin biwa") adalah makhluk dalam cerita rakyat Jepang yang disebut fiktif dalam sumber ini.
claims.quote: The Biwa-bokuboku (Japanese: 琵琶牧々; meaning "Biwa goblin") is a fictitious being from Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: Its head resembles a biwa lute.
claims.statement_id: Kepalanya menyerupai kecapi biwa.
claims.quote: The Biwa-bokuboku is described as an anthropomorphic being with the head of a traditional biwa.

claims.statement: Some stories have it play music at night while lamenting its neglect.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebagian cerita, ia memainkan musik pada malam hari sambil meratapi pengabaian pemiliknya.
claims.quote: The Biwa-bokuboku comes to life at night and sits calmly in a tatami room, singing and plinking while lamenting the neglect of his former owner.

claims.statement: It belongs to the group of animated objects called tsukumogami.
claims.statement_id: Ia tergolong benda hidup yang disebut tsukumogami.
claims.quote: The Biwa-bokuboku belongs to a special group of yōkai: the Tsukumogami (Japanese: 付喪神, lit. 'artifact ghosts').

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: Biwa-bokuboku is a Japanese yōkai in Toriyama Sekien's yōkai picture collection 『百器徒然袋』, a yōkai of the biwa.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: Biwa-bokuboku adalah yōkai Jepang dalam kumpulan gambar yōkai 『百器徒然袋』 karya Toriyama Sekien, yaitu yōkai berupa biwa.
claims.quote: 琵琶牧々（びわぼくぼく）は、鳥山石燕による妖怪画集『百器徒然袋』にある日本の妖怪の一つで、琵琶の妖怪。

claims.statement: It is drawn as a biwa that has transformed into a biwa-hōshi or zatō (blind biwa player); its body is like a human but its head is a biwa, with eyes closed and leaning on a cane.
claims.statement_id: Ia digambarkan sebagai biwa yang berubah menjadi biwa-hōshi atau zatō (pemain biwa buta); tubuhnya seperti manusia tetapi kepalanya biwa, matanya tertutup, dan ia bertumpu pada tongkat.
claims.quote: 琵琶が琵琶法師・座頭のすがたに変化した姿で描かれている。体は人間のようだが、頭部は琵琶であり、目を閉じ杖をついている。

claims.statement: In his caption Sekien states that the name 「牧々」 comes from 「牧馬」 (Bokuba), a biwa known as a famous instrument.
claims.statement_id: Dalam keterangannya, Sekien menyebut bahwa nama 「牧々」 berasal dari 「牧馬」 (Bokuba), biwa terkenal yang dianggap pusaka.
claims.quote: 石燕による解説文には「玄上牧馬と言へる琵琶はいにしへの名器にしてふしぎたびたびありければ そのぼく馬（牧馬）のびは（琵琶）の転にして ぼくぼくといふにや」とあり、この妖怪の「牧々」という名称は琵琶の名器として知られる「牧馬」から名前がついているとしている。

claims.statement: It is thought to have been modeled on the biwa yōkai pulling a koto yōkai in the Muromachi-period scroll 『百鬼夜行絵巻』, and Koto-furunushi appears on the same spread as Biwa-bokuboku.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap digambar berdasarkan yōkai biwa yang menarik yōkai koto dalam gulungan 『百鬼夜行絵巻』 dari zaman Muromachi, dan pada halaman yang sama dengan Biwa-bokuboku dimuat pula Koto-furunushi.
claims.quote: 室町時代の妖怪絵巻『百鬼夜行絵巻』に描かれている琴の妖怪を引っ張っている琵琶の妖怪がモデルになって描かれたと考えられており、琵琶牧々と同じ見開きには琴古主が掲載されている。

claims.statement: The ukiyo-e artist Tsukioka Yoshitoshi drew a work apparently based on Sekien's Biwa-bokuboku in the color print 『百器夜行』 (1865).
claims.statement_id: Seniman ukiyo-e Tsukioka Yoshitoshi tampaknya menggambar karya yang mengacu pada Biwa-bokuboku Sekien dalam cetakan berwarna 『百器夜行』 (1865).
claims.quote: 浮世絵師・月岡芳年は錦絵『百器夜行』（1865年）に石燕の琵琶牧々を参考にしたと見られる絵を描いている。

claims.statement: The Kamakura-period court-practice book 『禁秘抄』 records two famous biwa, Genjō and Bokuba; Genjō is said to have leapt out by itself when the palace burned, and an oni enchanted by its tone stole it and lowered it on a cord from Suzaku Gate.
claims.statement_id: Kitab 『禁秘抄』 dari zaman Kamakura mencatat dua biwa termasyhur, Genjō dan Bokuba; Genjō konon melompat keluar sendiri saat istana terbakar, dan oni yang terpesona oleh bunyinya mencurinya lalu menurunkannya dengan tali dari Gerbang Suzaku.
claims.quote: 鎌倉時代の有職故実書『禁秘抄』には、「玄上（げんじょう）」と「牧馬（ぼくば）」という琵琶の名器があり、特に玄上の方は、内裏が焼失したときにひとりでに外へ飛び出したり、その音色に魅せられた鬼がこれを盗み出して、朱雀門から紐で吊り下ろしたといった不思議なことがあった、という逸話が記されている。

claims.statement: Yokai.com: the biwa bokuboku is a biwa that has grown a human body and is dressed like a blind priest, wielding a cane.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: Biwa bokuboku adalah biwa yang tumbuh tubuh manusia dan berpakaian seperti pendeta buta sambil memegang tongkat.
claims.quote: The biwa bokuboku is a biwa that has grown a human body and is dressed like a blind priest, wielding a cane.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: a biwa of extremely fine construction, upon reaching an advanced age, transforms into the self-playing biwa instrument known as a biwa bokuboku; this musical tsukumogami wanders playing music in the street for money.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: biwa yang dibuat sangat baik, setelah mencapai usia lanjut, berubah menjadi biwa yang bermain sendiri; tsukumogami musikal ini berkeliaran memainkan musik di jalan demi uang.
claims.quote: A biwa of extremely fine construction, upon reaching an advanced age, transforms into the self-playing biwa instrument known as a biwa bokuboku. This musical tsukumogami wanders playing music in the street for money.

claims.statement: Yokai.com: these tsukumogami take their name from a legendary biwa named Bokuba, said to play magically on its own when nobody was looking.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com: nama tsukumogami ini berasal dari biwa legendaris bernama Bokuba, yang konon bermain sendiri secara ajaib bila tak ada yang melihat.
claims.quote: These tsukumogami get their name from a legendary biwa named Bokuba. This magnificent instrument was said to magically play on its own when nobody was looking.

claims.statement: Kotobank (Daijisen Plus): a yōkai drawn in the picture collection of the Edo-period painter Toriyama Sekien; a kind of tsukumogami, a biwa that has transformed into a biwa-hōshi.
claims.statement_id: Kotobank (Daijisen Plus): yōkai yang digambar dalam kumpulan gambar karya pelukis zaman Edo Toriyama Sekien; sejenis tsukumogami, yaitu biwa yang berubah menjadi sosok biwa-hōshi.
claims.quote: 江戸時代の画家、鳥山石燕(せきえん)の画集「画図百器徒然袋」に描かれた妖怪。付喪神(つくもがみ)の一種で、琵琶が琵琶法師の姿に化けたもの。

claims.statement: According to English Wikipedia, tsukumogami may also meet other tsukumogami and throw noisy parties, or leave home and stroll around in search of others with whom to commiserate.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Inggris, tsukumogami juga dapat berkumpul dengan sesamanya untuk berpesta gaduh, atau meninggalkan rumah berkeliling mencari teman senasib.
claims.quote: Alternatively, they meet with other Tsukumogami and throw noisy parties or they leave home and stroll around in search of others with whom to commiserate.

claims.statement: According to English Wikipedia, the Biwa-bokuboku was modeled after the biwa (琵琶), a short-necked, wooden lute.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Inggris, Biwa-bokuboku dimodelkan dari biwa (琵琶), lute kayu berleher pendek.
claims.quote: The Biwa-bokuboku was modeled after the biwa (琵琶), a short-necked, wooden lute.

claims.statement: Chimimōryō is a term for supernatural beings of mountains and waterways.
claims.statement_id: Chimimōryō adalah istilah bagi makhluk gaib pegunungan dan perairan.
claims.quote: Chimei wangliang, or Chimimōryō (Chinese: 魑魅魍魉; pinyin: Chīmèi wǎngliǎng; Japanese: 魑魅魍魎 [ちみもうりょう]; rōmaji: chimimōryō), is a term that refers to monsters of the mountains and monsters of the rivers.

claims.statement: The term originates in ancient Chinese writings.
claims.statement_id: Istilah ini berasal dari tulisan Tiongkok kuno.
claims.quote: The term originated in China roughly 2,500 years ago in ancient chronicles such as the Zuo Zhuan.

claims.statement: Older legends portray such spirits as harmful to people.
claims.statement_id: Legenda lama menggambarkan roh-roh tersebut membahayakan manusia.
claims.quote: It originates from ancient Chinese legends about the spirits that harm people in the mountains and swamps, and its original meaning is "all kinds of Yaoguai (demons and ghosts)".

claims.statement: Wangliang (魍魎; mōryō in Japanese), one component of the term, are considered to be spirits from mountains and rivers, and trees and rocks.
claims.statement_id: Wangliang (魍魎; mōryō dalam bahasa Jepang), salah satu unsur istilah itu, dianggap roh dari gunung dan sungai, serta pohon dan batu.
claims.quote: Wangliang (魍魎; mōryō in Japanese) are considered to be spirits from mountains and rivers, and trees and rocks.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: 魑魅魍魎 (chimi-mōryō) means monsters of mountains and monsters of rivers, and various yōkai; chimi are mountain apparitions and mōryō river apparitions, and the name is commonly used for all the apparitions of mountains and rivers.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: 魑魅魍魎 (chimi-mōryō) adalah monster gunung dan monster sungai serta beragam yōkai; chimi adalah makhluk gaib gunung dan mōryō makhluk gaib sungai, dan nama ini umumnya dipakai untuk semua makhluk gaib gunung dan sungai.
claims.quote: 魑魅魍魎（ちみもうりょう）とは、山の怪物や川の怪物。様々な妖怪変化。魑魅は山の怪、魍魎は川の怪であり、一般には山河全ての怪として魑魅魍魎の名で用いられることが多い。

claims.statement: Chimi is said to be a monster born of the strange vapors of mountain forests, with a human face and an animal body, that leads people astray; the Heian-period dictionary 『和名類聚抄』 classes it as a kind of oni called sudama, and the Edo-period encyclopedia 『和漢三才図会』 calls it a mountain god.
claims.statement_id: Chimi disebut monster yang lahir dari hawa aneh hutan gunung, berwajah manusia dan bertubuh binatang, serta menyesatkan orang; 『和名類聚抄』 zaman Heian menggolongkannya sejenis oni bernama sudama, dan 『和漢三才図会』 zaman Edo menyebutnya dewa gunung.
claims.quote: 魑魅とは、山林の異気（瘴気）から生ずるという怪物のことといわれている。顔は人間、体は獣の姿をしていて、人を迷わせる。平安時代中期の辞書『和名類聚抄』ではスダマという和名の鬼の一種とされ、江戸時代の百科事典『和漢三才図会』では山の神とされる。

claims.statement: Mōryō are regarded as spirits of rivers, trees and rocks; they arise from the vital energy of all natural things and bewitch people, are said to eat the dead, and look like young children standing on two legs, with dark red skin, red eyes, long ears, beautiful hair and a human-like voice.
claims.statement_id: Mōryō dianggap roh sungai, pohon, dan batu; ia lahir dari hawa semua benda alam dan menipu manusia, konon memakan orang mati, berwujud seperti anak kecil yang berdiri dengan dua kaki, berkulit merah kehitaman, bermata merah, bertelinga panjang, berambut indah, dan bersuara seperti manusia.
claims.quote: 魍魎は川や木石の精霊とされる。山・水・木・石などあらゆる自然物の精気から生じ、人を化かす。また、死者を食べるとも言われ、姿かたちは幼児に似ていて、2本足で立ち、赤黒色の皮膚をして、目は赤く、耳は長く、美しい髪と人に似た声をしている。

claims.statement: In 『和漢三才図会』 mōryō is a water god and in the 『春秋左氏伝』 a god of marshes; it is said to fear tigers and can be avoided by placing a tiger image and cypress.
claims.statement_id: Dalam 『和漢三才図会』 mōryō adalah dewa air, dan dalam 『春秋左氏伝』 dewa rawa; ia konon takut harimau dan dapat dihindari dengan menaruh patung harimau dan pohon cemara.
claims.quote: 『和漢三才図会』では水神、古代中国の書『春秋左氏伝』では水沢の神とされる。虎を恐れるとされ、虎の像と柏を置いておくと避けられる。

claims.statement: Etymology has many theories; according to the 『史記』 (Annals of the Five Emperors), 魑 is a tiger-shaped mountain god and 魅 a swamp god with a boar head and human form, from which the image of a monster combining various beasts' traits is surmised to have grown.
claims.statement_id: Asal kata punya banyak teori; menurut 『史記』 (Lima Kaisar), 魑 adalah dewa gunung berbentuk harimau dan 魅 dewa rawa berkepala babi hutan bertubuh manusia, dari sini diduga muncul citra monster berbagai sifat hewan.
claims.quote: 語源に関しては諸説あるが、古代中国の妖怪か精の一種とされる。『史記』（五帝本紀）によると、魑は虎の形をした山神、魅は猪頭人形の沢神とされ、ここから色々な獣の属性を併せ持った怪物のイメージが膨らんだ、と推測される。

claims.statement: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten: 「魑魅」 is a monster born of the vapors of mountains and forests and 「魍魎」 a spirit of mountains, rivers, trees and rocks; together the word means various yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten: 「魑魅」 adalah makhluk gaib yang lahir dari hawa gunung dan hutan, dan 「魍魎」 roh gunung, sungai, pohon, dan batu; secara umum berarti beragam yōkai.
claims.quote: ( 「魑魅」は山林の気から生じるばけもの、「魍魎」は山川や木石の精霊 ) いろいろな妖怪変化。種々のばけもの。

claims.statement: Heibonsha: a note to China's 《左伝》 says that 魑魅 is something born of the strange vapors of mountains and rivers that harms people.
claims.statement_id: Heibonsha: catatan atas 《左伝》 Tiongkok menyatakan bahwa 魑魅 adalah sesuatu yang lahir dari hawa aneh gunung dan sungai dan mencelakai orang.
claims.quote: 中国の《左伝》の注に〈魑魅は山川の異気の生む所にして人に害をなすもの〉

claims.statement: Heibonsha: since these are local spirits that do not submit to the centralized order of gods, meeting them without any preparation was considered dangerous.
claims.statement_id: Heibonsha: karena roh-roh ini bersifat lokal dan tidak tunduk pada tatanan dewa yang tersentralisasi, bertemu mereka tanpa persiapan dianggap berbahaya.
claims.quote: これらは地方的な精霊であるため，中央集権的な神々の体制には服さず，それゆえ，人々が何の準備もなくこうした精霊と遭遇するのは危険であるとされた。

claims.statement: Kotobank: the phrase is also written 「魑魅罔両」, which seems to be the original form, but as an idiom 「魑魅魍魎」, with all four characters given a matching form, is used more often.
claims.statement_id: Kotobank: istilah ini juga ditulis 「魑魅罔両」, yang tampaknya bentuk aslinya, tetapi sebagai idiom lebih banyak dipakai 「魑魅魍魎」 dengan keempat karakter berbentuk serasi.
claims.quote: 「魑魅罔両」とも書き、こちらのほうが本来のようです。でも、熟語としては、四字とも字形をそろえた「魑魅魍魎」が多く使われます。

claims.statement: Kotobank: in the 「春秋左氏伝」 explanation, 「魑」 is a mountain god, 「魅」 a monster and 「魍魎」 a water god; other books explain it differently, so it need not be taken too strictly.
claims.statement_id: Kotobank: menurut penjelasan 「春秋左氏伝」, 「魑」 adalah dewa gunung, 「魅」 monster, dan 「魍魎」 dewa air; kitab lain menjelaskannya berbeda sehingga tak perlu dipahami terlalu ketat.
claims.quote: では「魑」は山の神、「魅」は怪物、「魍魎」は水の神と説明します。他の書物ではまた説明が違うので、あまり厳密に考えなくてもかまわないでしょう。

claims.statement: In modern Japanese, 「魑魅魍魎」 often no longer means mere monsters but people who are as inscrutable as monsters.
claims.statement_id: Dalam bahasa Jepang modern, 「魑魅魍魎」 sering tidak lagi berarti sekadar makhluk gaib, melainkan orang-orang yang tak jelas jati dirinya seperti makhluk gaib.
claims.quote: 現代日本語で「魑魅魍魎」と言えば、単なるばけものではなく、多くは、ばけもののように得体の知れない人間たちを指します。

claims.statement: Zuo Zhuan text (Wang Sunman's reply to the Prince of Chu): when Xia had virtue, tripods were cast with images of things so that the people would know the spirits and the harmful; so people entering rivers, marshes, mountains and forests would not meet harmful things, and 螭魅罔兩 could not meet them.
claims.statement_id: Teks Zuo Zhuan (jawaban Wang Sunman kepada Pangeran Chu): ketika Xia berbudi, tripod dicetak dengan gambar segala hal agar rakyat mengenali yang gaib dan merugikan; maka orang yang memasuki sungai, rawa, gunung, dan hutan tidak bertemu hal yang merugikan, dan 螭魅罔兩 tidak dapat menjumpai mereka.
claims.quote: 昔夏之方有德也，遠方圖物，貢金九牧，鑄鼎象物，百物而為之備，使民知神姦。故民入川澤山林，不逢不若，螭魅罔兩，莫能逢之。

claims.statement: Context: King Ding sent Wang Sunman to receive the Prince of Chu; the prince asked about the size and weight of the tripods, and was answered that what matters is virtue, not the tripods.
claims.statement_id: Konteksnya: Raja Ding mengutus Wang Sunman menyambut Pangeran Chu; sang pangeran menanyakan ukuran dan berat tripod, dan dijawab bahwa yang menentukan adalah kebajikan, bukan tripod.
claims.quote: 定王使王孫滿勞楚子。楚子問鼎之大小輕重焉。對曰：「在德不在鼎。

claims.statement: Harionago is a Japanese yōkai said to prey on young men.
claims.statement_id: Harionago adalah yōkai Jepang yang konon memangsa pria muda.
claims.quote: a yokai in Japanese folklore that preys on young men.

claims.statement: She is said to appear on roads in Shikoku.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon muncul di jalanan Shikoku.
claims.quote: Harionago appears along roads on the island of Shikoku as an attractive young woman with long black hair.

claims.statement: Stories give her long hair tipped with hooks.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah memberinya rambut panjang berujung kait.
claims.quote: The strands of her hair are prehensile and tipped with sharp barbed hooks.

claims.statement: A tale says she attacks a man who laughs back at her.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menyebut ia menyerang pria yang membalas tawanya.
claims.quote: When a man approaches her on a pathway, she laughs and, if he laughs in return, she attacks the man with her barbed hair.

claims.statement: Once she has trapped him, she devours him.
claims.statement_id: Setelah berhasil menjerat korbannya, ia memakannya.
claims.quote: Once she has him trapped, she devours him.

claims.statement: In one story the man survived by breaking free and locking himself in his house; Harionago left many deep gashes in the wooden door before giving up.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu kisah, sang pria selamat dengan melepaskan diri dan mengunci dirinya di rumah; Harionago meninggalkan banyak goresan dalam di pintu kayu sebelum menyerah.
claims.quote: In one story, the man was able to survive the encounter by breaking free and locking himself in his house. Harionago left many deep gashes in the wooden door before giving up.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia describes 針女 (harionago or harionna, also given as nureonago and waraionago) as a yōkai from the Uwajima area of southern Ehime that appears in a book by Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang menyebut 針女 (harionago atau harionna), juga disebut nureonago dan waraionago, sebagai yōkai dari wilayah Uwajima di Ehime selatan yang tercantum dalam buku Mizuki Shigeru.
claims.quote: 針女（はりおなご、はりおんな）または濡れ女子（ぬれおなご）、笑い女子（わらいおなご）は、水木しげるの著書にある、愛媛県南部の宇和島地方に伝わる妖怪。

claims.statement: She resembles a human woman, but the ends of her long, disheveled hair are fitted with fishhook-shaped hooks; she is said to have appeared often at Sakuraoka in Jōhen (now Ainan).
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya mirip perempuan manusia, tetapi ujung rambutnya yang panjang dan awut-awutan dilengkapi kait berbentuk kail; ia disebut sering muncul di Sakuraoka, Jōhen (kini Ainan).
claims.quote: 人間の女性の姿に似ているが、長いざんばら髪の先端に鈎針状の鉤が備わっている。 城辺町（現・愛南町）の桜岡にしきりと現れたといい、

claims.statement: She is said to have appeared often at Sakuraoka in Jōhen (now Ainan); on night roads she smiles at men, chases whoever smiles back while whipping her hair about, and catches him with the hooks of her hair.
claims.statement_id: Konon ia sering muncul di Sakuraoka, Jōhen (kini Ainan); di jalan malam ia tersenyum kepada pria, mengejar yang membalas senyumnya sambil mengibaskan rambut, dan menangkapnya dengan kait rambut.
claims.quote: 城辺町（現・愛南町）の桜岡にしきりと現れたといい、夜道で男に微笑みかけ、笑い返した者を髪を振り乱しながら追いかけ、髪の鉤で捕らえる。

claims.statement: Because 針女 shares many features with the Uwajima yōkai 濡女子 (nure-onago), the yōkai researcher Murakami Kenji conjectures that Mizuki named it 針女 after emphasizing the features of the nure-onago.
claims.statement_id: Karena ciri-ciri 針女 banyak kesamaannya dengan yōkai Uwajima 濡女子, peneliti yōkai Murakami Kenji menduga Mizuki memberi nama 針女 setelah menonjolkan ciri 濡女子.
claims.quote: 針女の特徴は、宇和島地方の妖怪「濡女子」と共通点が多いことから、妖怪研究家村上健司は、水木が濡女子の特徴を強調した上で「針女」と命名したものと推測している。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, in the dark they are indistinguishable from ordinary young women, unusual only for their loose, disheveled hair.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, dalam gelap mereka tak dapat dibedakan dari perempuan muda biasa, hanya rambutnya yang terurai awut-awutan yang tampak ganjil.
claims.quote: In the dark, they are indistinguishable from ordinary young women, unusual only for their loose, disheveled hair.

claims.statement: It is technically possible for a very fast runner to escape a hari onago, provided his home is close enough and has a sturdy door or gate.
claims.statement_id: Secara teknis seorang pelari yang sangat cepat dapat lolos dari hari onago, asalkan rumahnya cukup dekat dan berpintu atau bergerbang kokoh.
claims.quote: It is technically possible for a very fast runner to escape a hari onago, providing his home is close enough and has a sturdy door or gate.

claims.statement: If he gets safely indoors before her hooks catch him, he may survive until sunrise, when yōkai vanish.
claims.statement_id: Jika ia sempat masuk ke dalam rumah sebelum terkena kait, ia mungkin bertahan hingga matahari terbit, saat para yōkai lenyap.
claims.quote: If he can get himself safely indoors before her hooks catch him, he may be able to survive until sunrise—when yōkai vanish.

claims.statement: Yokai.com writes the name as 針女子 (はりおなご), translated "hook girl", with the alternate name hari onna ("hook woman").
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis nama ini 針女子 (はりおなご), berarti "gadis kait", dengan nama lain hari onna ("perempuan kait").
claims.quote: 針女子 はりおなご Translation: hook girl Alternate names: hari onna (“hook woman”)

claims.statement: If one flees into a house and shuts a sturdy door firmly, the 針女 vanishes by morning, but countless scars, apparently from the hooks of her hair, are said to remain outside the door.
claims.statement_id: Jika orang berlari masuk rumah dan menutup pintu yang kokoh rapat-rapat, 針女 menghilang pada pagi hari, tetapi konon tertinggal banyak bekas goresan di luar pintu yang diduga akibat kait rambutnya.
claims.quote: 家の中に逃げ込み、頑丈な扉をしっかりと閉めておけば、朝方には針女は消えてしまうが、扉の外には髪の鉤で付けられたであろう、無数の傷跡が残っているという。

claims.statement: Amenohoakari is a Japanese kami linked with the sun and farming.
claims.statement_id: Amenohoakari adalah kami Jepang yang dikaitkan dengan matahari dan pertanian.
claims.quote: Amenohoakari (天火明) is a kami of sun and agriculture in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: An old genealogy classifies his descendants among heavenly lineages.
claims.statement_id: Silsilah lama menggolongkan keturunannya sebagai garis keturunan surgawi.
claims.quote: The Shinsen Shōjiroku marks his descendants as descendants of kami (天孫族, tensonzoku).

claims.statement: Some sections of the Nihon Shoki name Ninigi as his father.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa bagian Nihon Shoki menyebut Ninigi sebagai ayahnya.
claims.quote: However, in volumes two, three, five, and seven of the Nihon Shoki, Ninigi-no-Mikoto is said to be his father.

claims.statement: The Kujiki identifies him with Nigihayahi.
claims.statement_id: Kujiki mengidentifikasikannya dengan Nigihayahi.
claims.quote: The Kujiki treats Amenohoakari as an alternate name for Nigihayahi, the ancestral kami of the Hozumi and Mononobe clans, though this interpretation raises many questions in terms of genealogy and domain.

claims.statement: Japanese Wikipedia: 天火明命 (Ame no Hoakari no Mikoto) is a deity in Japanese mythology who, in the classification of the 『新撰姓氏録』, is a 「天孫」 of the 「神別」 category.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Jepang: 天火明命 (Ame no Hoakari no Mikoto) adalah dewa dalam mitologi Jepang yang menurut klasifikasi 『新撰姓氏録』 termasuk 「天孫」 dari kategori 「神別」.
claims.quote: 天火明命（あめのほあかりのみこと）は、日本神話に登場する神。『新撰姓氏録』による分類では「神別」の「天孫」。

claims.statement: In the main text of the 『日本書紀』 he is a child of Ninigi and Konohanasakuya-hime, the third child after Hosusori (Umisachihiko) and Hikohohodemi (Yamasachihiko).
claims.statement_id: Dalam teks utama 『日本書紀』, ia adalah anak Ninigi dan Konohanasakuya-hime, anak ketiga setelah Hosusori (Umisachihiko) dan Hikohohodemi (Yamasachihiko).
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』の本文では、瓊瓊杵尊と木花開耶姫の子とし、第一子が火闌降命（ホスソリ＝海幸彦）、第二子が彦火火出見尊（ヒコホホデミ＝山幸彦）、第三子を火明命（ホアカリ）とする。

claims.statement: According to the 『古事記』 and the sixth and eighth variant versions of the 『日本書紀』, he was born to Ame no Oshihomimi and 万幡豊秋津師比売命, daughter of 高木神; he is the elder brother and Ninigi the younger.
claims.statement_id: Menurut 『古事記』 dan versi varian keenam serta kedelapan 『日本書紀』, ia lahir dari Ame no Oshihomimi dan putri 高木神, 万幡豊秋津師比売命; ia kakak dan Ninigi adik.
claims.quote: 『古事記』および『日本書紀』の第六・第八の一書によれば、天火明命は天忍穂耳命と高木神の娘の万幡豊秋津師比売命との間に生まれた子とし、天火明命が兄で、邇邇芸命は弟とされる。

claims.statement: Some argue the identification with Nigihayahi raises great doubts on grounds of generations and areas of activity; by contrast the 『播磨国風土記』 (Harima Fudoki) makes him a child of Ōnamuchi and 弩都比売.
claims.statement_id: Ada pendapat bahwa penyamaan dengan Nigihayahi menimbulkan banyak keraguan dari segi generasi dan wilayah kegiatan; sebaliknya 『播磨国風土記』 (Harima Fudoki) menyebutnya anak Ōnamuchi dan 弩都比売.
claims.quote: このことについて、世代関係や活動地域から疑問が大きいとする説もある。 一方、『播磨国風土記』では大汝命と弩都比売との子とする。

claims.statement: The 天孫 line moved from Takamagahara to Owari and Tanba provinces and he is regarded as ancestral deity of many clans such as the Owari, Tsumori, Amabe and Tanba; his name is also recorded as founder in the 『海部氏系図』.
claims.statement_id: Garis 天孫 berpindah dari Takamagahara ke Provinsi Owari dan Tanba, dan ia dipandang sebagai leluhur banyak klan seperti Owari, Tsumori, Amabe, dan Tanba; namanya juga tercatat sebagai pendiri dalam 『海部氏系図』.
claims.quote: 天孫系は高天原から尾張国や丹波国にも移り、尾張氏・津守氏・海部氏・丹波氏など多くの氏族の祖神とされ、『海部氏系図』（あまべしけいず）にも始祖としてその名が記されている。

claims.statement: As the names 「天照国照」 and 「火明」 show, he is a personification of sunlight and heat; the 『古事記伝』 reads 「ホアカリ」 as 「穂赤熟」 (ears of grain ripening red), so he is worshiped as a sun and agricultural god.
claims.statement_id: Seperti terlihat dari namanya, ia adalah personifikasi sinar dan panas matahari; 『古事記伝』 menafsirkan 「ホアカリ」 sebagai 「穂赤熟」 (bulir padi yang matang memerah), sehingga ia dipuja sebagai dewa matahari dan pertanian.
claims.quote: 名前の「天照国照」「火明」からわかるように太陽光や熱の神格化である。また、『古事記伝』では「ホアカリ」は「穂赤熟」で、稲穂が熟して赤らむ意味としており、天皇に繋る他の神と同様、稲に関係のある名前でもあり、太陽神・農業神として信仰されている。

claims.statement: Although his name contains 「天照」, he is a different deity from 「天照大神」 (Amaterasu); at Moto-Ise Kono Shrine the principal deity is 「天照国照彦火明命」 and 「天照大神」 is a co-enshrined deity, treated as separate.
claims.statement_id: Walau namanya memuat 「天照」, ia dewa yang berbeda dari Amaterasu; di Kuil Kono (Moto-Ise), dewa utamanya 「天照国照彦火明命」 sedangkan 「天照大神」 dipuja sebagai dewa pendamping, keduanya dibedakan.
claims.quote: 「天照」の名があるが「天照大神」とは別の神である。元伊勢の籠神社では、主祭神を「天照国照彦火明命」とし、相殿神に「天照大神」としてそれぞれ別の神としている。

claims.statement: Kono Shrine (Miyazu, Kyoto Prefecture) enshrines him as 「彦火明命」, and the Amabe clan, regarded as his descendants, has held the head priesthood hereditarily from antiquity to the present.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Kono (Miyazu, Prefektur Kyoto) memujanya sebagai 「彦火明命」, dan klan Amabe, yang dianggap keturunannya, mewarisi jabatan kepala pendeta dari zaman kuno hingga kini.
claims.quote: 籠神社（京都府宮津市） - 「彦火明命」として祀られる。その子孫とされる海部氏が、古代から現在まで宮司を世襲している。

claims.statement: His other names include 天照国照彦火明命 (『日本書紀』), 天火明命 (『古事記』), 彦火明命 and 火明命 (『日本書紀』).
claims.statement_id: Nama-nama lainnya antara lain 天照国照彦火明命 (『日本書紀』), 天火明命 (『古事記』), 彦火明命, dan 火明命 (『日本書紀』).
claims.quote: 天照国照彦火明命（あまてるくにてるひこほあかりのみこと、『日本書紀』、真清田神社由緒記） 天火明命（あめのほあかりのみこと、『古事記』、真清田神社由緒記） 彦火明命 火明命（ほあかりのみこと、『日本書紀』）

claims.statement: Nihongi (Aston's translation): when the flames first broke out a child named Ho-no-susori no Mikoto was born; when the flame reached its height a child named Ho-no-akari no Mikoto was born.
claims.statement_id: Nihongi (terjemahan Aston): ketika api mulai berkobar lahir seorang anak bernama Ho-no-susori; ketika nyala api mencapai puncak lahir anak bernama Ho-no-akari no Mikoto.
claims.quote: At this time, when the flames first broke out, a child was born who was named Ho-no-susori no Mikoto ; next when the flame reached its height, a child was born who was named Ho-no-akari no Mikoto.

claims.statement: Nihongi: the child of Ama-no-ho-no-akari no Mikoto was called Kaguyama no Mikoto, the ancestor of the Ohari no Muraji.
claims.statement_id: Nihongi: anak Ama-no-ho-no-akari no Mikoto bernama Kaguyama no Mikoto, yang menjadi leluhur Ohari no Muraji.
claims.quote: The child of Ama-no-ho-no-akari no Mikoto was called Kaguyama no Mikoto. He is the ancestor of the Ohari no Muraji.

claims.statement: Nihongi: in one version a child named Ama-teru-kuni-teru Hiko-ho no akari no Mikoto was born, the ancestor of the Ohari no Muraji.
claims.statement_id: Nihongi: dalam salah satu versi, seorang anak bernama Ama-teru-kuni-teru Hiko-ho no akari no Mikoto lahir dan menjadi leluhur Ohari no Muraji.
claims.quote: and by her as consort had a child named Ama-teru-kuni-teru Hiko-ho no akari no Mikoto. He is the ancestor of the Ohari no Muraji.

claims.statement: Aston's note in the Nihongi: Ho no akari means "fire-light".
claims.statement_id: Catatan Aston dalam Nihongi: Ho no akari berarti "cahaya api".
claims.quote: Ho no akari means fire- light.

claims.statement: Kodansha (Nihon Jinmei Daijiten): a deity appearing in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, a child of Ninigi, regarded as ancestor of the Owari clan, said to have been born when the flames grew bright; in another version a child of Ame no Oshihomimi.
claims.statement_id: Kodansha (Nihon Jinmei Daijiten): dewa yang tampak dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki, anak Ninigi, dianggap leluhur klan Owari, konon lahir ketika api menyala terang; menurut versi lain ia anak Ame no Oshihomimi.
claims.quote: 記・紀にみえる神。 瓊瓊杵尊(ににぎのみこと)の子。尾張氏の祖先とされる。炎があかるくなったときに生まれたという。別伝では天忍穂耳尊(あめのおしほみみのみこと)の子。

claims.statement: Daijisen: in Japanese mythology, a child of Ame no Oshihomimi and ancestral deity of the Owari no Muraji.
claims.statement_id: Daijisen: dalam mitologi Jepang, anak Ame no Oshihomimi dan leluhur Owari no Muraji.
claims.quote: 日本神話で、 天忍穂耳尊 あまのおしほみみのみこと の子。 尾張連 おわりのむらじ の祖神。

claims.statement: Kerakera-onna is a Japanese yōkai pictured by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Kerakera-onna adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambar Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: 倩兮女（けらけらおんな）、けらけら女は、鳥山石燕による江戸時代の妖怪画集『今昔百鬼拾遺』に描かれている日本の妖怪。

claims.statement: The picture appears in an Edo-period illustrated yōkai book.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya muncul dalam buku yōkai dari zaman Edo.
claims.quote: 倩兮女（けらけらおんな）、けらけら女は、鳥山石燕による江戸時代の妖怪画集『今昔百鬼拾遺』に描かれている日本の妖怪。

claims.statement: The image shows a giant woman in a kimono.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi itu menampilkan perempuan raksasa berkimono.
claims.quote: 着物姿の巨大な女性が、塀越しに口をひらいて笑う姿が描かれており、石燕による解説文は以下の通り添えられている。

claims.statement: She is drawn laughing over a wall.
claims.statement_id: Ia tampak tertawa dari balik dinding.
claims.quote: 着物姿の巨大な女性が、塀越しに口をひらいて笑う姿が描かれており、石燕による解説文は以下の通り添えられている。

claims.statement: Toriyama Sekien likened the figure peering over a wall to the beauty in an old tale, and suggested the "kerakera-onna" might be the spirit of a lewd woman who toyed with many people.
claims.statement_id: Toriyama Sekien membandingkan sosok yang mengintip dari balik pagar dengan perempuan cantik dalam sebuah kisah lama, dan menduga "kerakera-onna" adalah roh perempuan cabul yang mempermainkan banyak orang.
claims.quote: 塀（墻・牆）からのぞき込んでいる姿をその故事中の美女に比しており、石燕はこれをもって「倩兮女」を多くの人を弄んだ淫婦の霊ではなかろうかと述べている。

claims.statement: Before Sekien, Edo-period printed books such as kurohon and the ezōshi Heike Bakemono Taiji often featured the head of a woman laughing "kerakera".
claims.statement_id: Sebelum Sekien, buku cetak zaman Edo seperti kurohon dan ezōshi Heike Bakemono Taiji berulang kali memuat kepala perempuan yang tertawa kerakera.
claims.quote: 石燕の「倩兮女」以前にも、江戸時代の版本には黒本や絵草紙『平家化物たいぢ』などにはけらけらと笑う女の首がたびたび登場している。

claims.statement: The Konjaku Hyakki Shūi gives no detailed features, but yōkai literature from the Shōwa and Heisei eras explains that it frightens people on deserted roads with its laughter, which only that one person can hear, and the faint-hearted faint on hearing it.
claims.statement_id: Konkon Hyakki Shūi tidak memerinci ciri-cirinya, tetapi pustaka yōkai sejak era Shōwa dan Heisei menjelaskan bahwa ia menakuti orang yang berjalan di jalan sepi dengan tawa; tawa itu hanya terdengar oleh satu orang dan orang berhati lemah pingsan mendengarnya.
claims.quote: 『今昔百鬼拾遺』には詳細な特徴などは述べられていないが、昭和・平成以降の妖怪関連の文献では、人通りのない道を歩いている者に笑いかけて脅かす者で、笑い声によって人の不安をかきたてるもの、また笑い声はその1人だけにしか聞こえず、気が弱い人は笑い声を聞いただけで気を失ってしまうという解説がなされている。

claims.statement: The folklorist Fujisawa Morihiko, in Yōkai Gadan Zenshū Nihon-hen (1929), describes a big-faced ugly woman appearing taller than the fence and laughing; hence it is often explained as a giant female yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Folklorist Fujisawa Morihiko dalam Yōkai Gadan Zenshū Nihon-hen (1929) menjelaskannya sebagai perempuan buruk rupa bermuka besar yang tampak lebih tinggi dari pagar dan tertawa; karena itu ia sering dijelaskan sebagai yōkai perempuan raksasa.
claims.quote: 民俗学者・藤沢衛彦の著書『妖怪画談全集 日本篇』（1929年）では「見上ぐれば垣より高く大面相の醜女現はれてげらげらげらと笑ふ」と解説されており、しばしば巨大な女性の妖怪と解説されていることがある。

claims.statement: In Tosa Province (Kōchi Prefecture) a yōkai called "Warai-onna" ("laughing woman") is handed down, which shares the trait of being a woman yōkai that laughs.
claims.statement_id: Di Provinsi Tosa (Prefektur Kōchi) diwariskan yōkai "Warai-onna" (perempuan tertawa), yang sama-sama yōkai perempuan yang mengeluarkan tawa.
claims.quote: 土佐国（高知県）には「笑い女」という妖怪が伝承されており、これは笑い声をたてる女の妖怪であるという点で共通している。

claims.statement: The dictionary describes a yōkai in the form of a giant middle-aged woman who is said to laugh "kerakera" over a wall, recorded in works such as Edo-period painter Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Hyakki Shūi.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menggambarkannya sebagai yōkai berwujud perempuan paruh baya raksasa yang tertawa kerakera dari balik pagar, dengan catatan dalam kumpulan gambar Toriyama Sekien, Konjaku Hyakki Shūi, antara lain.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。巨大な中年女の姿で、塀越しにけらけらと笑うとされる。江戸時代の画家、鳥山石燕(せきえん)の画集「今昔百鬼拾遺」などに記述がある。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, when a man passes a lonely street or alley haunted by a kerakera onna, she unleashes a horrible shrill cackle that only he can hear.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ketika seorang lelaki melewati jalan atau lorong sepi yang dihantui kerakera onna, ia melepaskan tawa melengking mengerikan yang hanya terdengar olehnya.
claims.quote: When a man passes a lonely street or alley haunted by a kerakera onna, she unleashes a horrible, shrill cackle that can only be heard by him.

claims.statement: Yokai.com says their name comes from the cackling sound of their laughter.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut namanya berasal dari bunyi tawa terkekeh mereka.
claims.quote: Their name comes from the cackling sound of their laughter.

claims.statement: Konaki-jiji is a yōkai associated with the mountains of Tokushima.
claims.statement_id: Konaki-jiji adalah yōkai yang dikaitkan dengan pegunungan Tokushima.
claims.quote: Konaki-jiji (子泣き爺; also romanized konaki-jijii or konakijijii) is a yōkai — a supernatural creature from Japanese folklore — originating in the mountain regions of Tokushima Prefecture on the island of Shikoku.

claims.statement: Its name evokes an old man crying like a baby.
claims.statement_id: Namanya mengingatkan pada kakek yang menangis seperti bayi.
claims.quote: The name is typically translated as "old man crying like a baby" or "baby-crying old man," combining ko naki (子泣き, "child crying") with jijii (爺, "old man").

claims.statement: One story says it becomes extremely heavy after a traveler picks it up.
claims.statement_id: Menurut satu cerita, tubuhnya menjadi sangat berat setelah diangkat pejalan.
claims.quote: The konaki-jiji is notable for its deceptive method of attack: it lures compassionate travelers by mimicking the sound of an infant crying in the wilderness, then, once picked up, becomes supernaturally heavy, crushing its victim to death.

claims.statement: Accounts allow it to appear as either an old man or a baby.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah memberinya wujud kakek atau bayi.
claims.quote: The Konaki-jiji is said to be able to take the appearance of an old man or a baby.

claims.statement: Konaki-jiji is one of the yōkai described in the folklorist Yanagita Kunio's Yōkai Dangi; it is originally an old man said to cry like a newborn on night roads.
claims.statement_id: Konaki-jiji adalah salah satu yōkai yang dicatat dalam buku Yōkai Dangi karya folklorist Yanagita Kunio; pada dasarnya berwujud lelaki tua yang dikatakan menangis seperti bayi di jalan malam.
claims.quote: 民俗学者の柳田國男の著書『妖怪談義』に記述のある妖怪の一つで、本来は老人の姿だが、夜道で赤ん坊のような産声をあげるとされている。

claims.statement: Yanagita regarded these features as close to those of the obariyon and the ubume, and pointed to them as an invention.
claims.statement_id: Yanagita menilai ciri-ciri itu mirip obariyon dan ubume, dan menunjuknya sebagai rekaan.
claims.quote: しかし、柳田はこうした特徴について、おばりよんや産女に近いものとして、創作と指摘している。

claims.statement: According to the Anan local historian Takita Masahiro, it has been found that no Konaki-jiji legend actually exists in the Tokushima region said to be its home.
claims.statement_id: Menurut sejarawan lokal Anan, Takita Masahiro, legenda Konaki-jiji ternyata tidak benar-benar ada di wilayah Prefektur Tokushima yang disebut sebagai tempat asalnya.
claims.quote: 阿南市の郷土史家の多喜田昌裕によれば、伝承地とされる徳島県地方では、実際には子泣き爺の伝説は存在しないことが判明している。

claims.statement: In 2001 Takita and local volunteers certified Yamashiro-chō (now Miyoshi), Tokushima, as the legend's birthplace; a stone statue named "児啼爺" and a monument by Kyōgoku Natsuhiko were erected there.
claims.statement_id: Pada 2001, Takita dan sukarelawan setempat menetapkan Yamashiro-chō (kini Miyoshi), Tokushima, sebagai tempat asal legendanya; dibangun patung batu bernama "児啼爺" dan prasasti oleh Kyōgoku Natsuhiko.
claims.quote: 2001年には多喜田と地元の有志団により、徳島県三好郡山城町（現・三好市）が伝承の発祥地と認定され、現地には「児啼爺」の名の石像と、京極夏彦による「児啼爺の碑」が建てられ、同年に山城町にて除幕式が行われた。

claims.statement: Since Mizuki Shigeru's manga and anime GeGeGe no Kitarō portrayed it as a fine supporting character helping the hero Kitarō, it has become suddenly famous as a yōkai on the side of justice.
claims.statement_id: Sejak digambarkan dalam manga dan anime GeGeGe no Kitarō karya Mizuki Shigeru sebagai tokoh pendukung yang membantu Kitarō, ia mendadak terkenal sebagai yōkai yang berpihak pada kebenaran.
claims.quote: 特に水木しげるの漫画・アニメ『ゲゲゲの鬼太郎』で主人公の鬼太郎をサポートする名脇役として描かれて以降は、正義の妖怪として一躍有名な存在となっている。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, konaki jijii are mountain-dwelling spirits that look like old men, carrying walking sticks and wearing straw raincoats over oversized baby clothes.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, konaki jijii adalah roh penghuni gunung yang tampak seperti lelaki tua, membawa tongkat jalan dan memakai jas hujan jerami di atas pakaian bayi berukuran kebesaran.
claims.quote: Konaki jijii are mountain-dwelling spirits who look like old human men. They carry walking sticks and wear straw raincoats on top of over-sized baby clothes.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, when someone hugs the crying spirit it rapidly grows heavier and clings to the victim, who cannot pull free.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, bila orang memeluk roh yang menangis itu, ia dengan cepat menjadi makin berat dan menempel pada korban yang tidak bisa melepaskan diri.
claims.quote: When they hug the crying spirit, it rapidly becomes heavier and heavier. The konaki jijii clings to its victim, who is unable to pull themself free.

claims.statement: Yokai.com says it is thought to be a yōkai invented by combining two different folktales.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut ia diduga yōkai yang tercipta dari penggabungan dua cerita rakyat yang berbeda.
claims.quote: It is thought to be a yōkai that was invented by combining two different folktales into a new form.

claims.statement: Yokai.com says the pattern of tricking passersby into helping a crying baby and then crushing them is shared by several other yōkai across Japan, such as obariyon, ubume and nure onna.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut pola menipu orang agar menolong bayi yang menangis lalu menindihnya serupa dengan beberapa yōkai lain di Jepang, seperti obariyon, ubume, dan nure onna.
claims.quote: This pattern of behavior—tricking passersby into helping a crying baby and then crushing them like a stone—is shared by several yōkai across Japan, such as obariyon, ubume, and nure onna.

claims.statement: In Shikoku a yōkai called "gogyanaki" is handed down which, like Konaki-jiji, is said to cry like a newborn baby.
claims.statement_id: Di Shikoku diwariskan yōkai "gogyanaki" yang, seperti Konaki-jiji, dikatakan menangis seperti bayi baru lahir.
claims.quote: 子泣き爺と同様、赤ん坊のような産声をあげるという「ごぎゃ泣き（ごぎゃなき）」という妖怪が四国に伝わっている。

claims.statement: Kudan is a Japanese prophetic yōkai with human and bovine features.
claims.statement_id: Kudan adalah yōkai peramal Jepang dengan ciri manusia dan sapi.
claims.quote: The kudan (件; literally "matter"; or "human-faced bovine"). is a yōkai of a "prophecy beast" type, whose news or urban legend has been disseminated in Japan since the Edo Period.

claims.statement: An 1836 illustrated handbill reported an alleged appearance in Tango Province.
claims.statement_id: Selebaran bergambar tahun 1836 melaporkan kemunculannya di Provinsi Tango.
claims.quote: The human-faced, bovine-bodied kudan that allegedly appeared in "Mount Kurahashi", Tango Province (in today's Kyoto Prefecture) in the year Tenpō 7 (1836) was reported in a contemporary kawaraban.

claims.statement: That story predicts a good harvest and recommends displaying its image.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu meramalkan panen baik dan menyarankan orang memasang gambarnya.
claims.quote: It predicted bountiful harvest in the ensuing years, and instructed people to paste up the picture image of itself for the home to ward off evil and prosper.

claims.statement: Its written name combines characters for person and cow.
claims.statement_id: Namanya ditulis dengan gabungan aksara untuk manusia dan sapi.
claims.quote: The kanji for kudan consists of two characters, the ninben/hito (亻/人; 'person' radical), and ushi (牛; 'cow' or 'bull'), aptly representing its human-bovine composite nature (i.e., human-headed and bovine-bodied).

claims.statement: The kudan is generally depicted with a human head and a bovine body.
claims.statement_id: Kudan umumnya digambarkan berkepala manusia dan bertubuh sapi.
claims.quote: The kudan is generally depicted as having the head of a human and the body of a bovine.

claims.statement: An early attestation of the kudan is in the diary Mikkyoku nichijō dated Bunsei 2 (1819), about a human-headed, human-speaking calf that declared it should be named "kudan".
claims.statement_id: Catatan awal tentang kudan terdapat dalam diary Mikkyoku nichijō bertanggal Bunsei 2 (1819), tentang anak sapi berkepala manusia yang berbicara dan menyatakan namanya harus "kudan".
claims.quote: An early attestation of kudan occurs in the aforementioned Mikkyoku nichijō (『密局日乗』) dated to Bunsei 2 (1819), where a human language-speaking and human-headed calf declared it should be given the name "kudan".

claims.statement: The kudan is typical of the so-called prophecy beasts (yogenjū) of Japanese folklore, which not only portend plague or bounty but prescribe how to avoid being stricken.
claims.statement_id: Kudan tergolong "binatang peramal" (yogenjū) dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, yang tidak hanya meramalkan wabah atau panen melimpah tetapi juga memberi cara menghindari bencana.
claims.quote: The kudan is typical of the so-called prophesy beasts (予言獣, yongenjū) of Japanese folklore, which not only portend plague or bounty, but prescribe the method on how to avoid being stricken.

claims.statement: The kudan may derive from the Chinese luck beast Bai Ze (Hakutaku in Japanese), as formally theorized by the sociologist Kenji Sato.
claims.statement_id: Kudan mungkin berasal dari makhluk pembawa untung Tiongkok Bai Ze (Hakutaku dalam bahasa Jepang), seperti yang diteorikan secara formal oleh sosiolog Kenji Sato.
claims.quote: The kudan may derive from the Chinese luck beast Bai Ze (pronounced "Hakutaku" in Japanese), as has been formally theorized by sociologist Kenji Sato

claims.statement: Wikipedia says the idiom "kudan no gotoshi" is much older (Heian period) than the monster (late Edo period), so a relationship between phrase and monster has been refuted as an anachronism.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia menyebut ungkapan "kudan no gotoshi" jauh lebih tua (zaman Heian) daripada makhluknya (akhir zaman Edo), sehingga kaitan antara frasa dan makhluk itu dibantah sebagai anakronisme.
claims.quote: However while the kudan monster dates to the late Edo Period, the idiom is much older, dating to the Heian period, so the relationship between the phrase and the monster has been refuted as an anachronism.

claims.statement: After the shogunate ended and the Meiji era began, the kudan was still mentioned in writings, and Lafcadio Hearn heard of travelling showmen displaying an alleged stuffed kudan.
claims.statement_id: Setelah zaman keshogunan berakhir dan era Meiji dimulai, kudan masih disebut dalam tulisan, dan Lafcadio Hearn mendengar tentang pemain keliling yang memamerkan spesimen kudan yang diawetkan.
claims.quote: After the shogunate ended and the Meiji era began, the kudan was still mentioned in writings and Lafcadio Hearn heard about travelling showmen displaying an alleged stuffed specimen of a kudan.

claims.statement: The kutabe or kudabe is considered an equivalent (subclass) of the kudan, though its legend is set specifically at Tateyama in Etchū Province (now Toyama Prefecture).
claims.statement_id: Kutabe atau kudabe dianggap setara (subkelas) kudan, tetapi legendanya berlatar khusus di Tateyama, Provinsi Etchū (kini Prefektur Toyama).
claims.quote: The kutabe or kudabe is considered an equivalent (subclass) of the kudan, though kutabe's legend is set specifically in Tateyama in Etchū Province (Mount Tate, in today's Toyama Prefecture).

claims.statement: The kudan news in the kawaraban dated Tenpō 7 (1836) is the earliest extant written folkloric material on the kudan proper.
claims.statement_id: Berita tentang kudan dalam kawaraban bertanggal Tenpō 7 (1836) adalah bahan tertulis folkloris tertua yang masih ada tentang kudan.
claims.quote: dated Tenpō 7 (1836) is the earliest extant written folkloric material on the "kudan" proper.

claims.statement: A writer argues that the kudan and the ushi-onna ought to be distinguished: the kudan is a calf born from cattle, whereas the ushi-onna is a daughter of human parents.
claims.statement_id: Seorang penulis berpendapat kudan dan ushi-onna perlu dibedakan: kudan adalah anak sapi yang lahir dari sapi, sedangkan ushi-onna adalah putri orang tua manusia.
claims.quote: argues that the kudan and the ushi-onna ought to be distinguished, due to a number of differences: the kudan is a calf born from cattle, the ushi-onna is a daughter of human parents

claims.statement: In the Taishō era the novelist Hyakken Uchida published a short novel entitled Kudan (1921).
claims.statement_id: Pada era Taishō, novelis Hyakken Uchida menerbitkan novel pendek berjudul Kudan (1921).
claims.quote: In the Taisho era, novelist Hyakken Uchida published a short novel entitled Kudan (1921)

claims.statement: The dictionary describes the kudan as a half-human, half-bovine yōkai that in the first few days after birth prophesies disasters and epidemics and is said to die once it has spoken.
claims.statement_id: Kamus menggambarkan kudan sebagai yōkai berwujud setengah manusia setengah sapi yang, dalam beberapa hari setelah lahir, meramalkan bencana dan wabah lalu dikatakan mati setelah selesai berbicara.
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。半人半牛の姿で、生まれて数日の間に災害や疫病の予言をし、言い終えると死んでしまうとされる。

claims.statement: Another dictionary entry defines the kudan as a yōkai with a human head and a bovine body, said to prophesy epidemics and disasters.
claims.statement_id: Kamus lain memberi definisi kudan sebagai yōkai berkepala manusia dan bertubuh sapi yang dikatakan meramalkan wabah dan bencana.
claims.quote: 頭が人、体が牛の形をした妖怪。疫病の流行や災害などについて予言するといわれる。

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, kudan can speak human languages from the day they are born and give one or more prophecies immediately after birth.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, kudan dapat berbicara bahasa manusia sejak lahir dan segera memberikan satu atau lebih ramalan.
claims.quote: Kudan are able to speak human languages from the day they are born. Immediately upon being born, a kudan gives one or more prophecies.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, because of its reputation for honesty, images of kudan were used as talismans for good luck, prosperity, and protection from sickness and disaster.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, karena reputasinya yang jujur, gambar kudan dipakai sebagai jimat keberuntungan, kemakmuran, dan perlindungan dari penyakit dan bencana.
claims.quote: Because of its reputation for honesty, images of kudan were used as talismans for good luck, prosperity, and protection from sickness and disaster.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, in the Edo period newspapers added the words "kudan no gotoshi" ("as if a kudan had said it") to lend a story credibility.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, pada zaman Edo surat kabar menambahkan kata "kudan no gotoshi" ("seolah kudan yang mengatakannya") agar cerita lebih dipercaya.
claims.quote: During the Edo period, newspapers looking to add credibility to a story would include the words “kudan no gotoshi,” or, “as if a kudan had said it” to their articles.

claims.statement: Sakyo Komatsu also wrote a piece of fiction entitled Kudan no haha ("kudan's mother") (1968).
claims.statement_id: Sakyo Komatsu juga menulis cerita fiksi berjudul Kudan no haha ("ibu kudan") (1968).
claims.quote: Sakyo Komatsu also wrote a piece of fiction entitled Kudan no haha (「くだんのはは」 ; lit. "kudan's mother") (1968)

claims.statement: Okuri-inu is a doglike yōkai in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Okuri-inu adalah yōkai mirip anjing dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: The Okuri-inu (送り犬) (literally, 'escorting dog') is a kind of yōkai.

claims.statement: Its regional forms include both dogs and wolves.
claims.statement_id: Bentuk daerahnya mencakup anjing maupun serigala.
claims.quote: There are stories of the okuri-inu from the Tōhoku region to Kyushu, but depending on the area it can be a wolf not a dog, and there are numerous differences in its behaviour.

claims.statement: It follows people walking mountain paths at night.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengikuti pejalan di jalan pegunungan pada malam hari.
claims.quote: The okuri-inu closely follows people who are walking along mountain paths at nighttime.

claims.statement: One story says it attacks if the traveler falls.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menyebut ia menyerang ketika pejalan terjatuh.
claims.quote: If by chance the person falls over they will be immediately eaten up, but if they pretend to be having a short rest they will not be attacked.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the okuri inu follows lone travelers late at night, stalking them at a safe distance and following footstep for footstep as long as they keep walking; if the traveler trips or stumbles it pounces and rips them to shreds.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, okuri inu mengikuti pelancong yang sendirian larut malam di jalan, menjaga jarak aman, mengikuti langkah demi langkah selama mereka terus berjalan; bila pelancong tersandung, ia menerkam dan mencabik-cabiknya.
claims.quote: The okuri inu follows lone travelers late on the road at night. It stalks them, keeping a safe distance, but following footstep for footstep, as long as they keep walking. If the traveler should trip or stumble, the okuri inu will pounce on them and rip them to shreds.

claims.statement: Yokai.com calls the okuri inu somewhat of a blessing and a curse: it pounces with supernatural speed if one falls, but so ferocious that while it follows someone no other dangerous yokai or wild animals come close.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menyebut okuri inu sebagai berkah sekaligus kutukan: ia menerkam dengan kecepatan supernatural bila orang jatuh, tetapi karena sangat garang, selama ia mengikuti seseorang tidak ada yōkai atau binatang buas berbahaya lain yang mendekat.
claims.quote: The okuri inu is somewhat of a blessing and a curse. On the one hand, if one should trip and fall, it will pounce with supernatural speed and gobble him or her up. On the other hand, they are so ferocious that while they are following someone, no other dangerous yokai or wild animals will come close.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the okuri inu has a special relationship with another yokai, the yosuzume, whose nocturnal song is often a warning that an okuri inu is following you.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, okuri inu punya hubungan khusus dengan yōkai lain, yosuzume; nyanyian malam burung ini sering menjadi peringatan bahwa okuri inu sedang mengikuti.
claims.quote: The okuri inu has a special relationship with another yokai, the yosuzume. This eerie bird's nocturnal song is often a warning that an okuri inu is following you.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, a person who stumbles can survive by faking it as deliberate, so that the okuri inu is tricked into thinking they were just taking a short rest and does not pursue.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, bila seseorang tersandung, ia bisa selamat dengan berpura-pura itu disengaja sehingga okuri inu mengira ia hanya beristirahat sebentar dan tidak mengejar.
claims.quote: if you fake it so it looks like you did it on purpose, the okuri inu will be tricked into thinking you were just taking a short rest, and it won't pursue.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, after making it out of the mountains safely one should turn around and call out "Thanks for seeing me off!", after which that okuri inu will never follow again.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, setelah keluar dari pegunungan dengan selamat, orang sebaiknya berbalik dan berseru "Terima kasih sudah mengantar!", dan okuri inu itu tidak akan mengikutinya lagi.
claims.quote: If you should make it out of the mountains safely, you should turn around and call out, "Thanks for seeing me off!" Afterwards, that okuri inu will never follow you again.

claims.statement: Yokai.com gives 送り犬 (おくりいぬ) with the translation "sending-off dog", the alternate name okuri ōkami ("sending-off wolf"), and dark mountain passes and forested roads as habitat.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis 送り犬 (おくりいぬ) dengan terjemahan "anjing pengantar", nama lain okuri ōkami ("serigala pengantar"), dan habitat jalur gunung gelap serta jalan berhutan.
claims.quote: Okuri inu 送り犬 おくりいぬ Translation: sending-off dog Alternate names: okuri ōkami (sending-off wolf) Habitat: dark mountain passes, forested roads

claims.statement: In an account recorded by Wikipedia, a woman who gave birth on a mountain path was surrounded by many okuri-inu, which instead of attacking protected the mother and child from the wolves lurking in the mountain.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebuah catatan yang dimuat Wikipedia, seorang perempuan yang melahirkan di jalan gunung dikelilingi banyak okuri-inu; alih-alih menyerang, mereka melindungi ibu dan anak itu dari serigala yang berkeliaran di gunung.
claims.quote: Night fell, and many okuri-inu gathered around. Terrified, the woman said "If you're going to eat us then eat us!", but rather than attacking, they actually protected the mother and child from the wolves that lurked in the mountain.

claims.statement: Wikipedia records the yōkai investigator Kenji Murakami's hypothesis that the okuri-ōkami is actually the Japanese wolf and that tales of strange goings on or protection are merely convenient interpretations of the wolf's nature and traits.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat hipotesis peneliti yōkai Kenji Murakami bahwa okuri-ōkami sebenarnya adalah serigala Jepang, dan kisah keganjilan atau perlindungan hanyalah tafsir yang memudahkan atas sifat serigala itu.
claims.quote: Yōkai investigator Kenji Murakami, too, has hypothesised that the okuri-ōkami is actually the Japanese wolf, and that tales of strange goings on or protecting people are merely convenient interpretations of the Japanese wolf's nature and traits.

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that from the Kantō region to the Kinki region, and in Kōchi, there are legends of okuri-ōkami ("sending-off wolf").
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa dari wilayah Kantō hingga Kinki, juga di Kōchi, ada legenda okuri-ōkami ("serigala pengantar").
claims.quote: From the Kantō region to the Kinki region, along with Kōchi Prefecture, there are legends of okuri-ōkami (送り狼 ; literally, 'sending-off wolf').

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that in Koumi, yama-inu are classified as either okuri-inu or mukae-inu ("welcoming dog"), with okuri-inu said to protect people and mukae-inu attacking them.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa di Koumi, yama-inu digolongkan sebagai okuri-inu atau mukae-inu ("anjing penyambut"); okuri-inu disebut melindungi orang, sedangkan mukae-inu menyerang.
claims.quote: in Koumi, yama-inu (see above) are classified either as okuri-inu or mukae-inu (迎え犬 ; literally, 'welcoming dog'), with okuri-inu being said to protect people like the case from Shioda, and mukae-inu attacking people.

claims.statement: Ōmononushi is a kami associated with Mount Miwa in Japan.
claims.statement_id: Ōmononushi adalah kami yang dikaitkan dengan Gunung Miwa di Jepang.
claims.quote: Ōmononushi (Japanese: 大物主神, romanized: Ōmononushi-no-Kami; historical orthography: Ohomononushi) is a kami in Japanese mythology associated with Mount Miwa (also known as Mount Mimoro) in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture.

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki link him closely to Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki menghubungkannya erat dengan Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: He is closely linked in the imperial myth cycle recorded in the Kojiki (c. 712 CE) and the Nihon Shoki (720 CE) with the earthly kami Ōkuninushi (Ōnamuchi); indeed, the latter text treats 'Ōmononushi' as another name for or an aspect—more precisely, the spirit or mitama—of Ōnamuchi. Ōmononushi's chief place of worship is Ōmiwa Shrine located at the foot of Mount Miwa, which serves as the

claims.statement: He is also worshiped at other shrines.
claims.statement_id: Ia juga dipuja di kuil-kuil lain.
claims.quote: In addition, he is also enshrined in some other shrines such as Ōsugi Shrine in Ibaraki Prefecture.

claims.statement: One tradition identifies the deity of Kotohira Shrine with him.
claims.statement_id: Satu tradisi menyamakan dewa Kuil Kotohira dengannya.
claims.quote: The deity of Kotohira Shrine (Kotohira-gū) in Kotohira, Kagawa Prefecture, popularly known as Konpira Daigongen (金毘羅大権現), is also currently identified with Ōmononushi.

claims.statement: According to Heibonsha, "mono" means a spirit or demonic thing and "nushi" means chief; per the Mount Miwa legend in the Kiki chronicles this deity had a snake body and lived in a rock cave; under Emperor Sujin his curse caused a plague, and when his descendant Ōtataneko was made to worship him, the realm became stable.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Heibonsha, "mono" berarti makhluk gaib dan "nushi" berarti pemimpin; menurut legenda Gunung Miwa dalam Kiki, dewa ini berwujud ular dan tinggal di gua batu; pada masa Kaisar Sujin kutukannya menimbulkan wabah, dan ketika keturunannya Ōtataneko memujanya, negeri menjadi tenteram.
claims.quote: モノは魔物をいい,ヌシは頭領の意。記紀の伝える三輪山伝説によると,この神は蛇体であり岩窟に住んでいた。また崇神天皇の代にこの神のたたりで疫病がはやり人民が飢え苦しんだので,その子孫の大田田根子に祭らせたところ,天下は安定したともいう。

claims.statement: Heibonsha calls Ōmononushi one of the most strongly indigenous earthly deities (kunitsukami) of the Yamato region; he stands out as an emanation of Ōkuninushi who helped build the land and, after the transfer of the land, led the earthly deities to guard the court.
claims.statement_id: Heibonsha menyebut Ōmononushi sebagai salah satu kunitsukami paling berakar di wilayah Yamato; ia menonjol sebagai penjelmaan Ōkuninushi yang membantu pembangunan negeri dan, setelah penyerahan negeri, memimpin para kunitsukami melindungi istana.
claims.quote: 魔物の頭目として大和地方でもっとも土着性の強い国津神(くにつかみ)の一つだが,このオオモノヌシが記紀神話の伝承の中でとくに目だつのは,大国主神(おおくにぬしのかみ)の分身として国作りに協力し,国譲りの後はもろもろの国津神を率いて宮廷を守護したとされている点である。

claims.statement: Nipponica calls him the ancestral deity of the Miwa clan, with rich myths of sacred marriage with Seyadatarahime and Yamato-Totohimomosohime; he is also a snake god, a thunder god and a god of farming.
claims.statement_id: Nipponica menyebutnya dewa leluhur klan Miwa, dengan banyak mitos pernikahan sakral dengan Seyadatara-hime dan Yamatototohimomoso-hime; ia juga dewa ular, dewa petir, dan dewa pertanian.
claims.quote: しかし、実際は三輪(みわ)氏の祖神である。この神には勢夜陀多良比売(せやだたらひめ)や倭迹迹日百襲姫命(やまとととひももそひめのみこと)との聖婚を語る神話が豊かに伝承されている(古事記、日本書紀)。蛇神、雷神でもあり、農耕神でもある。

claims.statement: According to the Yamakawa Nihonshi Shōjiten, he appeared as a curse-bringing deity in the time of Emperor Sujin and also manifests as a red-painted arrow, a snake and thunder.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yamakawa Nihonshi Shōjiten, ia muncul sebagai dewa pengutuk pada masa Kaisar Sujin dan juga menampakkan diri sebagai panah bercat merah, ular, dan petir.
claims.quote: 崇神(すじん)天皇のとき祟り神として現れ,また丹塗矢・蛇・雷などとして顕現してもいる。

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that the name Ōmononushi is translated either as "Great Thing Master" (literal rendering of the characters) or "Great Spirit Master" (mono taken as spirit or supernatural entity).
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa nama Ōmononushi diterjemahkan sebagai "Penguasa Benda Agung" (terjemahan harfiah aksara) atau "Penguasa Roh Agung" (mono dimaknai roh atau makhluk gaib).
claims.quote: The name 'Ōmononushi' ... is translated either as 'Great Thing Master' (after a literal translation of the characters used in his name) or 'Great Spirit Master' (with mono being taken as meaning 'spirit' or 'supernatural entity').

claims.statement: Wikipedia lists Ōmononushi as a god of nation-building, agriculture, business, medicine, brewing and seafaring.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia memerinci Ōmononushi sebagai dewa pembangunan negara, pertanian, bisnis, pengobatan, pembuatan minuman keras, dan pelayaran.
claims.quote: Ōmononushi-no-Kami Mitama of Ōkuninushi; god of nation-building, agriculture, business, medicine, brewing, and seafaring

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, another god "illuminating the sea" appeared before Ōkuninushi and promised to help if worshipped; Ōkuninushi enshrined him on Mount Mimoro (Mount Miwa) in Yamato.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, dewa lain yang "menerangi laut" muncul di hadapan Ōkuninushi dan berjanji membantu bila dipuja; Ōkuninushi memuliakannya di Gunung Mimoro (Gunung Miwa) di Yamato.
claims.quote: another god "illuminating the sea" appears before Ōkuninushi, promising to aid him in his task if he (Ōkuninushi) will worship him. Ōkuninushi, in accordance with the god's wish, then enshrined him in Mount Mimoro (Mount Miwa) in the land of Yamato.

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, in a revelation Ōmononushi claimed responsibility for the pestilence and announced it would not stop until he was offered due worship by a man named Ōtataneko.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, melalui wahyu Ōmononushi mengaku bertanggung jawab atas wabah dan menyatakan wabah takkan berhenti sebelum ia dipuja sebagaimana mestinya oleh seorang bernama Ōtataneko.
claims.quote: In it, Ōmononushi claimed responsibility for the pestilence and announced that it would not stop until he was offered due worship by a man named Ōtataneko

claims.statement: According to Wikipedia, Seyadatarahime bore a daughter after being impregnated by Ōmononushi, who took the form of a red arrow.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia, Seyadatarahime melahirkan seorang putri setelah dihamili Ōmononushi, yang mengambil wujud panah merah.
claims.quote: Seyadatarahime (勢夜陀多良比売) who bore a daughter after she was impregnated by Ōmononushi, who took the form of a red arrow

claims.statement: Ouni is a yōkai pictured by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Ouni adalah yōkai yang digambar Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: The ouni (苧うに) is a yōkai depicted in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien.

claims.statement: The illustration gives it long hair and a face resembling a demon woman.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasinya memberi sosok itu rambut panjang dan wajah mirip perempuan iblis.
claims.quote: It is a yōkai with a face like that of a demon woman (kijo) torn from mouth to ear, and its entire body is covered in hair.

claims.statement: Sekien left no explanation of its nature.
claims.statement_id: Sekien tidak menjelaskan sifat makhluk itu.
claims.quote: There is no explanatory text from Sekien, so it is unclear what kind of yōkai this is.

claims.statement: Researchers have not found a clear older folk legend about this figure.
claims.statement_id: Para peneliti belum menemukan legenda rakyat lama yang jelas tentang sosok ini.
claims.quote: There are no folk legends or records that are clearly about the ouni (or the "wauwau" based on Sekien's), so it is presently not clear what kind of yōkai they were intending to depict, but starting in the Heisei period, inferring from how there are many tales that seem highly related to the previous "o" and the yamauba, there have started to be many illustrated references, books, and oth

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, ouni looks like an ugly old woman with an angry face and a body covered in long black hair; she is a kind of yamauba, or mountain hag, who lives deep in the mountains and only occasionally appears before humans.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ouni tampak seperti perempuan tua buruk rupa berwajah marah dengan tubuh tertutup rambut hitam panjang; ia sejenis yamauba (nenek gunung) yang tinggal jauh di pegunungan dan hanya sesekali menampakkan diri kepada manusia.
claims.quote: Ouni looks like an ugly old woman with an angry face and a body covered in long, black hair. She is a kind of yamauba, or mountain hag. She lives deep in the mountains, away from civilization, and only occasionally appears before humans.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, unlike most yamauba, ouni are friendly toward humans who treat them kindly, and occasionally visit rural houses or mountain huts late at night.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, tidak seperti kebanyakan yamauba, ouni bersahabat dengan manusia yang memperlakukannya dengan baik, dan sesekali mengunjungi rumah desa atau pondok gunung larut malam.
claims.quote: Unlike most yamauba, ouni are friendly towards humans who treat them kindly. They occasionally visit rural houses or mountain huts late at night.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, if the household is kind and invites her in, during the night she spins an enormous amount of thread for the family and then vanishes without a trace.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, bila penghuni rumah ramah dan mengundangnya masuk, pada malam hari ia memintal benang dalam jumlah sangat banyak bagi keluarga itu lalu lenyap tanpa jejak.
claims.quote: If they are kind and invite her in, during the night she spins an enormous amount of thread for the family and then vanishes without a trace.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, ouni's name comes from the Japanese word for ramie, a fibrous plant used to make thread, and peat, the rotten muck of swamps from rotting plant matter.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, nama ouni berasal dari kata Jepang untuk rami (ramie), tanaman berserat untuk benang, dan gambut, lumpur busuk rawa dari bahan tanaman yang membusuk.
claims.quote: Ouni's name comes from the Japanese word for ramie, a fibrous plant that is used to make thread, and peat, the rotten muck found in swamps that comes from rotting plant matter.

claims.statement: Yokai.com gives 苧うに (おうに) with the translation "ramie peat", the alternative name wauwau, and deep in the mountains as habitat.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis 苧うに (おうに) dengan terjemahan "gambut rami", nama lain wauwau, dan habitat jauh di pegunungan.
claims.quote: Ouni 苧うに おうに Translation: ramie peat (named for her resemblance to these plants) ALTERNATIVE NAMES: wauwau Habitat: deep in the mountains

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that the "o" (苧) in "ouni" refers to the ramie plant or to bundles of string made from ramie, hemp and the like, so it is said Sekien named it "ouni" because it evokes a yōkai with head and body hair made of layers of this "o".
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa "o" (苧) dalam "ouni" menunjuk rami atau gulungan benang dari rami dan semacamnya, sehingga dikatakan Sekien menamainya "ouni" karena membayangkan yōkai berambut kepala dan tubuh dari lapisan "o".
claims.quote: The "o" (苧) in "ouni" refers to the ramie plant or to bundles of string made from ramie, hemp, among others, so it is said that Sekien gave it the name "ouni" because it conjures up the image of a yōkai with head and body hair made of layers of this "o".

claims.statement: Wikipedia notes that in the Hyakkai Zukan (1737, Sawaki Suushi), an Edo-period yōkai emaki, it is called "wauwau", and Edo-period yōkai emaki usually present it under that name.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat bahwa dalam Hyakkai Zukan (1737, Sawaki Suushi), gulungan yōkai zaman Edo, ia bernama "wauwau", dan gulungan yōkai zaman Edo biasanya menampilkannya dengan nama itu.
claims.quote: In the Hyakkai Zukan (1737, Sawaki Suushi), a yōkai emaki from the Edo period, it is given by the name "wauwau", and Edo period yōkai emaki would usually present it under that name.

claims.statement: Wikipedia records a tale from Kotaki, Echigo Province, in which a yamauba appeared and helped spin, biting the hemp to draw out strings and spinning bundles of string at a speed unbelievable for humans.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia mencatat tuturan dari Kotaki, Provinsi Echigo, tempat seorang yamauba muncul, ikut membantu memintal, menggigit rami dan menarik benang, lalu memintal gulungan benang dengan kecepatan tak masuk akal bagi manusia.
claims.quote: the following example is from Kotaki, Nishikubiki, Echigo Province (now Itoigawa, Niigata Prefecture). ... a yamauba appeared and said "I'll also spin some" and started to help along. The yamauba bit the hemp and drew out strings and then spun bundles of string at a speed unbelievable for humans.

claims.statement: Sazae-oni is a shellfish-like creature in Japanese myth.
claims.statement_id: Sazae-oni adalah makhluk menyerupai kerang dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Sazae-oni (栄螺鬼, lit. shellfish ogre) are creatures from Japanese mythology, resembling large mollusks.

claims.statement: One account says an old sea snail becomes such an obake.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu kisah menyebut siput laut tua berubah menjadi obake ini.
claims.quote: They are a type of obake that forms when turban snails, especially Turbo sazae, reach 30 years of age.

claims.statement: A well-known tale involves pirates who rescue a woman from the sea.
claims.statement_id: Cerita terkenal melibatkan perompak yang menyelamatkan perempuan dari laut.
claims.quote: The most popular legend of the Sazae-oni is that of a group of pirates who rescued a drowning woman from the sea and took her back to the ship.

claims.statement: Another story places it at a coastal inn in human form.
claims.statement_id: Kisah lain menempatkannya di penginapan pesisir dalam wujud manusia.
claims.quote: Other legends of these creatures depict them wandering into coastal or seaside inns whilst in human guise, whereupon they devour the innkeeper in the night and then escape before morning.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, sazae oni are monstrous turban snails that haunt the seas and appear on moonlit nights, dancing on the water's surface like exotic dancers or dragons.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, sazae oni adalah siput turbo monster yang menghantui laut dan muncul pada malam berbulan, menari di permukaan air seperti penari eksotis atau naga.
claims.quote: Sazae oni are monstrous turban snails which haunt the seas. They appear on moonlit nights, dancing on the water's surface like exotic dancers or dragons.
